An open-source way to connect your AI to your files, tools, and apps.

Today we're sharing **Ganju** — an open-source platform that connects AI
assistants to the things you actually work with: your documents, your tools, and
your apps.

## Why we built it

AI assistants are great at reasoning but blind to your context. Wiring them up to
your data usually means running servers, writing glue code, and worrying about
security. Ganju removes all of that: create a connection, add your content and
tools, and your AI is ready — in minutes, no code required.

## What you can do

- Search and answer from your own files.
- Let your AI use real tools: email, calendar, web search, Slack, and more.
- Turn the same setup into a bot on Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, or Discord.

It's open source under Apache-2.0 — run it yourself, or let us host it for you.

Every project's Home dashboard shows what your assistant is doing: activity across channels and MCP clients, tool health with the calls behind each number, unused tools, data triggers, and a recent-activity feed.

Every project opens on its **Home** dashboard (select **Home** at the top of
the rail). It's where you see how your assistant is actually being used: activity
over time, how each tool is doing, what's going unused, and who did what.

## Why it matters

- **See real usage, not guesses.** Watch conversations per day and spot when
  your assistant is busy, or quiet.
- **Know which channels and clients matter.** Each [channel](/docs/channels/)
  and [MCP client](/docs/mcp/) is its own line, so you can tell where your
  traffic comes from.
- **Catch broken tools early.** Tool health shows errors, slow calls, and the
  model fumbling a tool's inputs, with every call one click away.
- **Keep the tool list lean.** Tools nobody used in 30 days are listed with a
  **Disable** button.

## What's on Home

From top to bottom:

1. The project's name and description, and its **MCP URL** (see
   [MCP clients](/docs/mcp/)).
2. **Build your bot with the Assistant**: only on a brand-new Pro or
   Enterprise project.
3. **Activity**: the chart.
4. Three counters: **Resources**, **Tools**, **Prompts**.
5. **Tool health**: per-tool calls, errors, and latency, plus errors, data
   sections, and unused tools.
6. **Recent activity**: a feed of individual runs.

## Activity

The **Activity** card charts conversations per day on your channels and
connected apps, including the messages that come in. Switch the range between
**7d**, **30d**, and **90d**, and the view between **Line**, **Area**, and
**Bar**. Each channel and each MCP client gets its own series in the legend
(with its total for the range); click a legend entry to hide or show it.

> Only your bot's **replies** count toward billing; the incoming messages in
> this chart are free. See [Settings → Billing & plan](/docs/settings/#billing--plan).

![The project Home: MCP URL, the Activity chart by channel, and the Resources, Tools and Prompts counters](/images/project-home.webp)

## Counters

Below the chart, three cards summarize what the project holds and how much it's
used. Each links straight to that section:

- **Resources**: how many you have, total size stored, and how many reads.
- **Tools**: how many are turned on and how many calls they've received.
- **Prompts**: how many you've defined and how many times they've run.

## Tool health

**Tool health** shows how each tool did over the selected range, from MCP
clients and channel bots alike. One row per tool:

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Tool** | The tool's name. **Off** if it's turned off now; **Not on this server** if no tool has that name any more (it was removed, or the model made it up). |
| **Calls** | How many times it was called. |
| **Errors** | How many of those failed. |
| **p95** | 95% of calls finished faster than this. |
| **Last used** | When it was last called. |
| **Signals** | Hints that the model is struggling with it (see below). |

The **Signals**:

- **bad arguments**: calls whose arguments didn't match the tool's input
  schema. Clearer descriptions of the inputs usually fix these.
- **retries**: called again right after it failed, or with the very same
  arguments.
- **gave up**: after this tool failed, the model called a different tool
  instead.

![Tool health: calls, errors, p95 and last use per tool, Most common errors and Tables synced from a spreadsheet](/images/home-tool-health.webp)

### Drill into a call

Click a tool to see **Calls to …**, filtered by **All** or **Errors** (with
**Load more**). Click a call to see it whole: where it came from (a channel's
bot or an **MCP client**), its **Arguments**, its **Result** or **Error**, or
**Rejected before it ran**. From there:

- **Open session** lists every tool call, prompt, and resource read in that
  session, oldest first.
- **Open conversation** jumps to the channel conversation the call happened in.

### More sections in Tool health

Under the table, Tool health adds what applies to the project:

- **Most common errors**: the errors seen most often in the range, with how
  many times each happened.
- **Index suggestions**: for projects with [Data](/docs/data/), a column that
  queries keep filtering or sorting on, reading many rows to return a few
  ("An index would help"), or an index no query used in 30 days.
- **Tables synced from a spreadsheet**: each synced table, its source file, and
  when it last synced (or was refused).
- **Database triggers**: each [trigger](/docs/data/triggers/) with its
  **Runs**, **Failed**, **p95**, **Last run**, and how many events it skipped
  (the trigger was off or deleted, or the plan no longer includes Data). Click
  one to see its runs.
- **Unused in 30 days**: tools that are on but weren't called once in 30 days
  (built-in tools, MCP servers, functions, HTTP endpoints). Every enabled tool
  is sent to the model on every turn, so select **Disable** to turn one off.
  You can turn it back on from **Tools**. On Free, if the project is at its tool
  limit, the confirmation warns that you'll have to turn another tool off before
  you can turn this one back on.

## Recent activity

The **Recent activity** feed is a running log of individual events: who
**read** a resource, **ran** a tool, or **used** a prompt, which source it came
from (a channel like Telegram, or an MCP client), and when. It's the quickest way
to confirm your assistant is doing what you expect.

![The Recent activity feed: who ran or read what, from which channel, and when](/images/home-recent-activity.webp)

## Other places to look

- **Channels → a channel → Conversations**: every exchange on that channel,
  with the tools and resources each reply used. See
  [Channels](/docs/channels/).
- **Settings → Billing & plan**: replies, storage, custom tool calls,
  Assistant credits, and Data usage for the whole organization. See
  [Settings](/docs/settings/#billing--plan).
- **The CLI**: the recent calls to your own functions, with their `ctx.log`
  output:

```bash
ganju logs                       # the last 20 calls
ganju logs --tool lookup-order   # only this one
ganju logs --limit 100
ganju logs --follow              # keep polling for new calls
```

## How long it's kept

Tool-call arguments and results are kept for 90 days, channel conversation
history for 365 days, and the "who ran what, when" audit rows behind Recent
activity for 365 days.

Describe what your bot should know or do in your own words, and the assistant builds it with you, tests it, and changes nothing until you press Apply.

The **Assistant** tab is where you build your bot by talking about it. Tell it
what you want ("tell customers if a pizza is sold out", "take orders and email
them to me", "book appointments in my Google Calendar") and it plans the work
with you, builds it, tries it, and hands you one card to apply. You never see
code, and nothing your customers see changes until you press **Apply**.

The assistant is part of the **Pro** and **Enterprise** plans; on Free the tab
shows **Build your bot by describing it** with **Upgrade**. It answers in the
language you write in, Spanish or English.

![The Assistant tab: the owner asks for new opening hours and the assistant answers with its plan, four questions and a credit estimate](/images/assistant-chat.webp)

## Start a chat

Write what your bot should do in the box at the bottom (**Enter** sends,
**Shift + Enter** adds a line), or pick one of the suggestions on an empty
chat: **Tell customers if we are open right now**, **Answer questions from my
menu**, **Take orders and email them to me**, **Book appointments in my Google
Calendar**.

![A new chat in the Assistant tab: "What should your bot do?" with four suggestions, the past chats list and the month's credits](/images/assistant-empty.webp)

## What it can change

- **Actions**: small programs your bot runs, like checking stock or saving a
  booking. The assistant writes and tests them for you, and can put them back
  the way they were on an earlier day. Under the hood they are
  [functions](/docs/tools/functions/), which the **Tools** page shows
  read-only.
- **[Data](/docs/data/)**: your project's tables, columns and rows, saved
  queries, [triggers](/docs/data/triggers/) such as "email me each new
  order", [schedules](/docs/data/schedules/) such as "every night
  at 9, email me today's orders", and the database's time zone, which
  schedules run in.
- **Knowledge**: notes and websites your bot searches, under **Knowledge →
  [Resources](/docs/resources/)**. Files come from you: when it needs one, it
  asks you to upload it.
- **[Prompts](/docs/prompts/)** and **[tools](/docs/tools/)**: the catalog's
  Gmail, Outlook, Google Calendar and Slack through accounts you connect with
  one click, other catalog tools, and
  [HTTP endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/).
- **[Bot instructions](/docs/channels/#tell-your-bot-how-to-answer)**: how
  your bot answers, like "answer in two sentences" or "always in Spanish".

What it **can't** change: channels, the bot's model, members, billing, API
tokens, and organization or project settings. Ask it for one of those and it
tells you where to change it yourself.

It can also **answer questions about the [CLI](/docs/tools/cli/)**, the
command line your developer uses: how to install it, deploy, test, set up CI
or manage the database. It reads the CLI docs first and answers with the
commands and a link.

## How a request goes

1. **It plans first.** For anything new, it says back what it understood, asks
   about the gaps in one message ("When the stock is 0, should the bot say it's
   sold out or offer something else?"), and estimates the credits it will use.
2. **It builds and tries.** You see each step as it works ("Looking at your
   project", "Writing an action", "Trying it"). Actions that send an email or
   save a row do it for real while testing, so it says so first and points
   tests at you or at rows clearly marked as tests. Before a scheduled email
   goes live, it sends you a sample so you can read it.
3. **You get one card.** Everything your bot or customers would see is
   collected into a **Ready to apply** card. See [The card](#the-card).
4. **You press Apply.** From that moment your bot uses it. The assistant then
   tests whatever needed the change to be live, and tells you what it found,
   before saying it works.

Nothing is half-applied: until you press **Apply**, what the assistant built is
only a draft. If it proposes a new card before you applied the last one, the
old card shows **Replaced by a newer change**.

## The card

![A "Ready to apply" card: a summary, the list of changes, the "Once applied, your bot can:" box and the Apply button](/images/assistant-change-card.webp)

A **Ready to apply** card lists, in plain words, every change it holds, and
under **Once applied, your bot can:** what your bot is able to do with it:

- **Only reads information**, or **Changes or sends things (it asks your
  customer first)**;
- **Read your tables** or **Read and change your tables**, naming them;
- **Reach** the outside websites an action calls;
- **Use your accounts**, such as Gmail or Google Calendar.

A card that holds something that can't fully come back says **This can't be
undone** or **Some of this can't be undone**, and marks each line that
**Deletes**.

After **Apply**, the card shows **Applied** and an **Undo** button.

### Undo

**Undo** puts your project back the way it was before the card. Most changes
come back step by step. A few are bigger, and the card warns you before you
apply them:

- Dropping a table or column, deleting rows, or changing a column's type is
  undone by putting the **whole database** back to just before it: anything
  saved after it is lost. Undo asks again before doing it (**Undo anyway**).
- A removed file's contents don't come back.
- A removed tool comes back without its key or sign-in, which you add again.
- A webhook trigger that comes back gets a new signing secret.

### Deleting

Deleting anything (a table, a column, rows, a note, a file, a prompt, a tool)
takes two steps. The assistant first asks you, naming exactly what would go
and what is lost with it, and stages it only after your yes. The card then asks
you to **type its name** before **Apply** works. When you'd rather turn
something off than delete it, it suggests that instead.

## Cards that need you

Some things only you can do. The assistant shows a card and stops until you're
done; your next message tells it how it went. **I'd rather not** on any of them
asks it for another way.

- **Connect your account**: **Connect Gmail** (or Google Calendar, Outlook,
  Slack…) signs you in to that account for the project.
- **A key the assistant needs**: it explains where to find the key, step by
  step. Paste it under **Paste the key here** and **Save it**. The value goes
  straight to your project; the assistant never sees it.
- **A file the assistant needs**: **Add it in Resources** takes you to upload
  it, then **Done, I added it**.

It never asks for your passwords, and never sees a key or a sign-in.

## Go back to an earlier version

Ask "put the actions back the way they were yesterday" or "undo what you
changed this morning" and the assistant finds the version of your actions that
was live then. It tells you what comes back and which actions added since
would go, and stages it as a card you apply like any other. If a developer
uploads your actions, it tells you their next upload will replace it.

For anything else on a card, **Undo** on that card is the way back.

## Time zone and schedules

The database has a time zone, and schedules ("every night at 9") and "today"
run in it. Before a first schedule, or when a schedule fires at the wrong hour,
the assistant checks the time zone, asks where your business is if it doesn't
know, and stages the change on the card. A schedule runs at most once a day,
every day or on the weekdays you choose, and a project can have up to five.
More in [Schedules](/docs/data/schedules/).

## Try it as a customer

**Try it** in the chat's header opens **Try it as a customer**, a panel that
talks to your real bot with everything that is turned on: the same bot your
channels answer with. Use it after applying a card to ask what a customer would
ask. **Start over** clears it.

![The "Try it as a customer" panel open beside the chat, with a customer question and the bot's answer](/images/assistant-try-it.webp)

## Credits

The assistant is billed in credits; one credit is $0.01 of AI cost. A new action
with its tables usually takes 30 to 60 credits for the whole job, and up to
about 90 when it also emails, checks your hours or handles payments; a change to
an action 10 to 50, and new knowledge or a small fix under 15. Each reply shows
what it used, and each chat its total.

Pro and Enterprise include **1,000 credits a month**. Past that, extra credits
are $2 per 100, up to a monthly limit an admin sets in **Settings → Billing &
plan** (2,000 extra by default; 0 stops at the included credits). The chats
list shows the month so far; when the credits run out, it says so.

Messages in **Try it as a customer** use credits too when your bot runs on our
AI model. Nothing else does.

### Your own Anthropic key

If your organization added an Anthropic model in **Settings → Models**, an admin
can switch **Pay with**, beside the month's credits, from **Ganju credits** to
that model. The assistant then runs on your key and uses no credits; only the
customer test chat still does.

## When an action stops working

For actions the assistant built, the Assistant tab shows a **Something stopped
working** banner when an action fails often (at least 5 failed calls, and 30%
of its calls, over the last day or since it was last changed) or when an
account it uses needs signing in again. **Fix it with the assistant** writes
the first message for you: it reads what went wrong, tells you why in plain
words, and proposes a fix as usual. An account that needs signing in again is
fixed by reconnecting it, not by changing anything.

The project's owner and the organization's admins also get an email, at most
once a day per project, and about the same problem again only after a week.
Turn it off in **Settings → Billing & plan**.

## Projects a developer deploys

When a project's actions were uploaded by a developer with the
[CLI](/docs/tools/cli/), the assistant doesn't replace their code. It reads it,
and answers a code change with **A change for your developer**: the changed
files, to **Copy** or **Download** and send them. They apply it and upload
again.

If the developer manages your tables from code, the card says so: their next
upload puts table and column changes back, so pass those on to them too.

When the assistant changed the actions since the developer's last upload, the
CLI warns the developer before their next deploy replaces them.

## Chats

Start a **New chat** for each new thing you build; past chats are in the list.
One chat answers at a time in each project, and sending many messages in a
minute asks you to wait a moment. If the assistant stops after many steps
without finishing, tell it to continue.

- After **30 days**, a message keeps what you and the assistant said, but what
  its tools returned and its working notes are removed, since they can hold your
  customers' data. An old chat still continues: the assistant picks up from what
  was said and checks your project again.
- A chat is deleted **90 days after its last message**.
- **Delete chat** in the chat's header deletes it now. What it changed in your
  project stays, but its changes can't be undone from there anymore.

- **[Functions](/docs/tools/functions/)**: what an action is underneath, if
  you're curious or work with a developer.
- **[Settings](/docs/settings/)**: your own models, the extra-credit limit and
  the alert email.

Ask “put the actions back the way they were yesterday” or “undo what you changed this morning” and the assistant finds the version of your actions that was live then. It tells you what comes back and which actions added since would go, and stages it as a card you apply like any other. If a developer uploads your actions, it tells you their next upload will replace it.

For anything else on a card, Undo on that card is the way back.

Time zone and schedules

The database has a time zone, and schedules (“every night at 9”) and “today” run in it. Before a first schedule, or when a schedule fires at the wrong hour, the assistant checks the time zone, asks where your business is if it doesn’t know, and stages the change on the card. A schedule runs at most once a day, every day or on the weekdays you choose, and a project can have up to five. More in Schedules.

Try it as a customer

Try it in the chat’s header opens Try it as a customer, a panel that talks to your real bot with everything that is turned on: the same bot your channels answer with. Use it after applying a card to ask what a customer would ask. Start over clears it.

Credits

The assistant is billed in credits; one credit is $0.01 of AI cost. A new action with its tables usually takes 30 to 60 credits for the whole job, and up to about 90 when it also emails, checks your hours or handles payments; a change to an action 10 to 50, and new knowledge or a small fix under 15. Each reply shows what it used, and each chat its total.

Pro and Enterprise include 1,000 credits a month. Past that, extra credits are $2 per 100, up to a monthly limit an admin sets in Settings → Billing & plan (2,000 extra by default; 0 stops at the included credits). The chats list shows the month so far; when the credits run out, it says so.

Messages in Try it as a customer use credits too when your bot runs on our AI model. Nothing else does.

Your own Anthropic key

If your organization added an Anthropic model in Settings → Models, an admin can switch Pay with, beside the month’s credits, from Ganju credits to that model. The assistant then runs on your key and uses no credits; only the customer test chat still does.

When an action stops working

For actions the assistant built, the Assistant tab shows a Something stopped working banner when an action fails often (at least 5 failed calls, and 30% of its calls, over the last day or since it was last changed) or when an account it uses needs signing in again. Fix it with the assistant writes the first message for you: it reads what went wrong, tells you why in plain words, and proposes a fix as usual. An account that needs signing in again is fixed by reconnecting it, not by changing anything.

The project’s owner and the organization’s admins also get an email, at most once a day per project, and about the same problem again only after a week. Turn it off in Settings → Billing & plan.

Projects a developer deploys

When a project’s actions were uploaded by a developer with the CLI, the assistant doesn’t replace their code. It reads it, and answers a code change with A change for your developer: the changed files, to Copy or Download and send them. They apply it and upload again.

If the developer manages your tables from code, the card says so: their next upload puts table and column changes back, so pass those on to them too.

When the assistant changed the actions since the developer’s last upload, the CLI warns the developer before their next deploy replaces them.

Chats

Start a New chat for each new thing you build; past chats are in the list. One chat answers at a time in each project, and sending many messages in a minute asks you to wait a moment. If the assistant stops after many steps without finishing, tell it to continue.

  • After 30 days, a message keeps what you and the assistant said, but what its tools returned and its working notes are removed, since they can hold your customers’ data. An old chat still continues: the assistant picks up from what was said and checks your project again.
  • A chat is deleted 90 days after its last message.
  • Delete chat in the chat’s header deletes it now. What it changed in your project stays, but its changes can’t be undone from there anymore.

Next

  • Data: the tables and triggers the assistant builds on.
  • Functions: what an action is underneath, if you’re curious or work with a developer.
  • Settings: your own models, the extra-credit limit and the alert email.

Deliver your assistant to real people on the apps they already use (Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack, and Discord), tune how it answers, and watch every conversation.

**Channels** are how you put your assistant in front of other people. Everything
you've built ([prompts](/docs/prompts/), [resources](/docs/resources/),
[tools](/docs/tools/) and [data](/docs/data/)) comes along automatically; you
just choose where people reach it. Connect a **messaging app** so clients and
teammates chat with your AI where they already are, or connect any
[MCP client](/docs/mcp/) for a power-user workflow.

## Why use channels

- **Meet people where they are.** No new app to install: your assistant lives in
  Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack, or Discord.
- **One assistant, delivered everywhere.** Every channel serves the same prompts,
  resources, tools and bot instructions, so answers stay consistent across apps.
- **Bring your own model.** Each channel can run on the system default or a
  language model you configure in [Settings](/docs/settings/).
- **Stay in control of cost.** Wait for people to finish typing before
  answering, and cap how many replies one customer gets a day.
- **Watch it work.** Every conversation is kept in the dashboard, with what the
  bot looked up and did for each answer.

## What's available

Ganju supports four messaging platforms. Each has its own page with step-by-step
instructions for creating the credentials it needs:

| Platform | What you need | Where it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **[Telegram](/docs/channels/telegram/)** | A bot token from @BotFather | Private chats; in groups when mentioned or replied to |
| **[WhatsApp](/docs/channels/whatsapp/)** | A Meta app with the WhatsApp Business Cloud API | One-to-one chats with your number |
| **[Slack](/docs/channels/slack/)** | A Slack app: bot token and signing secret | Direct messages; in channels when @mentioned |
| **[Discord](/docs/channels/discord/)** | A Discord application: bot token, application ID and public key | Direct messages; in servers when @mentioned |

## Connect a channel

Open **Channels** in the project's sidebar and select **Add channel**. The
**Connect channel** panel asks for:

1. **Platform**: Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp or Discord.
2. **Language model**: leave **System default**, or pick one of your
   organization's models (see [below](#choose-the-language-model)).
3. The platform's credentials. The panel shows what each field is and, for
   Slack, Discord and WhatsApp, the scopes, intents or webhook fields the app
   needs.

![The Connect channel panel: Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp and Discord, the Language model and the Bot token field](/images/channels-connect-panel.webp)

Select **Connect**. Ganju checks the credentials with the platform before saving
them (a wrong token is refused right away) and stores them encrypted. Then:

- **Telegram** is ready at once: Ganju registers the webhook and the command menu
  for you.
- **Slack**, **Discord** and **WhatsApp** need one more step: the channel's
  **Overview** shows a URL to paste back into that platform (the **Request URL**,
  **Interactions Endpoint URL** or **Callback URL**) with a copy button. Each
  platform page covers the exact steps.

A bot, Slack app, Discord application or WhatsApp number can be connected to only
one channel at a time.

## The Channels page

Each connected channel is a card with its bot name, the platform's icon, its
status (**Active** or **Disabled**) and a running count of conversations and
messages. Select a card to open it. The panel has an **Overview** and a
**Conversations** tab, and for WhatsApp a **Message templates** tab.

![The Channels page with Telegram, Slack, Discord and WhatsApp channels, Bot instructions and Add channel](/images/channels-page.webp)

## Channel settings

The **Overview** tab holds everything about one channel:

- **Status**: **Receiving messages** on, or **Paused**. While paused, the
  platform still sends messages to Ganju, but they're dropped until you turn it
  back on.
- **Language model**: change the model this channel uses.
- **Reply timing**: people often send one thought across several messages.
  Waiting for a pause lets the bot answer them all in one reply. Choose **Answer
  every message**, or wait **2**, **5** (recommended, the default), **10** or
  **30 seconds**. The bot never waits more than a minute from the first message,
  and a slash command is always answered right away.
- **Replies per customer**: how many replies one customer gets in 24 hours:
  **20**, **50** (recommended, the default), **100**, **200** or **No limit**.
  Past it, the customer is told once, and the bot stays quiet until the day frees
  up, so spam and all-day chats stop costing you messages and model time.
- **Customer memory**: turn on **Remember customers** and the bot keeps what
  each customer tells it about themselves (name, address, allergies, important
  dates) and uses it next time ("same address as always?"). It's off by default,
  works in private chats only, and customers can ask the bot to forget. You can
  clear it from a conversation.
- **Activity**: the channel's conversation and message counts.
- **Danger zone**: **Remove channel** disconnects it and deletes its
  conversation history. This can't be undone.

![A Telegram channel's Overview: the bot, Receiving messages, Language model, Reply timing and Replies per customer](/images/channel-overview.webp)

## Choose the language model

Every channel runs on a language model. By default that's the **System
default**, run by Ganju. On **Pro** and **Enterprise** you can bring your own:
your own provider and API key, added once in [Settings](/docs/settings/) and
picked per channel, when you connect it or later from its Overview. Until you
add one, the dropdown only offers the system default.

## Tell your bot how to answer

**Bot instructions**, a button at the top of the Channels page, say how your bot
answers on every channel of the project and in the assistant's
[Try it as a customer](/docs/assistant/#try-it-as-a-customer) panel: its
language, length and tone, or what it should always or never say. Write them as
short rules, one per line, and select **Save**:

```
Answer in two sentences at most.
Always answer in Spanish.
Call customers by their first name.
```

![The Bot instructions dialog with example instructions and the 2,000-character counter](/images/channels-bot-instructions.webp)

- They take up to **2,000 characters** (the counter under the box shows how many
  you've used) and work on any model, including the system default.
- On a model with its own system prompt, they're added after it.
- Ganju's own rules come first, so the instructions can't turn off, for example,
  the bot asking a customer before it changes something.
- Keep facts like prices and hours in [Resources](/docs/resources/) instead.

The project [assistant](/docs/assistant/) can also write them for you ("answer
more briefly", "always offer delivery"): it proposes the new text and you approve
it. The dialog reads them again every time you open it, so you always see the
latest version.

## What people can do in a chat

- **Just write.** The bot answers from your resources, uses your tools and
  data, and can send stored files as attachments. In group chats and channels it
  answers only when it's mentioned (or, on Telegram, replied to); in private
  chats it answers everything.
- **Run a prompt.** Each [prompt](/docs/prompts/) is a slash command; the text
  after it fills the prompt's first variable.
- **Send a voice note.** The bot transcribes it and answers as if it were typed.
  Notes longer than five minutes get a reply saying so instead.
- **Confirm sensitive actions.** Before a tool changes something, the bot asks,
  with **Yes / No** buttons where the app has them, and only the person asked
  can answer.
- **Link their account.** `/link` is reserved: it gives the person a code to
  connect their chat account to their Ganju account. For safety it works only
  in a private chat (on Slack and Discord the reply is visible only to them).

With [citations](/docs/resources/#cite-your-sources) on, answers list the
resources they used.

## Watch the conversations

Open a channel's **Conversations** tab to see every chat, each with its title
(the person's name for a private chat, the group or channel name otherwise), a
**Private**, **Group** or **Channel** tag, how many messages it has and when the
last one arrived.
Select one to read the thread:

- every message, with who sent it and when;
- under each answer, the tokens and time it took, and each **Tool**,
  **Resource** or **Prompt** the bot used; select one to see its input, output
  or error, with a link to open it in Tools, Resources or Prompts;
- the files the bot sent as attachments, and the **Sources** it cited (with the
  page number for PDFs);
- tags like **Voice note** or **Daily limit reached**;
- with customer memory on, what the bot **remembers about this customer**, with
  a **Forget** button.

![A conversation thread in the dashboard: the user's /start command and the assistant's answer listing the project's resources, tools and prompts](/images/channel-messages.webp)

For numbers across all channels (conversations, messages, tools), see
[Analytics](/docs/analytics/).

## Connect any MCP client

Messaging apps aren't the only way in. Under the hood your project is a **Model
Context Protocol (MCP) server**, so any MCP-compatible client (**Claude**,
**ChatGPT** or **Cursor**) can connect to the very same assistant, with all your
prompts, resources and tools. Channels are for the people you serve; MCP clients
are for wiring your AI into your own tools and workflows. Both point at one
project. See [MCP clients](/docs/mcp/).

## From the CLI

The [`ganju` CLI](/docs/tools/cli/) lists your WhatsApp message templates and
their status with Meta:

```bash
ganju channel templates
ganju channel templates --json
```

Channels themselves are connected and configured in the dashboard.

## Plan limits

- **Free**: one channel per project, and 100 bot messages a month across the
  organization, on the system default model.
- **Pro** and **Enterprise**: unlimited channels, messages metered past what the
  plan includes, and your own models.

See [Settings](/docs/settings/) for plans and usage.

## Troubleshooting

- **The bot never answers.** Check the channel is **Active** with **Receiving
  messages** on, then the platform-specific step: Slack's Request URL and bot
  events, Discord's Message Content intent, WhatsApp's Callback URL and
  `messages` field. On Slack, **Socket Mode** must be **off**. With it on, Slack
  sends events over its socket instead of to Ganju's Request URL.
- **It answers in DMs but not in a group.** Mention the bot (`@yourbot`). It
  ignores group chatter that isn't addressed to it.
- **It answers late.** That's **Reply timing** waiting for a pause. Pick a shorter
  wait, or **Answer every message**.
- **A customer stopped getting answers.** They probably hit **Replies per
  customer**; the conversation shows **Daily limit reached**. Raise the limit or
  wait for the day to free up.
- **"…is already connected to project…".** That bot, app or number is
  connected to another project's channel. Remove that channel first, or use a
  different bot.
- **Free plan: can't add a channel.** Free allows one channel per project.

What people can do in a chat
Connect a Discord application: reset the bot token, enable the message intents, invite the bot, paste the token, application ID and public key, then set the interactions endpoint for slash commands.

**Discord** connects through an application you create in the Discord Developer
Portal. You'll grab three values (the **bot token**, **Application ID** and
**Public key**), enable the message intents, and invite the bot. Free-form
messages reach Ganju over Discord's Gateway automatically; slash commands use the
**Interactions Endpoint URL** you set at the end.

## 1. Create an application and bot

1. Go to the [Discord Developer Portal](https://discord.com/developers/applications)
   and select **New Application**. Name it and accept the terms.
2. On **General Information**, copy the **Application ID** and the **Public key**.
3. Open the **Bot** tab and select **Reset Token**, then copy the **bot token**
   (treat it like a password; Discord shows it only once).

## 2. Enable intents and invite the bot

1. Under **Bot → Privileged Gateway Intents**, enable **Message Content Intent**
   and **Server Members Intent**. Without Message Content, the bot can only read
   DMs or messages where it's @mentioned.
2. Under **OAuth2 → URL Generator**, tick the **`bot`** and
   **`applications.commands`** scopes, then the **Send Messages**, **Read
   Message History** and **Attach Files** permissions. Open the generated URL
   and add the bot to your server.

## 3. Connect it in Ganju

In **Channels → Add channel**, pick **Discord**, choose a **Language model**,
and fill in:

![The Connect channel panel with Discord selected: Bot token, Application ID, Public key and the required intents](/images/new-channel-discord.webp)

- **Bot token**: from the **Bot** tab (Reset Token).
- **Application ID**: from **General Information**; used to register slash
  commands.
- **Public key**: from **General Information**; used to verify incoming
  interactions.

Select **Connect**. Ganju checks the token with Discord, registers the slash
commands and opens the Gateway connection right away, so the bot can already
reply to DMs and mentions.

## 4. Set the interactions endpoint

Native slash commands arrive separately. The channel's **Overview** shows
**Discord setup** with an **Interactions Endpoint URL** and a copy button. Paste
it into your application's **General Information → Interactions Endpoint URL**
and save. Discord verifies it against your public key on the spot.

## Slash commands

Ganju registers one slash command per [prompt](/docs/prompts/), named like the
command on the prompt's card, each with an optional **`text`** option that fills
the prompt's first variable. It also registers **`/link`**, which replies with an
account-linking code only you can see. The set is updated whenever you add,
rename or remove a prompt. Discord allows up to 100 commands; names are cut to
32 characters.

The answer to a slash command arrives in the same conversation once it's ready.

## How the bot behaves in Discord

- **Direct messages**: it answers every message.
- **Servers**: it answers only when **@mentioned**.
- **Voice messages** are transcribed and answered like text.
- **Sources**: with [citations](/docs/resources/#cite-your-sources) on, sources
  come as link buttons under the answer.
- **Files**: the bot can attach stored resources, up to 25 MB each (Discord's
  limit for bots on servers without boosts).
- **Confirmations**: before a tool changes something, the bot asks with Yes / No
  buttons that only the person asked can use.

Long answers are split into several messages (Discord allows 2,000 characters per
message).

## Troubleshooting

- **The bot is online but ignores messages in a server.** @mention it. If it
  still doesn't answer, check **Message Content Intent** is on.
- **No slash commands show up.** Re-invite the bot with the
  `applications.commands` scope, and set the Interactions Endpoint URL. Discord
  can take a few minutes to show new commands.
- **"Interactions endpoint URL could not be verified".** Check the **Public key**
  you pasted in Ganju is the one on **General Information**, and the channel is
  **Active**.
- **"Connect" fails right away.** The token is wrong or was reset. Reset it again
  and paste the new one.

Sources: [Discord Bots & Companion Apps (Discord docs)](https://docs.discord.com/developers/bots/overview),
[Application setup (discord.js)](https://discordjs.guide/legacy/preparations/app-setup)

Connect a Slack app: add the bot scopes, install it to your workspace, paste the bot token and signing secret, then set the Request URL for events and slash commands.

**Slack** connects through a Slack app you create once. You'll add a few bot
scopes, install the app to grab its **Bot User OAuth Token** and **Signing
secret**, paste both into Ganju, then set Ganju's **Request URL** as the app's
event endpoint (and for any slash commands).

## 1. Create a Slack app

1. Go to [api.slack.com/apps](https://api.slack.com/apps) and select **Create New
   App → From scratch**. Name it and pick your workspace.
2. Leave **Socket Mode** (under **Settings**) **off**. Ganju receives events over
   HTTP at its Request URL; with Socket Mode on, Slack never sends them there.

## 2. Add bot token scopes

Under **OAuth & Permissions → Bot Token Scopes**, add the **required** scopes:

- `app_mentions:read`: see messages that @mention the bot
- `im:history`: read direct messages to the bot
- `chat:write`: post replies
- `files:write`: send files as attachments
- `files:read`: download voice clips to transcribe them

Optionally add the **recommended** scopes so the bot shows names instead of raw
IDs: `users:read`, `channels:read`, `groups:read`.

An app installed before you added a scope needs to be **reinstalled** for it to
take effect. Until `files:read` is there, voice clips get a reply asking the
person to type instead.

## 3. Install and copy credentials

1. Still under **OAuth & Permissions**, select **Install to Workspace** and
   approve. Copy the **Bot User OAuth Token** (starts with `xoxb-`).
2. Under **Basic Information → App Credentials**, copy the **Signing secret**.
3. Open **App Home** and, under **Show Tabs**, enable the **Messages tab** and
   allow users to send messages from it, so people can DM the bot.

## 4. Connect it in Ganju

In **Channels → Add channel**, pick **Slack**, choose a **Language model**, and
paste the **Bot token** and **Signing secret**. The panel lists the required and
recommended scopes and the bot events to subscribe to. Select **Connect**.

![The Connect channel panel with Slack selected: Bot token, Signing secret and the required bot scopes](/images/new-channel-slack.webp)

Ganju checks the bot token with Slack and shows the workspace and bot name on
the channel. The signing secret is checked when Slack sends its first event.

## 5. Set the Request URL

After connecting, the channel's **Overview** shows **Slack setup** with a
**Request URL** and a copy button. Back in your Slack app:

1. Go to **Event Subscriptions** and toggle **Enable Events** on.
2. Paste Ganju's Request URL. Slack verifies it instantly.
3. Under **Subscribe to bot events**, add **`app_mention`** and **`message.im`**,
   then **Save Changes**. Reinstall the app if Slack asks you to.

Now DM the bot, or invite it to a channel (`/invite @yourbot`) and @mention it,
and it replies.

## 6. Add slash commands (optional)

Slack only accepts slash commands you've created in the app, so a
[prompt](/docs/prompts/) becomes a Slack command once you add it there:

1. In your Slack app, open **Slash Commands → Create New Command**.
2. **Command**: the prompt's command as shown on its card, like
   `/summarize_article`.
3. **Request URL**: the same Request URL from step 5.
4. Add a short description and save; reinstall the app if Slack asks.

The text after the command fills the prompt's first variable, and the answer is
posted in the conversation where the command was used. You can also add
`/link`, which replies with an account-linking code only you can see.

## How the bot behaves in Slack

- **Direct messages**: it answers every message.
- **Channels**: it answers only when **@mentioned**, and replies in a thread
  under that message, continuing the thread if there is one.
- **Voice clips** are transcribed and answered like text (needs `files:read`).
- **Sources**: with [citations](/docs/resources/#cite-your-sources) on, a short
  list of source links follows the answer.
- **Files**: the bot can upload stored resources as attachments.
- **Confirmations**: before a tool changes something, the bot asks; reply yes or
  no.

## Troubleshooting

- **The Request URL won't verify.** Make sure you pasted the URL from this
  channel's Overview exactly, and that the channel is **Active**.
- **Events never arrive.** Check **Socket Mode** is off, **Enable Events** is
  on, and both `app_mention` and `message.im` are subscribed.
- **"Sending messages to this app has been turned off".** Enable the
  **Messages tab** in **App Home**.
- **The bot ignores a channel.** Invite it to the channel and @mention it.
- **It shows user IDs instead of names.** Add the recommended scopes and
  reinstall the app.
- **"/command is not a valid command".** Create the slash command in the Slack
  app (step 6).

Connect a Telegram bot in a minute: create it with @BotFather, paste the token, and Ganju registers the webhook and the command menu for you.

**Telegram** is the quickest channel to set up. You create a bot with Telegram's
own **@BotFather**, copy the token it gives you, and paste it into Ganju. That's
it. Ganju registers the webhook and turns your prompts into the bot's command
menu automatically.

## 1. Create a bot with BotFather

1. Open Telegram and search for **@BotFather** (the verified account with the blue
   checkmark).
2. Start a chat and send **`/newbot`**.
3. Enter a **display name** for your bot (anything you like).
4. Enter a **username**. It must be unique and end in `bot` (e.g. `acme_support_bot`).
5. BotFather replies with your **bot token**, a long string like
   `123456789:AA...`. Copy it.

Treat the token like a password. Optionally, while you're in BotFather, give the
bot a description and a profile picture with `/setdescription` and
`/setuserpic`.

## 2. Connect it in Ganju

In your project, open **Channels → Add channel**, pick **Telegram**, choose a
**Language model** (or leave **System default**), paste the token into **Bot
token**, and select **Connect**.

![The Connect channel panel with Telegram selected and a single Bot token field](/images/new-channel-telegram-1.webp)

Ganju checks the token with Telegram, then:

- registers the bot's **webhook**, so there's no callback URL for you to set;
- registers your [prompts](/docs/prompts/) as the bot's **command menu**, and
  refreshes it whenever you add, rename or remove a prompt.

The channel goes **Active** immediately, with the bot's name and `@username` on
its card.

Ganju now receives the bot's messages through that webhook, so the same token
can't also run on another server or bot platform at the same time: the last
one to set a webhook wins.

## 3. Chat with it

Open your bot in Telegram (via the `t.me/<username>` link BotFather gave you) and
send a message. It replies using your resources, tools and
[bot instructions](/docs/channels/#tell-your-bot-how-to-answer).

- **Private chats**: the bot answers every message.
- **Groups**: add the bot to the group. It answers only when it's
  **@mentioned**, when someone **replies** to one of its messages, or when a
  command is addressed to it (`/command@yourbot`). Other group chatter is
  ignored.
- **Commands**: type **/** to see your prompts in the menu, with their
  descriptions. The text after a command fills the prompt's first variable.
  Telegram shows up to 100 commands.
- **Voice notes** and audio files are transcribed and answered like text; a
  caption counts as text sent with the note.
- **Sources**: with [citations](/docs/resources/#cite-your-sources) on, the
  answer comes with one button per source under it.
- **Files**: the bot can send stored resources (a PDF menu, a price list) as
  attachments.
- **Confirmations**: before a tool changes something, the bot asks with Yes / No
  buttons.

Long answers are split into several messages.

## Change or revoke the token

If the token leaks, revoke it in BotFather via **`/mybots` → your bot → API
Token → Revoke current token**. The old token stops working at once, and so does
the channel. To use the new token, remove the channel and connect it again.
Removing a channel deletes its conversation history.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Connect" fails right away.** The token is wrong or was revoked. Copy it
  again from BotFather (`/mybots` → your bot → API Token).
- **The bot doesn't answer in a group.** Mention it (`@yourbot`) or reply to one
  of its messages. Check also that BotFather lets it join groups
  (`/mybots` → your bot → Bot Settings → Allow Groups).
- **The bot stopped answering after you used the token elsewhere.** Another
  service replaced the webhook. Remove the channel and connect it again.
- **A prompt is missing from the menu.** Commands must start with a letter, and
  the menu can take a moment to refresh. Typing the command still works.

Sources: [From BotFather to 'Hello World' (Telegram)](https://core.telegram.org/bots/tutorial),
[Telegram Bot API](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api)

Connect the WhatsApp Business (Meta) Cloud API: create a permanent System User token, grab your phone number ID, point the webhook at Ganju, and manage message templates.

**WhatsApp** runs on Meta's **WhatsApp Business Cloud API**. Setup has a few more
steps than the other channels because it happens in the Meta dashboard, but it's
a one-time job. You'll create a Meta app, generate a **permanent** access token,
copy your **Phone number ID**, then paste Ganju's **Callback URL** back into Meta.

## 1. Create a Meta app with WhatsApp

1. In the [Meta for Developers](https://developers.facebook.com/) dashboard, create
   an app (type **Business**) and add the **WhatsApp** product.
2. Note your **Phone number ID** (a numeric string, *not* the phone number
   itself) and your **WhatsApp Business Account ID**. For your real number,
   both are under **WhatsApp → Production setup → Register your WhatsApp phone
   number**, where Meta labels the account "Messaging Account ID". The **API
   Setup** (or **Try it**) page shows Meta's free test number and its own test
   account: use those IDs only to try things with the test number.

## 2. Generate a permanent access token

The temporary token on the API Setup page expires in 24 hours, so create a
permanent one instead:

1. Open **Business Settings → System users** and add a **System user**.
2. Assign your app to it and generate a token with the
   **`whatsapp_business_messaging`** and **`whatsapp_business_management`**
   permissions. The first lets the bot send and receive messages; the second
   lets Ganju manage your message templates.
3. Set it to **never expire** and copy it. This is your **Access token**.

## 3. Connect it in Ganju

In **Channels → Add channel**, pick **WhatsApp**, choose a **Language model**,
and fill in the fields:

![The Connect channel panel with WhatsApp selected: Access token, Phone number ID and Verify token](/images/new-channel-whatsapp.webp)

- **Access token**: the permanent System User token from step 2.
- **Phone number ID**: from **WhatsApp → Production setup** (the ID, not the
  display number). API Setup shows only the test number's.
- **Verify token**: any value you choose; you'll enter the same string in Meta.
- **App secret**: from **App → Settings → Basic**, used to verify incoming
  webhooks.

Select **Connect**. Ganju checks that the token can act for that number, then
the channel's **Overview** shows **WhatsApp setup** with a **Callback URL** and a
copy button.

## 4. Point the Meta webhook at Ganju

1. In the Meta dashboard, go to **WhatsApp → Configuration → Webhooks**.
2. Paste Ganju's **Callback URL** and the **Verify token** you chose above, and
   verify.
3. Subscribe the webhook to the **`messages`** field, and to
   **`message_template_status_update`** if you'll use message templates.

Once verified, messages sent to your WhatsApp number reach your assistant.

Meta only forwards a number's messages once your app is **subscribed to its
WhatsApp Business account**. Ganju does that for you when you connect the
channel, and when you save a new token or account id in its **Message
templates** tab. If Meta's webhook **Test** button works but real messages never
arrive, the subscription is missing. That happens when Meta couldn't tell Ganju
which business account the token belongs to. Fill in the account's id in the
**Message templates** tab, or subscribe the app yourself with the same token:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://graph.facebook.com/v25.0/<WABA_ID>/subscribed_apps" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>"
```

## How the bot behaves in WhatsApp

- **One-to-one chats.** Every conversation is a private chat with your number;
  the bot answers every message.
- **Commands.** WhatsApp has no command menu: people type a
  [prompt's](/docs/prompts/) `/command` at the start of a message, followed by
  any text for its first variable.
- **Voice notes** are transcribed and answered like text.
- **Sources**: with [citations](/docs/resources/#cite-your-sources) on, a short
  **Sources** list of links follows the answer.
- **Files**: the bot can send stored resources as attachments, within Meta's
  sizes: documents up to 100 MB, images up to 5 MB, video and audio up to 16 MB.
- **Confirmations**: before a tool changes something, the bot asks with Yes / No
  reply buttons that only that customer can use.

Long answers are split into several messages.

## 5. Message templates

WhatsApp only lets a business write freely to a customer within **24 hours of
the customer's last message**. After that, only a **message template** Meta
approved reaches them. Your assistant never needs one, since it always answers
a message. Triggers and functions that message a customer later do, like "your
order is ready" the next morning.

Open the channel and the **Message templates** tab. There you can:

- **See your templates** with Meta's status: **Approved**, **In review**,
  **Rejected** (with Meta's reason), **Paused**, **Disabled** or **In appeal**,
  and when they were last synced. **Refresh** reads them from Meta again.
- **Create one** with **New template**: a **Name** (lowercase letters, digits
  and underscores, like `order_ready`), a **Language**, a **Category**
  (**Utility** or **Marketing**), an optional **Header** and **Footer** (up to 60
  characters each, no variables), the **Message** (up to 1,024 characters) and
  up to ten **Quick replies** (25 characters each). Variables are inserted with
  a label ("customer name", "order number") and become `{{1}}`, `{{2}}`, … (up to
  20); Meta asks for an example value for each. A **Preview** shows it as a
  WhatsApp message, and the rules Meta rejects most for are checked before it's
  sent: a variable at the very start or end, two variables side by side, too
  many variables for the text. Select **Send for review**.
- **Edit or delete** one. Meta reviews an edit again and limits how often an
  approved template can be edited; when it refuses, its message is shown as is.
  Deleting removes it in Meta too, triggers and functions that send it start
  failing, and Meta doesn't let you reuse the name for 30 days.

![A WhatsApp channel's Message templates tab with approved templates, Refresh and New template](/images/whatsapp-message-templates.webp)

**Templates need two things from Meta:**

- **The WhatsApp Business account.** Templates belong to the account, not to
  the number. Ganju asks Meta which one your token manages, so usually there's
  nothing to do; when Meta can't tell, the tab asks for the **WhatsApp Business
  account ID** (the app's **WhatsApp → Production setup → Register your
  WhatsApp phone number**, labelled "Messaging Account ID", or WhatsApp Manager
  → Account tools → Business account settings). Ganju checks it with Meta before
  saving it: an account that doesn't have the channel's number is refused, so
  you can't save the test number's account for a real number by mistake.
- **The `whatsapp_business_management` permission** on the token, besides
  `whatsapp_business_messaging`. A token made only to send messages lacks it;
  the tab says so and explains how to generate a new one in **Business
  Settings → System users**. Paste it in **New access token**: like the first
  one, it's stored encrypted and never shown again. The same box appears when
  the token expired or was revoked.

**Review and category.** Meta reviews each template in minutes to a day. It
may reject one, or move it from **Utility** to **Marketing** if it reads as
promotional. Keep Utility for updates the customer expects: "Your order
#{{1}} is ready for pickup". Without the `message_template_status_update`
webhook field, Ganju still checks templates in review every hour, and the
others once a day.

**Cost.** Meta bills template messages to your WhatsApp Business account at
its own rates, and Marketing costs more than Utility. Ganju doesn't charge for
them.

**What Ganju can send.** Ganju fills the variables of the message itself. A
template made in WhatsApp Manager with an image, video or document header, a
variable in the header, or a button that takes a value (a link with a
variable, a code) is listed as **Ganju can't send it**, and is left out of
triggers and `ctx.channels.templates()`. Static links, phone buttons and quick
replies are fine.

**When Ganju can't read your templates** (a token without
`whatsapp_business_management`), it still sends the template you name: Meta
checks it, and a run fails with Meta's own error when it isn't approved.

**Paused or disabled.** Meta pauses a template when customers block or report
its messages, and disables one that stays paused. Sends that use it fail with
that reason, and your organization's admins get an email when a template a
trigger or function uses is paused or disabled.

Templates are used from the [message the row's customer](/docs/data/triggers/)
trigger action and from [`ctx.channels.send`](/docs/data/functions/). From the
[CLI](/docs/tools/cli/), list them with their status:

```bash
ganju channel templates
```

## Troubleshooting

- **"Connect" fails right away.** The token can't act for that Phone number ID:
  check you copied the ID (not the number) from Production setup, and that the
  System User has the app and the WhatsApp account assigned.
- **The Callback URL won't verify.** The **Verify token** in Meta must match
  the one you typed in Ganju exactly.
- **Meta's Test works, real messages don't arrive.** The app isn't subscribed
  to the business account. See the end of step 4.
- **Messages stopped after a day.** You used the temporary token from API Setup.
  Generate a permanent System User token and paste it in the **Message
  templates** tab.
- **A trigger's message never reached the customer.** Past the 24-hour window,
  only an **Approved** template gets through. Check its status in **Message
  templates**.

Sources: [WhatsApp Cloud API: Get Started (Meta)](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/get-started),
[Creating a permanent WhatsApp access token](https://noem.ai/help/creating-a-permanent-access-token-for-whatsapp-business-api)

  1. In the Meta for Developers dashboard, create an app (type Business) and add the WhatsApp product.
  2. Note your Phone number ID (a numeric string, not the phone number itself) and your WhatsApp Business Account ID. For your real number, both are under WhatsApp → Production setup → Register your WhatsApp phone number, where Meta labels the account “Messaging Account ID”. The API Setup (or Try it) page shows Meta’s free test number and its own test account: use those IDs only to try things with the test number.

2. Generate a permanent access token

The temporary token on the API Setup page expires in 24 hours, so create a permanent one instead:

  1. Open Business Settings → System users and add a System user.
  2. Assign your app to it and generate a token with the whatsapp_business_messaging and whatsapp_business_management permissions. The first lets the bot send and receive messages; the second lets Ganju manage your message templates.
  3. Set it to never expire and copy it. This is your Access token.

3. Connect it in Ganju

In Channels → Add channel, pick WhatsApp, choose a Language model, and fill in the fields:

  • Access token: the permanent System User token from step 2.
  • Phone number ID: from WhatsApp → Production setup (the ID, not the display number). API Setup shows only the test number’s.
  • Verify token: any value you choose; you’ll enter the same string in Meta.
  • App secret: from App → Settings → Basic, used to verify incoming webhooks.

Select Connect. Ganju checks that the token can act for that number, then the channel’s Overview shows WhatsApp setup with a Callback URL and a copy button.

4. Point the Meta webhook at Ganju

  1. In the Meta dashboard, go to WhatsApp → Configuration → Webhooks.
  2. Paste Ganju’s Callback URL and the Verify token you chose above, and verify.
  3. Subscribe the webhook to the messages field, and to message_template_status_update if you’ll use message templates.

Once verified, messages sent to your WhatsApp number reach your assistant.

Meta only forwards a number’s messages once your app is subscribed to its WhatsApp Business account. Ganju does that for you when you connect the channel, and when you save a new token or account id in its Message templates tab. If Meta’s webhook Test button works but real messages never arrive, the subscription is missing. That happens when Meta couldn’t tell Ganju which business account the token belongs to. Fill in the account’s id in the Message templates tab, or subscribe the app yourself with the same token:

curl -X POST "https://graph.facebook.com/v25.0/<WABA_ID>/subscribed_apps" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>"

How the bot behaves in WhatsApp

  • One-to-one chats. Every conversation is a private chat with your number; the bot answers every message.
  • Commands. WhatsApp has no command menu: people type a prompt’s /command at the start of a message, followed by any text for its first variable.
  • Voice notes are transcribed and answered like text.
  • Sources: with citations on, a short Sources list of links follows the answer.
  • Files: the bot can send stored resources as attachments, within Meta’s sizes: documents up to 100 MB, images up to 5 MB, video and audio up to 16 MB.
  • Confirmations: before a tool changes something, the bot asks with Yes / No reply buttons that only that customer can use.

Long answers are split into several messages.

5. Message templates

WhatsApp only lets a business write freely to a customer within 24 hours of the customer’s last message. After that, only a message template Meta approved reaches them. Your assistant never needs one, since it always answers a message. Triggers and functions that message a customer later do, like “your order is ready” the next morning.

Open the channel and the Message templates tab. There you can:

  • See your templates with Meta’s status: Approved, In review, Rejected (with Meta’s reason), Paused, Disabled or In appeal, and when they were last synced. Refresh reads them from Meta again.
  • Create one with New template: a Name (lowercase letters, digits and underscores, like order_ready), a Language, a Category (Utility or Marketing), an optional Header and Footer (up to 60 characters each, no variables), the Message (up to 1,024 characters) and up to ten Quick replies (25 characters each). Variables are inserted with a label (“customer name”, “order number”) and become {{1}}, {{2}}, … (up to 20); Meta asks for an example value for each. A Preview shows it as a WhatsApp message, and the rules Meta rejects most for are checked before it’s sent: a variable at the very start or end, two variables side by side, too many variables for the text. Select Send for review.
  • Edit or delete one. Meta reviews an edit again and limits how often an approved template can be edited; when it refuses, its message is shown as is. Deleting removes it in Meta too, triggers and functions that send it start failing, and Meta doesn’t let you reuse the name for 30 days.

Templates need two things from Meta:

  • The WhatsApp Business account. Templates belong to the account, not to the number. Ganju asks Meta which one your token manages, so usually there’s nothing to do; when Meta can’t tell, the tab asks for the WhatsApp Business account ID (the app’s WhatsApp → Production setup → Register your WhatsApp phone number, labelled “Messaging Account ID”, or WhatsApp Manager → Account tools → Business account settings). Ganju checks it with Meta before saving it: an account that doesn’t have the channel’s number is refused, so you can’t save the test number’s account for a real number by mistake.
  • The whatsapp_business_management permission on the token, besides whatsapp_business_messaging. A token made only to send messages lacks it; the tab says so and explains how to generate a new one in Business Settings → System users. Paste it in New access token: like the first one, it’s stored encrypted and never shown again. The same box appears when the token expired or was revoked.

Review and category. Meta reviews each template in minutes to a day. It may reject one, or move it from Utility to Marketing if it reads as promotional. Keep Utility for updates the customer expects: “Your order #{{1}} is ready for pickup”. Without the message_template_status_update webhook field, Ganju still checks templates in review every hour, and the others once a day.

Cost. Meta bills template messages to your WhatsApp Business account at its own rates, and Marketing costs more than Utility. Ganju doesn’t charge for them.

What Ganju can send. Ganju fills the variables of the message itself. A template made in WhatsApp Manager with an image, video or document header, a variable in the header, or a button that takes a value (a link with a variable, a code) is listed as Ganju can’t send it, and is left out of triggers and ctx.channels.templates(). Static links, phone buttons and quick replies are fine.

When Ganju can’t read your templates (a token without whatsapp_business_management), it still sends the template you name: Meta checks it, and a run fails with Meta’s own error when it isn’t approved.

Paused or disabled. Meta pauses a template when customers block or report its messages, and disables one that stays paused. Sends that use it fail with that reason, and your organization’s admins get an email when a template a trigger or function uses is paused or disabled.

Templates are used from the message the row’s customer trigger action and from ctx.channels.send. From the CLI, list them with their status:

ganju channel templates

Troubleshooting

  • “Connect” fails right away. The token can’t act for that Phone number ID: check you copied the ID (not the number) from Production setup, and that the System User has the app and the WhatsApp account assigned.
  • The Callback URL won’t verify. The Verify token in Meta must match the one you typed in Ganju exactly.
  • Meta’s Test works, real messages don’t arrive. The app isn’t subscribed to the business account. See the end of step 4.
  • Messages stopped after a day. You used the temporary token from API Setup. Generate a permanent System User token and paste it in the Message templates tab.
  • A trigger’s message never reached the customer. Past the 24-hour window, only an Approved template gets through. Check its status in Message templates.

Sources: WhatsApp Cloud API: Get Started (Meta), Creating a permanent WhatsApp access token
