Give a project its own database (tables with typed columns, relations and search) that the assistant, your functions, the CLI and the API all read and write, with restore to any moment in the last 30 days.

Every project on **Pro** or **Enterprise** can have its own **database**: tables
with typed columns, relations between them, and full-text search. It is where a
menu, orders, bookings or stock live, so the assistant can look things up and
write them down, and your own code can too.

The assistant, your [functions](/docs/data/functions/), the
[CLI](/docs/data-api/#from-the-command-line), the [Data API](/docs/data-api/)
and the dashboard all use the same database, under the same rules. Nothing can
write to it around them.

> **Data or Resources?** Rows with fields (menus, orders, customers, bookings,
> stock) go in Data. Documents and pages the assistant reads and quotes go in
> [Resources](/docs/resources/).

## Create the database

Open **Data** in the project. With no database yet, the page explains what it
is for and shows **Name (optional)** and **Create database**. The name defaults
to the project's slug; you type it to delete the database later.

From the CLI:

```bash
ganju data create                 # named after the project's slug
ganju data create --name pizzeria
```

A project has one database. Most projects never need one, so nothing is
created until you ask. On Free, the page shows **Data is part of Pro** with
**See plans** instead.

## The Data page

Once the database exists, the page has a list on the left and the selected
item on the right:

- **Tables**, each with its row count. Search them with **Search tables**,
  create one with **+** (**New table**) or the upload icon (**New table from a
  file**).
- **Queries**: the [named queries](#named-queries).
- **Schedules**: the [schedules](/docs/data/schedules/), things that run every
  day or week at a set time.
- **Database settings** (the gear at the top): size, [time zone](#time-zone),
  download, restore and delete.

![The Data page: tables with row counts, Queries and Schedules on the left, and a table's Rows tab](/images/data-tables.webp)

A table opens on three tabs: **Rows**, **Schema** and **Triggers**.

## Tables and columns

A table holds one kind of thing (the dishes you sell, your orders, your
customers), with a column for each detail. Click **New table**, give it a
**Table name** (lowercase letters, digits and `_`, such as `order_lines`) and
its columns, or **New table from a file** to start from a spreadsheet: see
[Import a file](#import-a-file).

![The New table dialog: Table name, Label, Description and the first column](/images/data-new-table.webp)

| Type | In the dashboard | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | Text | Short text |
| `long_text` | Long text | Notes and descriptions |
| `integer` | Whole number | Whole numbers, with an optional minimum (stock can't go below 0) |
| `decimal` | Decimal number | Decimal numbers, with an optional minimum |
| `boolean` | Yes / no | Yes or no |
| `date` | Date | A day |
| `datetime` | Date and time | A moment, stored in UTC and shown in a time zone |
| `enum` | Options | One of a list of up to 100 options, such as `open`, `ready`, `delivered` |
| `json` | JSON | Any JSON value |
| `email`, `url`, `phone` | Email, URL, Phone | Text checked for that shape |
| `relation` | Relation | A row of another table (**Points at**). **When that row is deleted**: **Block the delete**, **Delete these rows too** or **Clear this column** |
| `file` | File | A file in [Resources](/docs/resources/), by its uri |

Each column has a **Name**, a **Type**, an optional **Label** (shown instead of
the name) and a **Description**, and can also be:

- **Required**: every row must have it.
- **Unique**: no two rows share a value.
- **Filterable**: indexed, so filters and sorts on it stay fast as the table
  grows. Relations and unique columns are indexed on their own.
- **Searchable**: included in full-text search. Search ignores accents, so
  "jalapeno" finds "jalapeño".

Under **More options**: a **Minimum** for numbers (writes below it are
refused) and a **Default**, used when a new row leaves the column empty.

A **File** column takes a file you **Upload** (it is kept in Resources, under
**Data attachments**) or one you **Pick from resources**. Its **Searchable in
resources** option indexes the files uploaded from then on, so the assistant's
resource search finds them. If the file is later deleted from Resources, the
row shows **File missing**.

Every row also has `id`, `created_at`, `updated_at` and a `version` that goes
up with each change. The database sets them.

The **Description** of a table and of each column tells the assistant what it
holds ("the pizzas we sell, with price and stock"). Write one: it is what the
assistant reads to know which table to use.

### Rows

The **Rows** tab is a grid. Sort and filter from each column's header, look
for text with **Search rows**, and page through the table. **Refresh** reloads
it, **Import** adds rows from a file, and **New row** opens an empty row.
Select several rows to **Delete** them together.

![A table's Rows tab: the grid, Refresh, Import and New row](/images/data-rows.webp)

Click a row to open it in a side panel, change its fields and save. The panel
shows when it was **Created** and **Updated** and its **Version**. A relation
field searches the other table as you type; it shows the other table's
**Display column** ("Margherita" instead of #12).

![The row panel: each column's field, Created, Updated and Version, with Save and Delete](/images/data-row-panel.webp)

If someone changed the row after you opened it, saving tells you who and
offers **Load latest version**. Deleting shows first what else would go: rows
that would be deleted too, cleared, or that block the delete.

### Schema

The **Schema** tab has:

- **Columns**, with their type and rules. **Add column**, or edit and drop
  one from its row. Changing a column's type checks every row first; if some
  don't fit, nothing changes and you get the list. On a table over 100,000 rows
  the change runs in the background, with its progress at the top.
- **Table settings**: name, label, description, **Display column**, and who
  sees it ([Who sees what](#who-sees-what)).
- **Source: spreadsheet**: keep the table in step with a spreadsheet. See
  [Sync a table from a spreadsheet](/docs/data/sheet-sync/).
- **Relations** to and from this table, and its **Indexes**.
- **Drop table**, which asks you to type its name.

Dropping a table or a column, or changing a type, can be undone right after:
**Undo** puts the whole database back to just before the change.

![A table's Schema tab: columns with their type and rules, and Table settings](/images/data-schema.webp)

### Index suggestions

Ganju watches how your tables are queried, without storing anything in your
database, and once a day suggests an index where one would pay off. A
suggestion shows at the top of the table's **Schema** tab with the numbers
behind it, for example: "340 queries this week filtered or sorted on `status`,
and each read about 12,000 rows to return 8."

A column is suggested when, over the last 7 days:

- it has no index;
- 50 or more queries filtered or sorted on it;
- those queries read on average 1,000 rows or more, and 20 or more for every
  row they returned.

**Add index** marks the column filterable and records it in the change log.
**Dismiss** hides the suggestion until its numbers double.

Ganju also flags an index that no query used in 30 days on a table that is
written to a lot, since every write updates the index too. It is only a flag:
nothing is removed. Turn off **Filterable** on the column if nothing needs it.

Open suggestions also show in the project's **Tool health** and in
`ganju data info`; `ganju data index add <id>` and
`ganju data index dismiss <id>` act on one.

## Import a file

**New table from a file** reads a CSV, TSV or Excel file (`.xlsx`, `.xls`)
whose first row holds the column names. It guesses each column's name and type
from the first 200 rows; fix any of them, or untick a column to leave it out,
before creating the table. A workbook with several sheets asks which **Sheet**.

**Import**, on a table's Rows tab, adds a file's rows to a table that exists:

- Each column of the file goes into the table column you choose, matched by
  name or label first. **Leave out** skips one.
- **Add the rows to the table**, or **Replace all rows in the table** (you
  type the table's name to confirm, and can **Undo import** right after).
- **Numbers in this file**: values like `28.000` read two ways, so pick how
  the file writes decimals when Ganju can't tell.
- A relation is matched by the other table's display column. **Values with
  no match** lets you pick the row each unknown value means.
- The **Preview** marks the rows with a problem; they are left out, and you
  can **Download the rows left out (CSV)** to fix and import again.

From the CLI, `ganju data import <table> <file>` does the same with CSV, Excel
and JSONL files. See [the command line](/docs/data-api/#from-the-command-line).

## Who sees what

Your own MCP clients, as the project's owner, the dashboard, the CLI and your
functions see every table and every row. **Channel bots** (the assistant
answering customers on WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack or Discord) see only what
each table's settings allow. In the table's **Schema** tab, under **Table
settings**:

- **Assistant access (channel bots)**:
  - **None**: bots don't see the table.
  - **Read** (the default): bots can look rows up, but not change them.
  - **Read and add**: bots can look rows up and add new ones, such as orders.
  - **Full**: bots can add, change and delete rows. Deletes still ask the
    customer to confirm.
- **Each customer sees only their own rows**: on channels, a row is tied to the
  customer whose conversation wrote it, so "my orders" means theirs. A bot
  never reads another customer's rows.
- **Keep row history** (on by default): who changed each row and when, for 90
  days. Read it with `ganju data history <table> <id>` or the
  [Data API](/docs/data-api/#history-restore-and-export).

Text a customer wrote into a row is treated as outside content, like a web
page: the assistant reads it, but doesn't follow instructions in it.

## The assistant's data tools

Once the project has a database, the assistant gets these tools, on every
channel and MCP client, without installing anything:

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `data-describe` | Lists the tables and columns it can see |
| `data-query` | Finds, filters, searches, counts and sums rows, or runs a [named query](#named-queries) |
| `data-write` | Adds, changes and deletes rows, several at once, all or nothing |
| `data-admin` | Creates and changes tables, columns and named queries, imports and exports. Only for the organization's admins, from their own MCP clients |

A channel bot's tools only reach the tables, and the rows, its settings allow.
On a channel, changing or deleting rows asks the customer first; adding rows,
such as placing an order, doesn't.

## Build it with the Assistant

The project's [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) can set the database up for you in
plain words: "make a table of the pizzas we sell with price and stock", "email
me each new order", "every night at 9, send me today's orders". It can:

- create the database, and set its [time zone](#time-zone);
- create, change and drop tables and columns, and add, change or delete rows
  (up to 200 at a time);
- save and delete [named queries](#named-queries), and run one to show you the
  answer;
- create, turn on or off and delete [triggers](/docs/data/triggers/) and
  [schedules](/docs/data/schedules/), and send you a test of an email before it
  is due.

Nothing changes until you apply it. The Assistant proposes a list of changes,
each in a plain line; you review it and click **Apply**, and anything that
deletes asks you to type the name of what goes. Data changes applied this way
can be undone with **Undo**. Undoing a dropped table or column, a type change,
or deleted rows puts the whole database back to just before that change, so
anything written since is replaced; the change says so before you apply it.

If a developer manages the tables from code with `ganju data schema push`, the
Assistant warns that their next push will put back a change made there.

## Named queries

Some reports the filters can't express: sales per dish last week, the customers
who haven't ordered in a month. Write those once as a **named query**: one
`SELECT` (or `WITH … SELECT`) over your tables, with parameters like `:from`.

```sql
SELECT m.name AS dish, sum(l.quantity) AS units, sum(l.quantity * l.price) AS revenue
FROM order_lines l
JOIN menu m ON m.id = l.dish
JOIN orders o ON o.id = l."order"
WHERE o.created_at >= :from AND o.created_at < :to
GROUP BY m.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC
```

Open **Queries** on the Data page and click **New query**. Give it a **Name**
(lowercase letters, digits and `_`), a **Description** and the SQL. Each
parameter under **Parameters** has a type (`text`, `integer`, `decimal`,
`boolean`, `date` or `datetime`) and can be **Required**; a value is checked
against its type before the query runs. A query is checked when it is saved:
it can only read, and only your tables. **Reads** lists the tables it reads,
and if it reads a whole large table, the dialog says which column to index.
**Run** tries it with values you type.

![The Queries view with its description and the New query button](/images/data-queries.webp)

A saved query runs by name from your functions (`ctx.data.run`), the CLI
(`ganju data run`), the API (`POST /query/:name/run`), a
[schedule](/docs/data/schedules/) and, if you turn on **The assistant can run
it**, from `data-query`. A query that reads a table where each customer sees
only their own rows is never offered to channel bots, since it would see every
customer's rows.

A run returns up to 100 rows by default, 500 at most, and 1 MB. A query that
would read the whole of a table over 200,000 rows is refused: filter on an
indexed column.

A project holds up to 100 named queries, each up to 10,000 characters of SQL
and 20 parameters. They are kept in `ganju.data.json` with the schema too,
under `"queries"`.

## Time zone

**Database settings → Time zone** sets the zone dates and times come back in
for the assistant, your functions and the API when they don't ask for one. A
date and time written without an offset is read in it too. It is also the zone
[schedules](/docs/data/schedules/) run in, and the midnight a
[time trigger](/docs/data/triggers/#time-triggers) on a date column counts
from. Without one, it is UTC. The dashboard always shows times in your
browser's zone.

![The Database settings dialog: size, Time zone, Download a copy and Restore to a point in time](/images/data-settings.webp)

From the CLI:

```bash
ganju data time-zone                  # prints it
ganju data time-zone America/Bogota
ganju data time-zone --clear          # back to UTC
```

Through the API it is `PATCH` on the database with `{ "timeZone":
"America/Bogota" }`, or `null` for UTC. The Assistant can set it too.

## Restore and download

All three are in **Database settings**:

- **Restore to a point in time**: bring the whole database back to how it was
  at any moment in the last 30 days. Everything written after that moment is
  replaced, and you can **Undo restore** right after. Trigger events still
  waiting to be sent are dropped, and the rows a restore brings back don't fire
  triggers.
- **Restore points**: before a large change, take one with
  `ganju data checkpoint` or `POST /checkpoint`, and restore to it to undo
  exactly that change.
- **Download a copy**: every table as its own JSONL or CSV file, plus the
  schema, prepared in the background. From the CLI:
  `ganju data export --format csv --out backup/`.

## Delete the database

**Database settings → Delete database** removes every table and row; you type
the database's name to confirm. For 7 days you can restore it (**Restore
database** on the Data page, or `ganju data restore`), or download a copy.
After that it goes for good. What the assistant and your functions read and
write there stops working at once.

## Limits

| | Per database |
| --- | --- |
| Size | 9 GB. Past it, writes that add data are refused; reads, deletes and downloads keep working |
| Tables | 50 |
| Columns | 93 per table |
| Options in an `enum` | 100 |
| Rows per page | 500, or 1 MB |
| One insert | 500 rows |
| One write | 50 operations and 5,000 rows, all or nothing |
| Named queries | 100 |
| Triggers and schedules | 50 in all, of which up to 10 time triggers and 5 schedules |
| Row history | 90 days |
| Restore | Any moment in the last 30 days |
| After a delete | 7 days to restore |

## Plans and billing

Data is part of **Pro** and **Enterprise**. If the organization moves to Free,
its databases stay, **read-only**: you can read and download everything, the
assistant and your functions can still read, and nothing can be changed until
you upgrade. Triggers and schedules pause.

A database whose organization stays on Free is deleted after a notice:

- **Day 30 on Free:** the owner and the admins get an email listing each
  database (project, size, tables), saying it is read-only and the date it will
  be deleted, with links to upgrade and to download a copy.
- **3 days before that date (day 41):** a reminder.
- **From day 44:** Ganju deletes it by hand. A copy is kept for 90 days; write
  to support if you need it.

Moving back to Pro or Enterprise at any point stops this and keeps everything.
Downloading a copy doesn't stop it. A Pro database that is simply idle is never
deleted.

**Settings → Billing & plan** shows a **Data** block for the current period: storage
(checked every hour) and the period's peak, rows read and written, requests and
trigger runs. This usage is measured but not billed yet; a price will be set
once there are real usage numbers, and announced before it applies.

  • Required: every row must have it.
  • Unique: no two rows share a value.
  • Filterable: indexed, so filters and sorts on it stay fast as the table grows. Relations and unique columns are indexed on their own.
  • Searchable: included in full-text search. Search ignores accents, so “jalapeno” finds “jalapeño”.

Under More options: a Minimum for numbers (writes below it are refused) and a Default, used when a new row leaves the column empty.

A File column takes a file you Upload (it is kept in Resources, under Data attachments) or one you Pick from resources. Its Searchable in resources option indexes the files uploaded from then on, so the assistant’s resource search finds them. If the file is later deleted from Resources, the row shows File missing.

Every row also has id, created_at, updated_at and a version that goes up with each change. The database sets them.

The Description of a table and of each column tells the assistant what it holds (“the pizzas we sell, with price and stock”). Write one: it is what the assistant reads to know which table to use.

Rows

The Rows tab is a grid. Sort and filter from each column’s header, look for text with Search rows, and page through the table. Refresh reloads it, Import adds rows from a file, and New row opens an empty row. Select several rows to Delete them together.

Click a row to open it in a side panel, change its fields and save. The panel shows when it was Created and Updated and its Version. A relation field searches the other table as you type; it shows the other table’s Display column (“Margherita” instead of #12).

If someone changed the row after you opened it, saving tells you who and offers Load latest version. Deleting shows first what else would go: rows that would be deleted too, cleared, or that block the delete.

Schema

The Schema tab has:

  • Columns, with their type and rules. Add column, or edit and drop one from its row. Changing a column’s type checks every row first; if some don’t fit, nothing changes and you get the list. On a table over 100,000 rows the change runs in the background, with its progress at the top.
  • Table settings: name, label, description, Display column, and who sees it (Who sees what).
  • Source: spreadsheet: keep the table in step with a spreadsheet. See Sync a table from a spreadsheet.
  • Relations to and from this table, and its Indexes.
  • Drop table, which asks you to type its name.

Dropping a table or a column, or changing a type, can be undone right after: Undo puts the whole database back to just before the change.

Index suggestions

Ganju watches how your tables are queried, without storing anything in your database, and once a day suggests an index where one would pay off. A suggestion shows at the top of the table’s Schema tab with the numbers behind it, for example: “340 queries this week filtered or sorted on status, and each read about 12,000 rows to return 8.”

A column is suggested when, over the last 7 days:

  • it has no index;
  • 50 or more queries filtered or sorted on it;
  • those queries read on average 1,000 rows or more, and 20 or more for every row they returned.

Add index marks the column filterable and records it in the change log. Dismiss hides the suggestion until its numbers double.

Ganju also flags an index that no query used in 30 days on a table that is written to a lot, since every write updates the index too. It is only a flag: nothing is removed. Turn off Filterable on the column if nothing needs it.

Open suggestions also show in the project’s Tool health and in ganju data info; ganju data index add <id> and ganju data index dismiss <id> act on one.

Import a file

New table from a file reads a CSV, TSV or Excel file (.xlsx, .xls) whose first row holds the column names. It guesses each column’s name and type from the first 200 rows; fix any of them, or untick a column to leave it out, before creating the table. A workbook with several sheets asks which Sheet.

Import, on a table’s Rows tab, adds a file’s rows to a table that exists:

  • Each column of the file goes into the table column you choose, matched by name or label first. Leave out skips one.
  • Add the rows to the table, or Replace all rows in the table (you type the table’s name to confirm, and can Undo import right after).
  • Numbers in this file: values like 28.000 read two ways, so pick how the file writes decimals when Ganju can’t tell.
  • A relation is matched by the other table’s display column. Values with no match lets you pick the row each unknown value means.
  • The Preview marks the rows with a problem; they are left out, and you can Download the rows left out (CSV) to fix and import again.

From the CLI, ganju data import <table> <file> does the same with CSV, Excel and JSONL files. See the command line.

Who sees what

Your own MCP clients, as the project’s owner, the dashboard, the CLI and your functions see every table and every row. Channel bots (the assistant answering customers on WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack or Discord) see only what each table’s settings allow. In the table’s Schema tab, under Table settings:

  • Assistant access (channel bots):
    • None: bots don’t see the table.
    • Read (the default): bots can look rows up, but not change them.
    • Read and add: bots can look rows up and add new ones, such as orders.
    • Full: bots can add, change and delete rows. Deletes still ask the customer to confirm.
  • Each customer sees only their own rows: on channels, a row is tied to the customer whose conversation wrote it, so “my orders” means theirs. A bot never reads another customer’s rows.
  • Keep row history (on by default): who changed each row and when, for 90 days. Read it with ganju data history <table> <id> or the Data API.

Text a customer wrote into a row is treated as outside content, like a web page: the assistant reads it, but doesn’t follow instructions in it.

The assistant’s data tools

Once the project has a database, the assistant gets these tools, on every channel and MCP client, without installing anything:

Tool What it does
data-describe Lists the tables and columns it can see
data-query Finds, filters, searches, counts and sums rows, or runs a named query
data-write Adds, changes and deletes rows, several at once, all or nothing
data-admin Creates and changes tables, columns and named queries, imports and exports. Only for the organization’s admins, from their own MCP clients

A channel bot’s tools only reach the tables, and the rows, its settings allow. On a channel, changing or deleting rows asks the customer first; adding rows, such as placing an order, doesn’t.

Build it with the Assistant

The project’s Assistant can set the database up for you in plain words: “make a table of the pizzas we sell with price and stock”, “email me each new order”, “every night at 9, send me today’s orders”. It can:

  • create the database, and set its time zone;
  • create, change and drop tables and columns, and add, change or delete rows (up to 200 at a time);
  • save and delete named queries, and run one to show you the answer;
  • create, turn on or off and delete triggers and schedules, and send you a test of an email before it is due.

Nothing changes until you apply it. The Assistant proposes a list of changes, each in a plain line; you review it and click Apply, and anything that deletes asks you to type the name of what goes. Data changes applied this way can be undone with Undo. Undoing a dropped table or column, a type change, or deleted rows puts the whole database back to just before that change, so anything written since is replaced; the change says so before you apply it.

If a developer manages the tables from code with ganju data schema push, the Assistant warns that their next push will put back a change made there.

Named queries

Some reports the filters can’t express: sales per dish last week, the customers who haven’t ordered in a month. Write those once as a named query: one SELECT (or WITH … SELECT) over your tables, with parameters like :from.

SELECT m.name AS dish, sum(l.quantity) AS units, sum(l.quantity * l.price) AS revenue
FROM order_lines l
JOIN menu m ON m.id = l.dish
JOIN orders o ON o.id = l."order"
WHERE o.created_at >= :from AND o.created_at < :to
GROUP BY m.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC

Open Queries on the Data page and click New query. Give it a Name (lowercase letters, digits and _), a Description and the SQL. Each parameter under Parameters has a type (text, integer, decimal, boolean, date or datetime) and can be Required; a value is checked against its type before the query runs. A query is checked when it is saved: it can only read, and only your tables. Reads lists the tables it reads, and if it reads a whole large table, the dialog says which column to index. Run tries it with values you type.

A saved query runs by name from your functions (ctx.data.run), the CLI (ganju data run), the API (POST /query/:name/run), a schedule and, if you turn on The assistant can run it, from data-query. A query that reads a table where each customer sees only their own rows is never offered to channel bots, since it would see every customer’s rows.

A run returns up to 100 rows by default, 500 at most, and 1 MB. A query that would read the whole of a table over 200,000 rows is refused: filter on an indexed column.

A project holds up to 100 named queries, each up to 10,000 characters of SQL and 20 parameters. They are kept in ganju.data.json with the schema too, under "queries".

Time zone

Database settings → Time zone sets the zone dates and times come back in for the assistant, your functions and the API when they don’t ask for one. A date and time written without an offset is read in it too. It is also the zone schedules run in, and the midnight a time trigger on a date column counts from. Without one, it is UTC. The dashboard always shows times in your browser’s zone.

From the CLI:

ganju data time-zone                  # prints it
ganju data time-zone America/Bogota
ganju data time-zone --clear          # back to UTC

Through the API it is PATCH on the database with { "timeZone": "America/Bogota" }, or null for UTC. The Assistant can set it too.

Restore and download

All three are in Database settings:

  • Restore to a point in time: bring the whole database back to how it was at any moment in the last 30 days. Everything written after that moment is replaced, and you can Undo restore right after. Trigger events still waiting to be sent are dropped, and the rows a restore brings back don’t fire triggers.
  • Restore points: before a large change, take one with ganju data checkpoint or POST /checkpoint, and restore to it to undo exactly that change.
  • Download a copy: every table as its own JSONL or CSV file, plus the schema, prepared in the background. From the CLI: ganju data export --format csv --out backup/.

Delete the database

Database settings → Delete database removes every table and row; you type the database’s name to confirm. For 7 days you can restore it (Restore database on the Data page, or ganju data restore), or download a copy. After that it goes for good. What the assistant and your functions read and write there stops working at once.

Limits

Per database
Size 9 GB. Past it, writes that add data are refused; reads, deletes and downloads keep working
Tables 50
Columns 93 per table
Options in an enum 100
Rows per page 500, or 1 MB
One insert 500 rows
One write 50 operations and 5,000 rows, all or nothing
Named queries 100
Triggers and schedules 50 in all, of which up to 10 time triggers and 5 schedules
Row history 90 days
Restore Any moment in the last 30 days
After a delete 7 days to restore

Plans and billing

Data is part of Pro and Enterprise. If the organization moves to Free, its databases stay, read-only: you can read and download everything, the assistant and your functions can still read, and nothing can be changed until you upgrade. Triggers and schedules pause.

A database whose organization stays on Free is deleted after a notice:

  • Day 30 on Free: the owner and the admins get an email listing each database (project, size, tables), saying it is read-only and the date it will be deleted, with links to upgrade and to download a copy.
  • 3 days before that date (day 41): a reminder.
  • From day 44: Ganju deletes it by hand. A copy is kept for 90 days; write to support if you need it.

Moving back to Pro or Enterprise at any point stops this and keeps everything. Downloading a copy doesn’t stop it. A Pro database that is simply idle is never deleted.

Settings → Billing & plan shows a Data block for the current period: storage (checked every hour) and the period’s peak, rows read and written, requests and trigger runs. This usage is measured but not billed yet; a price will be set once there are real usage numbers, and announced before it applies.

Next

  • Data from functions: ctx.data and ctx.channels in your own code.
  • Triggers and webhooks: run something when rows change.
  • Schedules: run something every day or week at a set time.
  • Sync a table from a spreadsheet: keep a menu, prices or stock in step with a Google Sheet, an Excel file or a CSV.
  • Data API: the same database over HTTP, and the ganju data commands.

Manage a project's database over HTTP (create tables, insert and search rows, write orders safely, run named queries, manage triggers and schedules, restore and export) with a personal access token, or from the ganju data commands.

Every project on **Pro** or **Enterprise** can have its own **database**: tables
with typed columns, relations between them, and full-text search. The **Data
API** is how you manage it from your own code. The dashboard and the CLI use the
same routes, so anything they can do, your code can do too. [Data](/docs/data/)
explains the database itself.

The full reference is an OpenAPI file:
[`https://api.ganju.ai/openapi/data.json`](https://api.ganju.ai/openapi/data.json).
Load it into Postman, Insomnia or a code generator.

## Authenticate

Create a personal access token for the project with the CLI, and send it as a
bearer token:

```bash
ganju token create "orders sync" --expires 90   # or --expires never
```

The token is printed once. `ganju token list` shows your tokens and
`ganju token revoke "orders sync"` stops one.

Every route lives under the project's database. The organization and project
ids are in your `ganju.json` once you've run `ganju link`:

```bash
export GANJU_TOKEN=ganju_pat_...
export DATA=https://api.ganju.ai/organization/<organizationId>/project/<projectId>/artifact/data
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GANJU_TOKEN" $DATA
```

A token only reaches the project it was made for. Each token can make 120
requests a minute to each route, within 300 a minute for your account in all.
Past that, the API answers `429` with a `Retry-After` header: wait a minute and
try again.

The examples below write `curl ...` for
`curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GANJU_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json"`.

## The database

| Route | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /` | The database: `status`, size, `timeZone`, its tables, open index suggestions (`indexAdvice`) and a table copy in progress (`copy`). `database` is `null` when the project has none |
| `POST /` | Create it: `{ "name"? }`, the project's slug by default. Safe to repeat. While a deleted database can still be restored, this is refused unless you send `"replaceDeleted": true`, which gives up that restore |
| `PATCH /` | Its settings: `{ "timeZone": "America/Bogota" }`, or `null` for UTC |
| `DELETE /` | Delete it: `{ "confirmName": "<database name>" }`. It can be restored for 7 days |
| `POST /restore` | Undo a delete, within those 7 days |

(`/` here is `$DATA` itself.)

```bash
curl -X POST ... $DATA -d '{ "name": "pizzeria" }'
curl -X PATCH ... $DATA -d '{ "timeZone": "America/Bogota" }'
```

The **time zone** is the one dates and times come back in for anyone who
doesn't ask for another, and the one a date and time without an offset is read
in. A row read can ask for its own with `?timeZone=Europe/Madrid`.

## Create a table

```bash
curl -X POST ... $DATA/table -d '{
  "name": "menu",
  "label": "Menu",
  "description": "The pizzas we sell, with price and stock",
  "displayColumn": "name",
  "access": "read",
  "columns": [
    { "name": "name",  "type": "text",    "required": true, "searchable": true },
    { "name": "price", "type": "integer", "min": 0 },
    { "name": "stock", "type": "integer", "min": 0, "default": 0 },
    { "name": "size",  "type": "enum",    "values": ["30cm", "40cm"] }
  ]
}'
```

A table takes:

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Lowercase letters, digits and `_`, starting with a letter, up to 63 characters |
| `label`, `description` | Shown instead of the name, and what the assistant reads (up to 100 and 300 characters) |
| `displayColumn` | What a relation to this table shows: `"name"` instead of the id |
| `access` | What channel bots may do: `none`, `read` (the default), `add` or `full`. See [Who sees what](/docs/data/#who-sees-what) |
| `customerScoped` | `true`: each customer sees only their own rows |
| `history` | Keep row history; `true` by default |
| `source` | Sync it from a spreadsheet: `{ "uri", "sheet"?, "key" }`. See [Sync a table from a spreadsheet](/docs/data/sheet-sync/) |
| `columns` | Up to 93 |

and each column:

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `type` | The type is `text`, `long_text`, `integer`, `decimal`, `boolean`, `date`, `datetime`, `enum`, `json`, `email`, `url`, `phone`, `relation` or `file` |
| `label`, `description` | As for a table |
| `required`, `unique`, `filterable`, `searchable` | `true` or `false` |
| `values` | For `enum`: the options, up to 100 |
| `table`, `onDelete` | For `relation`: the table it points at, and what deleting that row does: `restrict`, `cascade` or `set_null` |
| `min` | For `integer` and `decimal`: the lowest value allowed |
| `default` | Used when a new row leaves it empty |

Every row also has `id`, `created_at`, `updated_at` and `version`. The database
sets these; you never send them.

## Insert, read and search rows

```bash
# One row, or up to 500 at once with "rows"
curl -X POST ... $DATA/table/menu/row -d '{ "values": { "name": "Margherita", "price": 28000, "stock": 10 } }'
curl -X POST ... $DATA/table/menu/row -d '{ "rows": [{ "name": "Hawaiian" }, { "name": "Pepperoni" }] }'

# One row
curl ... $DATA/table/menu/row/12

# Filter, sort, search and page
curl ... "$DATA/table/menu/row?where=%7B%22price%22%3A%7B%22lt%22%3A30000%7D%7D&sort=-price&limit=50"
curl ... "$DATA/table/menu/row?q=pizza"
```

An insert answers `{ "ids": [...] }`. A list answers `{ table, rows, total,
nextCursor }`:

- **`where`** is JSON: `{"status":"open"}`, `{"price":{"lt":30000}}`,
  `{"name":{"contains":"pizza"}}`. The operators are `eq`, `ne`, `gt`, `gte`,
  `lt`, `lte`, `in`, `notIn`, `contains`, `startsWith` and `isNull`; combine
  them with `and` / `or`, and filter on a related row's column with
  `"customer.name"`.
- **`sort`** is a list of columns. Put `-` in front of a column to sort
  descending: `-created_at,name`.
- **`q`** searches the columns marked `searchable`, best matches first.
- **`include`** brings in related rows: `include=customer`.
- **`limit`** is 20 by default, up to 500. A page holds up to 500 rows and
  1 MB. When there are more, the answer has `nextCursor`; send it back as
  `cursor` to read the next page. `total` comes on the first page.
- **`timeZone`** returns dates and times in that zone instead of the
  database's.

A relation comes back as `{ id, label }`. A file column comes back as
`{ uri, id, title, mimeType }`, or `{ uri, missing: true }` when no resource has
the uri any more; write it with the uri.

In JavaScript:

```js
const res = await fetch(`${DATA}/table/menu/row?q=${encodeURIComponent('pizza')}`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.GANJU_TOKEN}` }
});
const { rows, nextCursor } = await res.json();
```

## Change and delete rows without losing edits

Each row has a `version` that goes up by one with every change. Send back the
version you read:

```bash
curl -X PATCH ... $DATA/table/menu/row/12 -d '{ "set": { "price": 30000 }, "version": 3 }'
curl -X PATCH ... $DATA/table/menu/row/12 -d '{ "set": { "stock": { "decrement": 2 } } }'
curl -X DELETE ... $DATA/table/menu/row/12 -d '{ "version": 4 }'
```

A change answers `{ row }`, and a delete `{ deleted }`. A number can change
relative to itself with `{ "increment": n }` or `{ "decrement": n }`.

Someone may change the row after you read it. If they do, the answer is **409**,
with the row as it is now in `details.current` and who changed it in
`details.updatedBy`. Reload and try again. To overwrite their change, send the
request without `version`.

Before deleting, you can ask what the delete would do to the rows that point
at it. Nothing is deleted:

```bash
curl -X POST ... $DATA/table/orders/delete-preview -d '{ "ids": [12, 13] }'
```

Leave out `ids` to preview deleting every row. The answer lists each column
that points at a deleted row, with how many rows it would delete (`cascade`),
clear (`set_null`) or that refuse the delete (`restrict`). Cascades are
followed all the way down, and `depth` says how many cascades away each one
is. `blocked` is true when a restrict would refuse the delete. Past 200,000
affected rows, `truncated` is true and each count is a lower bound.

## Write an order safely

`POST /write` takes a list of up to 50 inserts, updates and deletes across
tables, touching up to 5,000 rows. They all apply together, or none of them do.
A later step can use the id of an earlier insert as `{ "$ref": <step> }`, in its
values or as the `id` of the row it updates or deletes. An update or delete
names one row by `id`, or the rows a `where` matches; `expect` says how many
rows must change. An update can change a number relative to itself, with a
guard:

```bash
curl -X POST ... $DATA/write -d '{
  "operations": [
    { "op": "insert", "table": "orders", "values": { "customer": "Ana" } },
    { "op": "insert", "table": "order_lines",
      "values": { "order": { "$ref": 0 }, "product": 12, "qty": 2 } },
    { "op": "update", "table": "menu", "id": 12,
      "set": { "stock": { "decrement": 2 } }, "where": { "stock": { "gte": 2 } } }
  ]
}'
```

It answers `{ results }`, one per step: `{ op, table, id }` for an insert
(`ids` for several rows), `{ op, table, changed }` for an update or delete.

If two customers order the last pizza at the same time, one order goes through.
The other gets a 409 ("changed 0 rows, expected 1"), and none of its steps are
written.

## Change the tables

| Route | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /table` | Tables, columns and relations, and each synced table's last `sync` |
| `POST /table` | Create a table |
| `PATCH /table/:table` | Rename it, change its label, description or settings. A `null` puts a setting back to its default |
| `POST /table/:table/sync` | Sync a table that has a `source` from its spreadsheet now (five a minute) |
| `DELETE /table/:table` | Drop it. Send `{ "confirmName": "<table>" }` |
| `POST /table/:table/column` | Add a column |
| `PATCH /table/:table/column/:column` | Rename or change a column, including its type |
| `DELETE /table/:table/column/:column` | Drop a column |
| `POST /advice/:adviceId` | Add a suggested index: marks the column filterable |
| `DELETE /advice/:adviceId` | Dismiss an index suggestion until its numbers double |
| `DELETE /copy` | Dismiss a failed table copy |
| `GET /change` | The log of these changes: who, what, when (`?limit=`, `?cursor=`) |

A table's `source` (`{ "uri", "sheet", "key" }`) keeps its rows in step with a
spreadsheet or CSV in Resources, and makes them read-only to every other
writer; `{ "source": null }` stops it. See
[Sync a table from a spreadsheet](/docs/data/sheet-sync/).

Changing a column's type checks every value first. If any value doesn't fit, the
change is refused and the answer lists the first 10 rows that don't. Dropping a
table or a column, and changing a type, answers with a `bookmark`. To undo the
change, restore to it.

A type change copies the table, and so does dropping a relation column. Up to
100,000 rows that happens in the request. On a larger table the copy runs in
the background. The answer has `copy`, with how many rows are copied so far,
and the table keeps its old columns until the copy is done. Meanwhile reads
and writes to other tables work as usual. A 409 answers table changes, and
writes that would change the copied table's rows: inserts, updates and
deletes on it, and deletes in a table it points at with cascade or set null.
`GET` on the database
shows its progress in `copy`. If the copy fails, the table is left as it was
and `copy` shows the `error` until you dismiss it with `DELETE /copy`.

## History, restore and export

- **`GET /table/:table/row/:id/history`**: every change to a row in the last 90
  days, newest first, with who made it (`?limit=` up to 100, `?cursor=`). A
  change made with a token is shown as `cli:<token id>`.
- **`POST /checkpoint`**: a restore point at this exact moment. It answers
  with a `bookmark`; take one before a large change, such as replacing a
  table's rows, to undo exactly that change later.
- **`POST /restore-point`**: put the whole database back as it was at a time in
  the last 30 days (`{ "timestamp": "2026-10-20T15:00:00-05:00" }`), or at the
  `bookmark` a checkpoint, a dropped table or column, a type change or an
  earlier restore answered with (`{ "bookmark": "…" }`). The answer has an
  `undoBookmark` that undoes the restore. Calls in flight while it restarts
  fail.
- **`POST /export`**: start a copy of the database, `{ "format": "jsonl" }` or
  `"csv"`: one file per table, plus `schema.json`. It answers `{ exportId,
  status }`. Poll `GET /export` (or `?exportId=`) until its `status` is
  `done`, then download each file with
  `GET /export/file?exportId=<id>&table=<table>`. Leave out `table` to get
  `schema.json`. Exports also work during the 7 days after you delete the
  database.

## Named queries, triggers and schedules

| Route | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /query` | Named queries, each with its SQL, parameters, the tables it reads and its plan (`SCAN orders` means it reads the whole table) |
| `POST /query` | Save one: `{ "name", "description", "sql", "params", "assistant" }`. Saving under an existing name replaces it |
| `DELETE /query/:name` | Delete one |
| `POST /query/:name/run` | Run one: `{ "params": { "from": "2026-10-01T00:00:00-05:00" }, "limit": 100 }`. Answers `{ query, rows, truncated? }` |
| `GET /trigger` | Triggers and schedules, and `pending`: events not yet sent |
| `POST /trigger` | Save a trigger or a schedule |
| `PATCH /trigger/:name` | Turn it on or off: `{ "enabled": false }` |
| `DELETE /trigger/:name` | Delete one |
| `POST /trigger/deploy` | Replace the triggers a CLI deploy made: `{ "triggers": [...] }` |
| `GET /trigger/:name/run` | Its recent runs, up to 50 |
| `POST /trigger/:name/run/:runId/retry` | Send a failed or skipped run again |
| `GET /trigger/test-send` | Your own chats with the project's bots, where a test can go |
| `POST /trigger/test-send` | Send a test of a customer message or an email, built from a row |

Each query parameter in `params` is `{ "name", "type", "description"?,
"required"? }`, with `type` one of `text`, `integer`, `decimal`, `boolean`,
`date` or `datetime`. A run returns up to `limit` rows (100 by default, 500 at
most) and 1 MB.

```bash
curl -X POST ... $DATA/query -d '{
  "name": "sales_by_dish",
  "description": "Units and revenue per dish between two times",
```

## From the command line

The CLI's `ganju data` commands call these same routes, for the project in
`ganju.json`. Install it with `npm install -g @ganju/cli`, then `ganju login`
and `ganju link`. On a machine with no browser, set `GANJU_API_TOKEN` to a
personal access token instead (`ganju token create`): the CLI's writes are then
recorded as `cli:<token id>`, and it waits out a `429` on its own. Run
`ganju data` alone to list every command. Most commands take `--json` for
output a script can read.

### The database

```bash
ganju data create [--name <name>]       # Pro and Enterprise
ganju data info                         # status, size, time zone, tables, index suggestions
ganju data time-zone                    # prints the database's time zone
ganju data time-zone America/Bogota     # the zone dates and times come back in
ganju data time-zone --clear            # back to UTC
ganju data changes                      # the schema change log
ganju data checkpoint                   # a bookmark of right now, alone on stdout
ganju data export --format csv --out backup/   # jsonl by default
ganju data copy                         # a table copy running in the background
ganju data copy wait
ganju data copy dismiss                 # clear a failed one

# Index suggestions: add one, or dismiss it until its numbers double
ganju data index add <id>
ganju data index dismiss <id>
```

`ganju data create --replace` starts a new database while a deleted one can
still be restored, giving up that restore.

### Tables and columns

```bash
ganju data tables
ganju data table create menu --schema menu.json
ganju data table rename menu dishes
ganju data table sync menu              # read a synced table's sheet again now
ganju data column add menu notes long_text
ganju data column add menu size enum --input '{"values":["30cm","40cm"]}'
ganju data column rename menu notes description
ganju data column change menu price --input '{"type":"decimal"}' --yes
```

`table create` takes a file with `{ "columns": [...] }`, a list of columns, or
a `ganju.data.json` that has the table. `column change` and `column rm` wait for
a table copy to finish unless you pass `--no-wait`.

### Rows

```bash
ganju data rows menu --where 'price<30000' --where size=30cm --sort -price --limit 50
ganju data rows menu --search pizza --json
ganju data rows orders --include customer --all
ganju data get menu 12 [--include <relations>]
ganju data insert menu --input '{"name":"Margherita","price":28000}'
ganju data insert menu --input-file menu.jsonl
ganju data update menu 12 --input '{"stock":{"decrement":2}}' --version 3
ganju data delete orders 7 8 --yes
ganju data history orders 7
ganju data write --input-file ops.json  # {"operations":[...]}, all or nothing
```

`--where` takes `column=value` and `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `~` (contains),
`^=` (starts with). `status=[open,done]` matches any of the values, and
`note=null` finds empty ones. On a text, phone, email, URL, enum or date column
the value is always text, so `phone=3001234567` works as typed; elsewhere,
quotes keep a value as text: `code="007"`. Repeat `--where` to require several
conditions, or pass the JSON `where` itself: `--where '{"price":{"lt":30000}}'`.
`--limit` is up to 500 a page; `--cursor` reads the next page and `--all`
reads every page.

`delete` shows what a cascade would also remove, and refuses when a restrict
blocks it.

### Import a file

```bash
# A CSV, Excel or JSONL file, matched to the columns the way the dashboard does
ganju data import menu menu.csv
ganju data import menu menu.xlsx --sheet Menu
ganju data import menu menu.csv --map 'Price (COP)=price'
ganju data import menu menu.csv --decimal-mark ,
ganju data import menu menu.csv --replace --yes --confirm menu
```

`import` matches headers to columns by name or label (`--map` points one at a
column), reads numbers like "28.000" (`--decimal-mark` says how the file writes
decimals when it's unclear), matches relations by the name the other table
shows, and puts the rows it refused, with why, in a CSV you can fix and import
again (`--out` names it). A `--replace` refused as a whole changes nothing and
writes the whole file back with each row to blame marked. A date and time in
the file without an offset is read in your computer's time zone.

### Named queries

```bash
ganju data queries                              # the saved queries and what they read
ganju data query save --input-file sales.json   # { name, description, sql, params, assistant }
ganju data run sales_by_dish --input '{"from":"2026-10-01T00:00:00-05:00","to":"2026-11-01T00:00:00-05:00"}'
ganju data query rm sales_by_dish --yes
```

`run` returns up to `--limit` rows (100 by default, 500 at most), with dates
and times in your computer's time zone.

### Schema as code

`ganju data schema pull` writes the database's tables, and its named queries
under `"queries"`, to `ganju.data.json`, in the same shape as an export's
`schema.json`. Edit it and review it like code. `ganju data schema diff` shows
what would change, and `ganju data schema push` applies it (`--schema <file>`
uses another file):

```bash
ganju data schema diff
+ create table orders (customer, status)
+ add column menu.notes long_text
~ change table menu: label "Menu"
- change menu.price: type "decimal" (copies the table) (needs --yes)
- drop column menu.code (needs --yes)
```

Tables and columns are matched by name, and new tables are created in an
order where every relation's target exists first. New tables and columns and
changed settings are applied straight away. Drops and type changes are listed
and applied only with `--yes`, after a restore point that undoes them. A rename
in the file reads as a drop and an add: rename with
`ganju data column rename` or `ganju data table rename` instead.

Each push is noted in the change log, so the project's Assistant warns that a
change made in the dashboard will be put back by the next push.

Triggers and schedules aren't in `ganju.data.json`: list them under
`"triggers"` in `ganju.json` and `ganju deploy` publishes them. See
[Deploy triggers with the CLI](/docs/data/triggers/#deploy-triggers-with-the-cli).

### Destructive commands

Anything that drops, deletes or rewrites data needs `--yes` (`-y`). Dropping
the database or a table also needs its name, typed with `--confirm`:

```bash
ganju data column rm menu code --yes
ganju data table rm orders --yes --confirm orders
ganju data drop --yes --confirm acme-support
ganju data restore                              # undo the delete, within 7 days
ganju data restore --at 2026-10-30T09:15:00-05:00 --yes
ganju data restore --bookmark <bookmark> --yes  # the undo a drop printed
```

`--at` takes an ISO time with its offset (or `Z` for UTC). In a terminal, a
missing flag is asked for. In a script, it is refused.

## Errors

Errors are JSON with a readable `error` and a `code`, and `details` when there
is more to say:

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | The request isn't valid. `errors` lists each field, with its `path` and `message` |
| `401` | No session or token |
| `402` | The organization's plan doesn't include Data |
| `403` | The token is for another project, you aren't allowed in the project, or the database is read-only after a downgrade |
| `404` | No database, table or row by that name |
| `409` | A stale `version`, a guard that changed nothing, a change below a column's minimum, a constraint (for example, rows still point at this one), a synced table's rows, a full database, or a table copy still running |
| `429` | Too many requests for this token |

Every project on Pro or Enterprise can have its own database: tables with typed columns, relations between them, and full-text search. The Data API is how you manage it from your own code. The dashboard and the CLI use the same routes, so anything they can do, your code can do too. Data explains the database itself.

The full reference is an OpenAPI file: https://api.ganju.ai/openapi/data.json. Load it into Postman, Insomnia or a code generator.

Authenticate

Create a personal access token for the project with the CLI, and send it as a bearer token:

ganju token create "orders sync" --expires 90   # or --expires never

The token is printed once. ganju token list shows your tokens and ganju token revoke "orders sync" stops one.

Every route lives under the project’s database. The organization and project ids are in your ganju.json once you’ve run ganju link:

export GANJU_TOKEN=ganju_pat_...
export DATA=https://api.ganju.ai/organization/<organizationId>/project/<projectId>/artifact/data
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GANJU_TOKEN" $DATA

A token only reaches the project it was made for. Each token can make 120 requests a minute to each route, within 300 a minute for your account in all. Past that, the API answers 429 with a Retry-After header: wait a minute and try again.

The examples below write curl ... for curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $GANJU_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json".

The database

Route What it does
GET / The database: status, size, timeZone, its tables, open index suggestions (indexAdvice) and a table copy in progress (copy). database is null when the project has none
POST / Create it: { "name"? }, the project’s slug by default. Safe to repeat. While a deleted database can still be restored, this is refused unless you send "replaceDeleted": true, which gives up that restore
PATCH / Its settings: { "timeZone": "America/Bogota" }, or null for UTC
DELETE / Delete it: { "confirmName": "<database name>" }. It can be restored for 7 days
POST /restore Undo a delete, within those 7 days

(/ here is $DATA itself.)

curl -X POST ... $DATA -d '{ "name": "pizzeria" }'
curl -X PATCH ... $DATA -d '{ "timeZone": "America/Bogota" }'

The time zone is the one dates and times come back in for anyone who doesn’t ask for another, and the one a date and time without an offset is read in. A row read can ask for its own with ?timeZone=Europe/Madrid.

Create a table

curl -X POST ... $DATA/table -d '{
  "name": "menu",
  "label": "Menu",
  "description": "The pizzas we sell, with price and stock",
  "displayColumn": "name",
  "access": "read",
  "columns": [
    { "name": "name",  "type": "text",    "required": true, "searchable": true },
    { "name": "price", "type": "integer", "min": 0 },
    { "name": "stock", "type": "integer", "min": 0, "default": 0 },
    { "name": "size",  "type": "enum",    "values": ["30cm", "40cm"] }
  ]
}'

A table takes:

Field What it is
name Lowercase letters, digits and _, starting with a letter, up to 63 characters
label, description Shown instead of the name, and what the assistant reads (up to 100 and 300 characters)
displayColumn What a relation to this table shows: "name" instead of the id
access What channel bots may do: none, read (the default), add or full. See Who sees what
customerScoped true: each customer sees only their own rows
history Keep row history; true by default
source Sync it from a spreadsheet: { "uri", "sheet"?, "key" }. See Sync a table from a spreadsheet
columns Up to 93

and each column:

Field What it is
name, type The type is text, long_text, integer, decimal, boolean, date, datetime, enum, json, email, url, phone, relation or file
label, description As for a table
required, unique, filterable, searchable true or false
values For enum: the options, up to 100
table, onDelete For relation: the table it points at, and what deleting that row does: restrict, cascade or set_null
min For integer and decimal: the lowest value allowed
default Used when a new row leaves it empty

Every row also has id, created_at, updated_at and version. The database sets these; you never send them.

Insert, read and search rows

# One row, or up to 500 at once with "rows"
curl -X POST ... $DATA/table/menu/row -d '{ "values": { "name": "Margherita", "price": 28000, "stock": 10 } }'
curl -X POST ... $DATA/table/menu/row -d '{ "rows": [{ "name": "Hawaiian" }, { "name": "Pepperoni" }] }'

# One row
curl ... $DATA/table/menu/row/12

# Filter, sort, search and page
curl ... "$DATA/table/menu/row?where=%7B%22price%22%3A%7B%22lt%22%3A30000%7D%7D&sort=-price&limit=50"
curl ... "$DATA/table/menu/row?q=pizza"

An insert answers { "ids": [...] }. A list answers { table, rows, total, nextCursor }:

  • where is JSON: {"status":"open"}, {"price":{"lt":30000}}, {"name":{"contains":"pizza"}}. The operators are eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte, in, notIn, contains, startsWith and isNull; combine them with and / or, and filter on a related row’s column with "customer.name".
  • sort is a list of columns. Put - in front of a column to sort descending: -created_at,name.
  • q searches the columns marked searchable, best matches first.
  • include brings in related rows: include=customer.
  • limit is 20 by default, up to 500. A page holds up to 500 rows and 1 MB. When there are more, the answer has nextCursor; send it back as cursor to read the next page. total comes on the first page.
  • timeZone returns dates and times in that zone instead of the database’s.

A relation comes back as { id, label }. A file column comes back as { uri, id, title, mimeType }, or { uri, missing: true } when no resource has the uri any more; write it with the uri.

In JavaScript:

const res = await fetch(`${DATA}/table/menu/row?q=${encodeURIComponent('pizza')}`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.GANJU_TOKEN}` }
});
const { rows, nextCursor } = await res.json();

Change and delete rows without losing edits

Each row has a version that goes up by one with every change. Send back the version you read:

curl -X PATCH ... $DATA/table/menu/row/12 -d '{ "set": { "price": 30000 }, "version": 3 }'
curl -X PATCH ... $DATA/table/menu/row/12 -d '{ "set": { "stock": { "decrement": 2 } } }'
curl -X DELETE ... $DATA/table/menu/row/12 -d '{ "version": 4 }'

A change answers { row }, and a delete { deleted }. A number can change relative to itself with { "increment": n } or { "decrement": n }.

Someone may change the row after you read it. If they do, the answer is 409, with the row as it is now in details.current and who changed it in details.updatedBy. Reload and try again. To overwrite their change, send the request without version.

Before deleting, you can ask what the delete would do to the rows that point at it. Nothing is deleted:

curl -X POST ... $DATA/table/orders/delete-preview -d '{ "ids": [12, 13] }'

Leave out ids to preview deleting every row. The answer lists each column that points at a deleted row, with how many rows it would delete (cascade), clear (set_null) or that refuse the delete (restrict). Cascades are followed all the way down, and depth says how many cascades away each one is. blocked is true when a restrict would refuse the delete. Past 200,000 affected rows, truncated is true and each count is a lower bound.

Write an order safely

POST /write takes a list of up to 50 inserts, updates and deletes across tables, touching up to 5,000 rows. They all apply together, or none of them do. A later step can use the id of an earlier insert as { "$ref": <step> }, in its values or as the id of the row it updates or deletes. An update or delete names one row by id, or the rows a where matches; expect says how many rows must change. An update can change a number relative to itself, with a guard:

curl -X POST ... $DATA/write -d '{
  "operations": [
    { "op": "insert", "table": "orders", "values": { "customer": "Ana" } },
    { "op": "insert", "table": "order_lines",
      "values": { "order": { "$ref": 0 }, "product": 12, "qty": 2 } },
    { "op": "update", "table": "menu", "id": 12,
      "set": { "stock": { "decrement": 2 } }, "where": { "stock": { "gte": 2 } } }
  ]
}'

It answers { results }, one per step: { op, table, id } for an insert (ids for several rows), { op, table, changed } for an update or delete.

If two customers order the last pizza at the same time, one order goes through. The other gets a 409 (“changed 0 rows, expected 1”), and none of its steps are written.

Change the tables

Route What it does
GET /table Tables, columns and relations, and each synced table’s last sync
POST /table Create a table
PATCH /table/:table Rename it, change its label, description or settings. A null puts a setting back to its default
POST /table/:table/sync Sync a table that has a source from its spreadsheet now (five a minute)
DELETE /table/:table Drop it. Send { "confirmName": "<table>" }
POST /table/:table/column Add a column
PATCH /table/:table/column/:column Rename or change a column, including its type
DELETE /table/:table/column/:column Drop a column
POST /advice/:adviceId Add a suggested index: marks the column filterable
DELETE /advice/:adviceId Dismiss an index suggestion until its numbers double
DELETE /copy Dismiss a failed table copy
GET /change The log of these changes: who, what, when (?limit=, ?cursor=)

A table’s source ({ "uri", "sheet", "key" }) keeps its rows in step with a spreadsheet or CSV in Resources, and makes them read-only to every other writer; { "source": null } stops it. See Sync a table from a spreadsheet.

Changing a column’s type checks every value first. If any value doesn’t fit, the change is refused and the answer lists the first 10 rows that don’t. Dropping a table or a column, and changing a type, answers with a bookmark. To undo the change, restore to it.

A type change copies the table, and so does dropping a relation column. Up to 100,000 rows that happens in the request. On a larger table the copy runs in the background. The answer has copy, with how many rows are copied so far, and the table keeps its old columns until the copy is done. Meanwhile reads and writes to other tables work as usual. A 409 answers table changes, and writes that would change the copied table’s rows: inserts, updates and deletes on it, and deletes in a table it points at with cascade or set null. GET on the database shows its progress in copy. If the copy fails, the table is left as it was and copy shows the error until you dismiss it with DELETE /copy.

History, restore and export

  • GET /table/:table/row/:id/history: every change to a row in the last 90 days, newest first, with who made it (?limit= up to 100, ?cursor=). A change made with a token is shown as cli:<token id>.
  • POST /checkpoint: a restore point at this exact moment. It answers with a bookmark; take one before a large change, such as replacing a table’s rows, to undo exactly that change later.
  • POST /restore-point: put the whole database back as it was at a time in the last 30 days ({ "timestamp": "2026-10-20T15:00:00-05:00" }), or at the bookmark a checkpoint, a dropped table or column, a type change or an earlier restore answered with ({ "bookmark": "…" }). The answer has an undoBookmark that undoes the restore. Calls in flight while it restarts fail.
  • POST /export: start a copy of the database, { "format": "jsonl" } or "csv": one file per table, plus schema.json. It answers { exportId, status }. Poll GET /export (or ?exportId=) until its status is done, then download each file with GET /export/file?exportId=<id>&table=<table>. Leave out table to get schema.json. Exports also work during the 7 days after you delete the database.

Named queries, triggers and schedules

Route What it does
GET /query Named queries, each with its SQL, parameters, the tables it reads and its plan (SCAN orders means it reads the whole table)
POST /query Save one: { "name", "description", "sql", "params", "assistant" }. Saving under an existing name replaces it
DELETE /query/:name Delete one
POST /query/:name/run Run one: { "params": { "from": "2026-10-01T00:00:00-05:00" }, "limit": 100 }. Answers { query, rows, truncated? }
GET /trigger Triggers and schedules, and pending: events not yet sent
POST /trigger Save a trigger or a schedule
PATCH /trigger/:name Turn it on or off: { "enabled": false }
DELETE /trigger/:name Delete one
POST /trigger/deploy Replace the triggers a CLI deploy made: { "triggers": [...] }
GET /trigger/:name/run Its recent runs, up to 50
POST /trigger/:name/run/:runId/retry Send a failed or skipped run again
GET /trigger/test-send Your own chats with the project’s bots, where a test can go
POST /trigger/test-send Send a test of a customer message or an email, built from a row

Each query parameter in params is { "name", "type", "description"?, "required"? }, with type one of text, integer, decimal, boolean, date or datetime. A run returns up to limit rows (100 by default, 500 at most) and 1 MB.

    { "name": "from", "type": "datetime" },

  "table": "orders", "on": "update",
