Anything that drops, deletes or rewrites data needs --yes (-y). Dropping the database or a table also needs its name, typed with --confirm:

ganju data column rm menu code --yes
ganju data table rm orders --yes --confirm orders
ganju data drop --yes --confirm acme-support
ganju data restore                              # undo the delete, within 7 days
ganju data restore --at 2026-10-30T09:15:00-05:00 --yes
ganju data restore --bookmark <bookmark> --yes  # the undo a drop printed

--at takes an ISO time with its offset (or Z for UTC). In a terminal, a missing flag is asked for. In a script, it is refused.

Errors

Errors are JSON with a readable error and a code, and details when there is more to say:

Status When
400 The request isn’t valid. errors lists each field, with its path and message
401 No session or token
402 The organization’s plan doesn’t include Data
403 The token is for another project, you aren’t allowed in the project, or the database is read-only after a downgrade
404 No database, table or row by that name
409 A stale version, a guard that changed nothing, a change below a column’s minimum, a constraint (for example, rows still point at this one), a synced table’s rows, a full database, or a table copy still running
429 Too many requests for this token
Change and delete rows without losing edits
Read and write the project's database from your own functions with ctx.data, message customers and staff chats with ctx.channels, and keep a function for triggers and schedules only.

Your [functions](/docs/tools/functions/) reach the project's
[database](/docs/data/) through `ctx.data`. Every call goes through the
platform, under the same rules as the dashboard and the assistant: a row below
a column's minimum is refused, a write that must all happen either does or
doesn't, and each change is recorded as the function that made it.

There is no SQL from a function. For a report the filters can't express, save a
[named query](/docs/data/#named-queries) and run it by name.

## `ctx.data`

| Call | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `describe(table?)` | Tables, columns, row counts and descriptions; one table when named |
| `query({ table, where, search, sort, limit, cursor, include, aggregate, groupBy })` | Find rows, or count, sum and average them |
| `search(table, text, options?)` | Full-text search over a table's searchable columns, best matches first |
| `insert(table, values)` | One row; returns `{ id }`. Pass a list of rows (up to 500) to add several; returns `{ ids }` |
| `update(table, idOrWhere, set, { where?, expect? })` | Change one row by id, or the rows a filter matches; returns `{ changed }` |
| `delete(table, idOrWhere, { where?, expect? })` | Delete them; returns `{ changed }` |
| `write(operations)` | Up to 50 inserts, updates and deletes, applied together or not at all |
| `run(name, params?, { limit? })` | A named query, by name; returns `{ query, rows, truncated? }` |

### Filters

`where` uses the same filters as the Data API and the assistant:

```ts
{ status: 'open' }                              // equals
{ price: { lt: 30000 } }                        // eq, ne, gt, gte, lt, lte
{ status: { in: ['open', 'ready'] } }           // in, notIn (up to 50 values)
{ name: { contains: 'pizza' } }                 // contains, startsWith (any case)
{ note: { isNull: true } }                      // empty, or not
{ 'customer.name': 'Ana' }                      // a column of the related row
{ or: [{ status: 'open' }, { total: { gte: 100000 } }] }
```

Several keys must all hold; `or` matches any of its filters, and `and` groups
them. A date and time without an offset is read in the database's
[time zone](/docs/data/#time-zone).

### Reading rows

```ts
const { rows, nextCursor } = await ctx.data.query({
  table: 'orders',
  where: { status: 'open' },
  sort: ['-created_at'],
  include: ['customer'],
  limit: 50
});
```

- A page has 20 rows by default, up to 500 (or 1 MB). Pass `nextCursor` back as
  `cursor` to read the next one.
- `sort` is a list of up to 3 columns; `-` in front sorts descending.
- A relation column comes back as `{ id, label }`, and `include` brings the
  whole related row instead.
- A file column comes back as `{ uri, title, mimeType }`, or `{ uri, missing:
  true }` when the file was deleted from Resources. Read the file with
  `ctx.resources.read(uri)`; write the column with the uri.
- Dates and times come back in the database's time zone, with their offset.

To count or add up instead of listing, pass `aggregate`, and `groupBy` (up to
3 columns) for one result per group:

```ts
const { groups } = await ctx.data.query({
  table: 'orders',
  where: { created_at: { gte: '2026-11-01T00:00:00-05:00' } },
  aggregate: [{ fn: 'count' }, { fn: 'sum', column: 'total' }],
  groupBy: ['status']
});
```

`fn` is `count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min` or `max`. `times` multiplies before adding
up: `{ fn: 'sum', column: 'stock', times: 'unit_cost' }` is the value of the
stock.

### Writing rows

```ts
const { id } = await ctx.data.insert('orders', { customer: 7, status: 'open' });
await ctx.data.update('menu', 12, { stock: { decrement: 2 } }, { where: { stock: { gte: 2 } } });
await ctx.data.delete('orders', { status: 'cancelled' });
```

A number can change relative to itself with `{ increment: n }` or
`{ decrement: n }`. `where` in the options is a guard that must hold, and
`expect` says how many rows must change; when either fails, nothing is written
and the call throws.

A refused call throws, with a message written for a person: "menu.stock can't
go below 0".

## Write an order in one step

From the [data-orders example](https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju/tree/main/examples/data-orders):
the order, a line per dish pointing at it, and the stock taken down, in one
`write`. `{ $ref: 0 }` is the id the first insert created. Each stock change
carries a guard, so two customers ordering the last pizza can't both get it:
the second write fails whole, and nothing of it is saved.

```ts
import { defineTool } from '@ganju/sdk';

export default defineTool<{ dish: number; quantity: number }>(
  async (input, ctx) => {
    const { results } = await ctx.data.write([
      { op: 'insert', table: 'orders', values: { status: 'open' } },
      {
        op: 'insert',
        table: 'order_lines',
        values: { order: { $ref: 0 }, dish: input.dish, quantity: input.quantity }
      },
      {
        op: 'update',
        table: 'menu',
        id: input.dish,
        set: { stock: { decrement: input.quantity } },
        where: { stock: { gte: input.quantity } }
      }
    ]);
    return { order: (results[0] as { id: number }).id };
  }
);
```

Each result says what its step did: `{ op: 'insert', table, id }` (or `ids`
for several rows) and `{ op: 'update' | 'delete', table, changed }`.

## What a function may touch

Left alone, a function can read and write every table. Narrow it with `data` on
the tool in `ganju.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "sales-report",
  "entry": "src/salesReport.ts",
  "data": { "access": "read", "tables": ["menu", "orders", "order_lines"] }
}
```

- `access`: `read` or `write`.
- `tables`: the only tables it sees. The others don't exist for it, in filters
  and relations too.

The platform enforces this, not your script. Use it for any function a channel
bot calls after reading what a customer wrote. `tables` limits what the
function names, not what the schema does: deleting a row still deletes the rows
that point at it with "delete these rows too", in tables outside the list as
well.

**A function sees every row, including in tables where each customer sees only
their own.** When a channel bot calls a function, the call doesn't say which
customer is talking, and anything about the customer in its input came from the
model. Don't treat it as who they are.

Changes a function makes are recorded as `function:<name>` in the row's
history.

## `ctx.channels`

Message the project's customers and staff chats. Messages go out as the bot,
as plain text, and are recorded on the conversation, so the bot's next turn
knows what the customer was told. They aren't billed as assistant replies.

A function only gets `ctx.channels` when it asks for it: set `"channels": true`
on it in `ganju.json`, or turn on **Can message through channels** in its
dialog on the Functions tab. Without it, every call throws "… can't use
ctx.channels". `ganju deploy` lists the functions that have it. Versions
published before this setting existed keep `ctx.channels`; add it to
`ganju.json` before you deploy them again.

```json
{
  "name": "tell-customer",
  "entry": "src/tellCustomer.ts",
  "channels": true
}
```

```ts
// A customer the bot has spoken with, in their private chat
await ctx.channels.send({
  participantId: order.participant_id,
  text: `Your order #${order.id} is ready.`
});

// A chat the bot is in: a Telegram group, or a Slack or Discord channel
await ctx.channels.post({
  channelId: await ctx.secret('KITCHEN_CHANNEL_ID'),
  chatId: await ctx.secret('KITCHEN_CHAT_ID'),
  text: 'New order #42: 2× Margherita'
});
```

- **`send`** writes to the customer's latest private conversation, on the
  channel they used. The channel's daily limit per customer applies. A row in a
  table where each customer sees only their own rows carries the customer as
  `participant_id`. It returns `{ messageId, conversationId, channelId,
  platform, sent }`, where `sent` is `text` or `template`.
- **WhatsApp** only takes free text within 24 hours of the customer's last
  message. After that only a template Meta approved reaches them; pass it as
  `template: { name, language, params }`, with one value per variable. Give
  both `text` and `template` and Ganju picks per customer. Without a template,
  `send` throws: "Outside WhatsApp's 24-hour window … use an approved
  template." When it can read the account's templates, Ganju checks the
  template is approved before calling Meta, and
  throws with Meta's reason when it is in review, rejected, paused or
  disabled. Meta bills template messages to your own WhatsApp account.
  Telegram, Slack and Discord have no window and take the text.
- **`templates()`** lists the templates Meta approved on the project's
  WhatsApp channels that Ganju can send, each with its `channelId`, `name`,
  `language`, `category`, `text` and `variables` (`{ n, label, example }`), so
  a function can choose one. Templates are created in the channel's
  [Message templates](/docs/channels/whatsapp/#5-message-templates).
- **`post`** takes the channel's id from the dashboard and the platform's chat
  id, such as a Telegram group's `-1001234567890`. It doesn't post to
  WhatsApp.

## Functions only triggers run

A function a [trigger](/docs/data/triggers/) or a
[schedule](/docs/data/schedules/) runs (tell the kitchen, message the
customer, send the nightly report) shouldn't be a tool the assistant can call.
Set `"expose": false` on it in `ganju.json`, or turn off **Assistant can use
this function** in its dialog on the Functions tab:

```json
{
  "name": "tell-customer",
  "entry": "src/tellCustomer.ts",
  "expose": false,
  "channels": true,
  "data": { "access": "read", "tables": ["orders"] }
}
```

It is still deployed, and shows a **Triggers only** tag. The assistant never
sees it, on channels or MCP clients, and it doesn't count toward the project's
tool limit.

A trigger calls it with the event instead of the model's arguments:

```ts
import { defineTool, type TriggerEvent } from '@ganju/sdk';

export default defineTool<TriggerEvent>(async (event, ctx) => {
  const order = event.row;
  if (typeof order?.participant_id !== 'string') return { skipped: 'no customer' };
  const sent = await ctx.channels.send({
    participantId: order.participant_id,
    text: `Your order #${order.id} is ready. Thank you!`
  });
  return { sent: sent.sent };
});
```

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `event` | `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `time` (a [time trigger](/docs/data/triggers/#time-triggers)'s row came due) or `schedule` |
| `table` | The table's name; empty on `schedule` |
| `row` | The row after the change; `null` on delete and on `schedule`. On `time`, the row as it was when it came due |
| `previous` | The row before the change; `null` on insert, `time` and `schedule` |
| `actor` | Who made the change: `channel:<customer>`, `user:<id>`, `function:<name>`…; `null` on `time` |
| `eventId` | The same on every delivery of this event. Use it to skip a repeat |
| `triggerId` | The trigger that ran it |
| `dueAt` | On `time` and `schedule`: when it came due (ISO 8601, UTC) |
| `truncated`, `rowId` | Set when the row was too large to send. Read it with `ctx.data.query({ table, where: { id: rowId } })` |
| `date` | On `schedule`: the run's date in the database's time zone (`YYYY-MM-DD`) |
| `query`, `rows`, `rowCount` | On `schedule` with a query: its name, its rows (up to 200) and how many it returned (counted up to 500) |
| `rowsTruncated`, `rowCountMore` | On `schedule`: some rows were left out for size; there were more rows than counted |

A schedule's function gets the rows straight away:

```ts
export default defineTool<TriggerEvent>(async (event, ctx) => {
  const total = (event.rows ?? []).reduce((sum, r) => sum + Number(r.total ?? 0), 0);
  await ctx.channels.post({
    channelId: await ctx.secret('KITCHEN_CHANNEL_ID'),
    chatId: await ctx.secret('KITCHEN_CHAT_ID'),
    text: `${event.date}: ${event.rowCount ?? 0} orders, ${total} in sales`
  });
});
```

The row is content a customer may have written. Pass it to an AI model as
untrusted text, never as instructions.

Writes a triggered function makes are recorded as that trigger, never fire
that same trigger again, and can fire other triggers one level deeper. See
[Triggers and webhooks](/docs/data/triggers/#loops-and-chains).

Usage

Every ctx.data call counts as one database request on the billing page’s Data block, with the rows it read and wrote. A function a trigger or a schedule runs counts as a custom tool call, like one the assistant calls.
Write an order in one step
Run something every day or every week at a set time, in the database's time zone: email a saved query's rows, or hand them to a function or a webhook.

A **schedule** runs on the clock: every day, or every week on the days you
choose, at a set time in the database's [time zone](/docs/data/#time-zone).
It can carry the rows of a [saved query](/docs/data/#named-queries), such as
today's orders, and email them to you, or hand them to a function or a
webhook. "Every night at 9, email me today's orders." "Every Monday at 8, send
last week's sales to our system."

A schedule has no table and nothing has to be written for it to run. To react
when rows change, or a set time after a row's date, use a
[trigger](/docs/data/triggers/).

## Create one

Open **Schedules** in the list on the Data page and click **New schedule**.
The list shows each schedule as "Every day at 21:00" or "Every Monday,
Thursday at 08:00", with the query whose rows it sends.

1. **Name** and **Description**: optional. Lowercase letters, digits, `-` and
   `_`; left empty, one is made up.
2. **Repeats**: **Every day** or **Every week**. For every week, tick the
   days.
3. **At**: the time, such as 21:00, in the database's time zone. The view's
   help line names that zone; change it in **Database settings**.
4. **Rows from**: a saved query whose rows go with each run, or **No query:
   just the time**. Make the query first under **Queries**.
5. The query's parameters: a value, or one of the run's dates (below).
6. **Don't run when the query returns no rows**: skips the days with nothing.
7. **Then**: **Send an email**, **Run a function** or **Call a webhook**.

![The New schedule dialog: Name, Repeats, At, Rows from a saved query and Then "Send an email"](/images/data-schedule-dialog.webp)

Each schedule can be turned on and off, edited and deleted from the list, and
**Recent runs** shows each run with its status and error, and **Retry** for a
failed one. A database holds up to 5 schedules; they count toward its 50
triggers. Daily is the most often a schedule runs.

You can also ask the project's [Assistant](/docs/assistant/): "every night at
9, email me today's orders". It writes the query and the schedule, can send you
a test of the email before it is due, and you apply both.

## The run's dates

A query parameter can take the run's own date instead of a fixed value. Each is
worked out in the database's time zone:

| Value | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `{{today}}` | The run's date, such as `2026-11-13` |
| `{{yesterday}}` | The day before |
| `{{today_start}}` | The start of the run's day, as a UTC date and time |
| `{{today_end}}` | The end of the run's day (the next midnight), as a UTC date and time |
| `{{now}}` | The time the run is for, as a UTC date and time |

Use `{{today}}` and `{{yesterday}}` for a `date` column, and `{{today_start}}`
and `{{today_end}}` for a column such as `created_at`, stored in UTC.

A query for the day's orders, saved as `todays_orders` with two `datetime`
parameters:

```sql
SELECT customer, items, total FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= :from AND created_at < :to
ORDER BY created_at
```

If you later change a query a schedule runs so that its parameters no longer
match, saving the query warns you: change the schedule too, or its runs fail.

## Actions

- **Send an email**: up to 10 addresses. The text takes `{{date}}` (the run's
  date) and `{{count}}` (how many rows), and is followed by the rows, one per
  line. The subject defaults to the query's name and the date. The same
  confirmation as a trigger's email applies: members of the organization get
  it right away, other addresses confirm first. See
  [Actions](/docs/data/triggers/#actions).
- **Run a function**: the function gets the run as its event, with the rows.
  Keep it out of the assistant's tools with `"expose": false`; see
  [Data from functions](/docs/data/functions/#functions-only-triggers-run).
- **Call a webhook**: the run is POSTed as JSON and signed, like a trigger's.
  See [Verify a webhook](/docs/data/triggers/#verify-a-webhook).

## What a run sends

A function or webhook gets:

```json
{
  "eventId": "…",
  "triggerId": "trg_…",
  "trigger": "nightly-orders",
  "table": "",
  "event": "schedule",
  "rowId": 0,
  "row": null,
  "previous": null,
  "actor": null,
  "at": "2026-11-14T02:00:03Z",
  "dueAt": "2026-11-14T02:00:00Z",
  "date": "2026-11-13",
  "query": "todays_orders",
  "rows": [{ "customer": "Ana", "items": "2× Margherita", "total": 56000 }],
  "rowCount": 1
}
```

- `dueAt` is the time the run was for, in UTC; `date` is that day in the
  database's time zone.
- `rows` holds up to 200 rows and 48 KB; `rowsTruncated` says some were left
  out. `rowCount` counts up to 500 rows; `rowCountMore` says there were more.

A schedule is a trigger with `"on": "schedule"` and no `table` or `when`. List

```json
{
  "name": "nightly-orders",
  "on": "schedule",
  "every": "day",
  "at": "21:00",
  "query": "todays_orders",
  "params": { "from": "{{today_start}}", "to": "{{today_end}}" },
  "skipEmpty": true,
  "email": { "to": "you@example.com", "subject": "Orders {{date}}", "text": "{{count}} orders today:" }
}
```

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `every` | `day` or `week` |
| `days` | With `week`: some of `mon`, `tue`, `wed`, `thu`, `fri`, `sat`, `sun`. Monday when left out |
| `at` | A 24-hour time, such as `08:00` or `21:00` |
| `query` | Optional. A saved query's name |
| `params` | With `query`: a value per parameter, or one of [the run's dates](#the-runs-dates). Every required parameter needs one |
| `skipEmpty` | With `query`: `true` runs nothing when it returns no rows |
| one action | `email`, `function` or `webhook` |

[trigger](/docs/data/triggers/#deploy-triggers-with-the-cli).

## When it runs

- **Once per time.** Each due time runs once, even if the database restarts.
- **Missed runs.** A run missed at its time (the database was down) goes out
  once, late, if it is back within 6 hours, and is skipped after that.
- **Changing the time zone** restarts the clocks in the new zone; a time that
  already passed there today isn't sent late.
- **A query that fails** means nothing goes out for that time; the run list
  shows the query's error.
- **Skipped when empty.** With **Don't run when the query returns no rows**, a
  day with no rows leaves no run at all.
- **Delivery, retries** and turning off after 20 failures in a row work as for
  triggers: see [How events are delivered](/docs/data/triggers/#how-events-are-delivered).
  When Ganju turns a schedule off, the organization's admins get an email.
- **Plans.** Each run counts as a trigger run. If the organization's plan no
  longer includes Data, schedules pause.

Sync a table from a spreadsheet
Keep a table's rows in step with a Google Sheet, an Excel file or a CSV in Resources, matched by a key column, read again whenever the file changes, read-only everywhere else.

Many businesses already keep the menu, the prices or the stock in a
spreadsheet. A table **synced from a spreadsheet** keeps those rows in step
with it, so nobody types them twice: change a price in the sheet, and the row
in Ganju changes too.

The source is any spreadsheet or CSV in [Resources](/docs/resources/): a
Google Sheet imported from Drive, an Excel file from OneDrive, or a CSV, TSV,
`.xlsx`, `.xls` or OpenDocument spreadsheet you uploaded. The sync goes one
way: **the sheet wins**.

> **Sync or import?** To copy a file's rows in once and then edit them in
> Ganju, [import it](/docs/data/#import-a-file). To keep editing the
> spreadsheet and have Ganju follow, sync it.

## Set it up

1. Put the file in [Resources](/docs/resources/), if it isn't there yet.
2. Make sure the table has a **Unique** column that names the same row in the
   sheet and in the table, such as `sku` or `name`. That is the **key**.
3. Open the table on the **Data** page, go to its **Schema** tab, and under
   **Source: spreadsheet** click **Sync from a spreadsheet**.
4. Pick the **File**, the **Sheet** (empty for the first one) and the **Key
   column**, and click **Start syncing**.

The first sync runs right away. It makes the table what the sheet says, so
**rows whose key isn't in the sheet are deleted**.

The sheet's first row holds the headers. Each header is matched to a column by
its name or its label, the way an [import](/docs/data/#import-a-file)
matches them: `Precio` fills `price` when `price` is labelled "Precio".
Headers that match no column are ignored, and so are columns the sheet
doesn't have. Cells are read the way an import reads them: dates, numbers
such as `28.000`, `sí` / `no`, and a relation by the related row's display
value.

## When it syncs

- **When the file changes.** A Drive or OneDrive file is checked on its own
  [sync interval](/docs/resources/), and read again only when it changed. An
  uploaded file syncs when you replace it.
- **When you ask.** **Sync now**, on the table's Rows tab or under its source,
  fetches a Drive or OneDrive file again if it changed, then reads it. The
  **Sync now** of the item in Resources does the same. You can ask five times a
  minute.

Each sync, in one go:

- inserts the lines whose key is new,
- updates the rows whose values differ from their line,
- deletes the rows whose key is no longer in the sheet.

Rows that didn't change aren't written: they keep their version and get no
[history](/docs/data/#who-sees-what) entry. The changes are made by
`system:sheet-sync`, which is what row history shows, and they fire the
table's [triggers](/docs/data/triggers/): a price or stock change in the sheet
can still notify someone.

The table's Rows tab says where the rows come from and when they were last
synced ("Synced from Menú.xlsx · synced 5 minutes ago"). Under **Source:
spreadsheet**, **Last sync** says when it ran and how many rows it added,
updated and deleted.

![A synced table's Rows tab: "Synced from qa_menu" with Sync now, and New row and Import unavailable](/images/data-sheet-sync-rows.webp)

## Read-only while it syncs

A synced table's rows change only in the sheet. Adding, changing or deleting a
row is refused from everywhere, the dashboard, the API, the CLI, functions and
the assistant, with a message such as:

```
menu is synced from "Menú.xlsx"; change the sheet, or stop syncing it.
```

You can still change the table's columns and settings. The key column can't
be dropped, and it stays unique. **Stop syncing**, under the source, leaves the
rows as they are and makes them editable again. **Change** picks another file,
sheet or key.

## When a sync is refused

A sheet that doesn't fit is refused whole, and the table keeps its rows as
they were:

- the sheet has no column for the key, or for a required column;
- a key is empty, or appears on two lines;
- a value doesn't fit its column (text in a number column, a number below the
  column's minimum, an option that isn't in the list);
- a line deleted from the sheet is still pointed at by another table's rows.

The reason shows on the table's Rows tab and under its source, with the line
it was found on, and in **Tool health** on the project's overview. Fix the
sheet, then click **Sync now** or wait for the next change.

## Limits

- One file of up to **5 MB**, and up to **20,000** lines.
- One source per table; several tables may sync from the same file, each from
  its own sheet.
- A synced table can't be [customer-scoped](/docs/data/#who-sees-what): its
  rows come from the sheet, with no customer, so the bots wouldn't see them.
- A delete in another table that would cascade into a synced table's rows, or
  clear a relation in them, is refused; change the sheet first.

## From the Assistant, the API, the CLI and ganju.data.json

A table's `source` is a table setting: `uri` (the file's uri in Resources),
`sheet` (optional) and `key`.

```json
{
  "name": "menu",
  "source": { "uri": "gdrive://files/1AbC…", "sheet": "Precios", "key": "sku" },
  "columns": [
    { "name": "sku", "type": "text", "required": true, "unique": true },
    { "name": "name", "type": "text", "required": true },
    { "name": "price", "type": "integer", "min": 0 }
  ]
}
```

- **Data API**: `PATCH …/table/menu` with `{ "source": { … } }` starts
  syncing, and `{ "source": null }` stops it. `POST …/table/menu/sync` is
  **Sync now** (it answers `202` and runs in the background). Each table in
  `GET …/table` has `sync`: when the last sync ran, `ok` or `failed`, what it
  inserted, updated, deleted and left unchanged, and why it was refused. See
  the [Data API](/docs/data-api/#change-the-tables).
- **CLI**: in `ganju.data.json`, `ganju data schema push` sets or removes it
  like any other setting, and `ganju data schema pull` writes it out.
  `ganju data tables` shows where each synced table comes from and how its last
  sync went; `ganju data table sync menu` is **Sync now**.
- **Assistant**: ask the project's [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) to make a
  table from a spreadsheet in Resources and keep it synced; it proposes the
  table with its source, and you apply it.
- **MCP clients**: the `data-admin` tool can stop a sync, but setting one is
  done from the dashboard, the Assistant, the API or the CLI, where the file is
  checked.

From the Assistant, the API, the CLI and ganju.data.json

Run something when a table's rows change or a set time after a row's date (a function, a signed webhook, a chat message, an email or a message to the customer), and how testing, delivery, retries and webhook signatures work.

A **trigger** is a rule on a table: when a row is added, changed or deleted,
and a condition holds, Ganju runs one action. A new order posts to the
kitchen's group; an order that becomes `ready` messages the customer; every
change to `bookings` reaches your own system as a webhook.

Triggers fire for every write, wherever it came from: the assistant on a
channel, the dashboard, the CLI, the API, a function or a
[spreadsheet sync](/docs/data/sheet-sync/). A write that is undone (because a
guard failed, say) fires nothing.

A [time trigger](#time-triggers) fires when time passes instead, with nothing
written: an order still `pending` 30 minutes after it was placed, a booking
nobody confirmed by noon the day before.

A [schedule](/docs/data/schedules/) runs on the clock, every day or every week
at a set time, with no table: "every night at 9, email me today's orders".

## Create one

Open a table on the **Data** page, then its **Triggers** tab, and click **New
trigger**:

1. **Name** and **Description**: optional. A name is lowercase letters,
   digits, `_` and `-`, starting with a letter; left empty, one is made up.
2. **When**: **A row is added**, **A row changes**, **A row is deleted**, or
   **Time passes** (see [time triggers](#time-triggers)).
3. **Only if**: optional. A column, a test (**changes to**, **changes from**,
   **is**, **changes (any value)**) and a value, such as `status` **changes
   to** `ready`. **Advanced (JSON)** takes any [condition](#conditions).
4. **Then**: the [action](#actions).
5. **Runs a minute**: 60 by default, up to 600. Past it, events wait and go out
   later.

![The New trigger dialog: Name, When, Only if, Then "Run a function" and Runs a minute](/images/data-trigger-dialog.webp)

Each trigger shows as a card on the Triggers tab with what it does in one
line, such as "status changes to ready". From the card you can turn it on and
off, **Edit** it, **Delete** it, and open **Recent runs**: each event it
handled, with its status (**Running**, **Waiting**, **Done**, **Failed** or
**Skipped**), its attempts and error, and **Retry** to send a failed one again.
When events are waiting to go out, the tab says how many.

A database holds up to 50 triggers, schedules included. Dropping a table
deletes its triggers. Renaming a column renames it in the triggers that use it,
in their conditions and `{{column}}` texts. A column a trigger uses can't be
dropped until you change or delete that trigger.

You can also ask the project's [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) to make one ("when
an order becomes ready, message the customer"): it proposes the trigger and you
apply it.

## Conditions

A condition tests the row before and after the change:

| Test | In the dashboard | Holds when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{ "status": { "changedTo": "ready" } }` | changes to | `status` is now `ready` and wasn't before |
| `{ "status": { "changedFrom": "open" } }` | changes from | `status` was `open` and isn't now |
| `{ "price": { "changed": true } }` | changes (any value) | `price` has a different value |
| `{ "zone": { "equals": "north" } }` | is | `zone` is `north` (on the row after the change, or the deleted row) |

An added row has no "before", and a deleted row no "after", so each counts as
every column empty: an insert **changes to** the values it was created with,
and a delete **changes from** the values it had. On a trigger for changed
rows, `status` **changes to** `ready` fires once, when the order becomes ready,
not again on every later edit of a ready order.

Tests on several columns must all hold. `all` and `any` combine conditions:

```json
{
  "any": [
    { "status": { "changedTo": "ready" } },
    { "all": [{ "status": { "equals": "open" } }, { "total": { "changed": true } }] }
  ]
}
```

Values compare exactly: `3` and `3.0` match, `"3"` and `3` don't. `null`, or a
value left empty in the dashboard, means empty.

## Time triggers

Choose **Time passes** under **When**, then **How long** and from which time
of the row:

- **The row's time**: **When it was added (created_at)**, **When it last
  changed (updated_at)**, or a date or date and time column of the table, such
  as a booking's `starts_at`.
- **How long**: an amount in minutes, hours or days, from 5 minutes to 30
  days, **after** that time, or **before** it on a date or date and time
  column (a reminder the day before a booking). A date with no time counts
  from midnight in the database's [time zone](/docs/data/#time-zone).
- **Only if**: tested on the row as it is when it comes due, so the only test
  is **is** (`equals`). `status` **is** `pending` fires for an order still
  pending 30 minutes on, not for one already marked ready.

Each row fires once for each time it comes due. On `updated_at`, the next
change makes a new due time, so a trigger for "no change in 2 days" fires
again two days after each change. Rows that were already due when you saved
the trigger, or while it was off, don't fire: a new trigger doesn't send a
backlog.

Ganju looks for due rows every 5 minutes, so a run can start up to 5 minutes
after the due time. The column gets an index while a time trigger uses it,
and it can't be dropped, or changed to a type that isn't a date, until you
change or delete the trigger.

Limits: a database holds up to 10 time triggers, and each fires up to 100
events per check (the rest go out at the next one). A database's time
triggers share 2,000 events a day (UTC): once that is reached, every time
trigger with another row due that day is turned off, its card says why, and
the organization's admins get an email. A time trigger is also turned off
while its runs are paused (the plan no longer includes Data, or the month's
trigger runs are used up). Turn it back on when you're ready; it counts from
then, so what came due while it was off isn't sent.

In `ganju.json` and the API:

```json
{
  "name": "still-pending",
  "table": "orders",
  "on": "time",
  "after": { "column": "created_at", "minutes": 30 },
  "when": { "status": { "equals": "pending" } },
  "customer": { "text": "Your order #{{id}} is taking longer than usual; we're on it." }
}
```

`minutes` goes from 5 to 43,200 (30 days), and is negative for before:
`{ "column": "starts_at", "minutes": -1440 }` is a day before. The event's
`event` is `time`, `previous` and `actor` are `null`, and `dueAt` says when the
row came due.

## Schedules

Schedules run at a set time every day or every week, with no table, and can
carry a saved query's rows, such as today's orders. They have their own place
on the Data page and their own page here: [Schedules](/docs/data/schedules/).
They share the actions, delivery, retries and webhook signatures described on
this page.

## Actions

| Action | In the dashboard | In `ganju.json` | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Run a function | **Run a function** | `"function": "notify-kitchen"` | The function runs with the event. See [functions only triggers run](/docs/data/functions/#functions-only-triggers-run) |
| Call a webhook | **Call a webhook** | `"webhook": "https://example.com/hooks/orders"` | The event is POSTed as JSON, [signed](#verify-a-webhook) |
| Send a chat message | **Send a chat message** | `"chat": { "channelId": "…", "chatId": "-1001234567890", "text": "New order #{{id}}" }` | Posted to a Telegram group or a Slack or Discord channel the bot is in |
| Send an email | **Send an email** | `"email": { "to": ["kitchen@example.com"], "subject": "Order {{id}}", "text": "…" }` | Up to 10 addresses. The subject defaults to `<table>: {{id}}` |
| Message the customer | **Message the customer** | `"customer": { "text": "Your order #{{id}} is ready." }` | Sent to the customer whose conversation wrote the row, on the channel they used |

**Function** lists the functions deployed in the project, marking those that
are **triggers only** and any that is no longer deployed. **Channel** lists
the project's Telegram, Slack and Discord channels; **Chat id** is the
Telegram group's id (such as `-1001234`) or the Slack or Discord channel's id.
Texts are up to 2,000 characters.

In a message, `{{column}}` inserts that column's value from the row, as plain
text. `id`, `created_at`, `updated_at` and `participant_id` work too. Messages
are never formatted as markup: a row may hold text a customer wrote.

**Email** goes to the organization's members right away. Any other address
first gets one email from Ganju, naming the project and the organization, with
a link to confirm it wants these emails. Until it confirms, runs leave it out:
a run that reached someone else is **ok** and says who was left out, and one
that reached nobody is **skipped**. The dashboard and `ganju deploy` list who
still has to confirm. An organization sends at most 20 of these links a day;
the rest go out when the trigger is saved again. Every email to a confirmed
address has a link to unsubscribe, and supports one-click unsubscribe in mail
apps.

**Message the customer** needs a table where **each customer sees only their
own rows**, since that is how a row knows its customer. A row the owner typed in
has no customer, and its run fails saying so. The channel's daily limit per
customer applies.

On **WhatsApp**, free text only reaches a customer within 24 hours of their last
message. Turn on **Use a WhatsApp template**, pick one of the templates Meta
approved on the project's WhatsApp channels, and give each of its variables a
column of the row or a fixed text; the labels you gave the variables show next
to them. Templates are created in the channel's
[Message templates](/docs/channels/whatsapp/#5-message-templates). In
`ganju.json`, `params` has one value per variable, in order:

```json
"customer": {
  "text": "Your order #{{id}} is ready.",
  "template": { "name": "order_ready", "language": "es", "params": ["{{id}}"] }
}
```

Within the window the customer gets the text; outside it, the template. When it
can read the account's templates, Ganju checks the template is approved before
sending it: one in review, rejected,
paused or disabled fails the run with Meta's reason, and so do Meta's own
refusals (the customer turned off marketing messages, the number's quality was
limited), in words on the run list. Meta bills template messages to your own
WhatsApp account. A chat message can't go to WhatsApp.

Messages sent by a trigger are recorded on the conversation, so the bot's next
turn knows what the customer was told. They aren't billed as assistant replies.

## Test a message before saving

The trigger dialog can send what you wrote, saved or not, built from a row of
the table (**Newest row** by default, or one you pick under **Row**). It isn't
a run: it isn't listed under the trigger's runs and doesn't count toward any
limit per customer.

- **Message the customer**: **Test this message** sends it to your own chat
  with the bot. Link that chat first: from your phone, write to the project's
  bot, send `/link`, and open the link it answers with while signed in to
  Ganju. With more than one linked chat, pick one under **Send to**. **Send as
  the template** sends the WhatsApp template even inside the 24-hour window;
  off, a test decides between text and template the way a real run does.
- **Send an email**: the test goes only to your own account's address,
  whatever **To** says, with "[Test]" before the subject.

Click **Send a test**; the dialog shows what went out, and Meta's or the
channel's refusal when there is one. You can send five tests a minute.

The API has the same: `GET /trigger/test-send` lists your linked chats, and
`POST /trigger/test-send` sends one, with `{ table, customer, rowId?,
participantId?, asTemplate? }` or `{ table, email, rowId? }`.

## Deploy triggers with the CLI

List them under `"triggers"` in `ganju.json`, next to your functions, and
`ganju deploy` publishes both:

```json
{
  "tools": [ … ],
  "triggers": [
    { "table": "orders", "on": "insert", "function": "notify-kitchen" },
    {
      "name": "order-ready",
      "table": "orders",
      "on": "update",
      "when": { "status": { "changedTo": "ready" } },
      "function": "tell-customer"
    },
    { "table": "orders", "on": "update", "webhook": "https://example.com/hooks/orders", "rateLimit": 120 }
  ]
}
```

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Optional. Lowercase letters, digits, `_` and `-`, starting with a letter |
| `description` | Optional, up to 300 characters |
| `table` | The table. Left out on a schedule |
| `on` | `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `time` (with `after`, see [time triggers](#time-triggers)) or `schedule` (see [schedules](/docs/data/schedules/)) |
| `when` | Optional. A [condition](#conditions) |
| `after` | On `time`: `{ "column", "minutes" }` |
| `rateLimit` | Runs a minute, 1 to 600; 60 when left out |
| `enabled` | `true` or `false`. Left out, a deploy keeps it as it was |
| one action | `function`, `webhook`, `chat`, `email` or `customer`; exactly one |

- Without a `name`, one is made from the table, the event and the action:
  `orders-insert-notify-kitchen`. In the dashboard and the API, saving a
  trigger without a name always creates a new one, numbered when the name is
  taken (`orders-insert-webhook-2`), so it never replaces another.
- `ganju deploy` adds and updates the triggers listed and removes the ones it
  deployed before that aren't listed anymore. Triggers made in the dashboard are
  left alone, and a name used by both is refused. All of it applies, or none.
- **Renaming a column a deployed trigger uses:** run
  `ganju data column rename`, which renames it in the trigger too, then change
  ganju.json to the new name before the next deploy. A deploy that still names
  the old column is refused. `ganju data schema push` reads a renamed column as
  a drop and an add, and a drop is refused while a trigger uses the column.
- **Dropping one:** take it out of the trigger in ganju.json and deploy first,
  then drop the column.
- A trigger turned off in the dashboard, or by Ganju after failures, stays off
  through later deploys unless its entry says `"enabled": true`.
- Leave `"triggers"` out and a deploy doesn't touch the database's triggers.
  `"triggers": []` removes the ones the CLI deployed.
- A new webhook's signing secret is printed once.

In the dashboard, a deployed trigger shows **Managed by the CLI (ganju.json)**.
You change it in the file, but can still turn it off and on there.

## From the Data API

The [Data API](/docs/data-api/#named-queries-triggers-and-schedules) has the
same routes the dashboard uses:

| Route | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /trigger` | Every trigger and schedule, and `pending`: events not yet sent. Webhook secrets are never listed |
| `POST /trigger` | Save one (the shape above). A new webhook answers with its `secret`, once; addresses still to confirm come back as `confirming`. `"replace": false` refuses to save over a trigger of that name |
| `PATCH /trigger/:name` | Turn it on or off: `{ "enabled": false }`. Turning it on clears why Ganju turned it off |
| `DELETE /trigger/:name` | Delete it |
| `POST /trigger/deploy` | What `ganju deploy` sends: `{ "triggers": [...] }` |
| `GET /trigger/:name/run` | Its recent runs, newest first, up to 50 (`?limit=`) |
| `POST /trigger/:name/run/:runId/retry` | Run a failed or skipped event again, with the same `eventId` |
| `GET /trigger/test-send`, `POST /trigger/test-send` | [Test a message](#test-a-message-before-saving) |

## How events are delivered

- **At least once.** The same event can arrive twice. Every event has an
  `eventId`, the same on every delivery and on a **Retry**, so a receiver can
  skip one it already handled. The data-orders example keeps it on the row.
- **Order** is kept per row as far as possible, not across rows.
- **Retries.** A failed run is tried three more times, waiting longer each time.
  Some failures aren't retried, because trying again wouldn't change them: a
  function that isn't published, a customer outside WhatsApp's window, a
  chain that went too deep, a webhook URL that points at a private address.
- **Turned off after 20 failures in a row.** The trigger's card says why, and
  the organization's admins get an email. Turn it back on once the
  cause is fixed.
- **Rate.** A trigger's runs a minute count from when each run starts, so a
  backlog goes out at that rate too.
- **Large rows.** A row over 48 KB (in UTF-8 bytes) is sent without `row` and `previous`, with
  `truncated: true` and its `rowId`, to read it by id.
- **Restores.** Events still waiting when you restore the database are
  dropped, and the rows a restore brings back don't fire triggers.

### Loops and chains

- A function a trigger runs writes as that trigger (`trigger:<id>`), and those
  writes never fire the same trigger again. `notify-kitchen` can mark the
  order it just posted without posting it twice.
- Its writes can fire *other* triggers, one level deeper. A chain stops at
  three levels, and the run that would go deeper fails with that error.

## Verify a webhook

A webhook trigger gets a secret that starts with `whsec_`. It is shown once,
when the trigger is created (or printed once by `ganju deploy`). Keep it with
your receiver.

Each event is a `POST` with a JSON body:

```json
{
  "eventId": "…",
  "triggerId": "trg_…",
  "trigger": "orders-update-webhook",
  "table": "orders",
  "event": "update",
  "rowId": 42,
  "row": { "id": 42, "status": "ready", "total": 56000, … },
  "previous": { "id": 42, "status": "open", "total": 56000, … },
  "actor": "user:…",
  "at": "2026-11-03T15:04:05Z"
}
```

A time trigger's event has `"event": "time"`, `"previous": null`, `"actor":
null` and `dueAt`, when the row came due. A
[schedule's](/docs/data/schedules/#what-a-run-sends) has `"event":
"schedule"`, an empty `table`, `"row": null`, `dueAt`, `date` (the run's date
in the database's time zone) and, with a query, `query`, `rows` and
`rowCount` (`rowsTruncated` when some were left out). A row too large to send
comes with `"truncated": true`.

and these headers:

| Header | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `content-type` | `application/json` |
| `user-agent` | `Ganju-Webhooks/1` |
| `x-ganju-signature` | `t=<unix seconds>,v1=<signature>` |
| `x-ganju-event-id` | The `eventId` |
| `x-ganju-event` | `<table>.<event>`, such as `orders.update` or `orders.time`; `schedule` for a schedule |
| `x-ganju-trigger` | The trigger's name |

The signature is the hex HMAC-SHA256 of `<t>.<raw body>`, keyed with the
secret. To check it, recompute it over the body exactly as it arrived, before
parsing it, compare in constant time, and refuse an old `t`:

```js
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import express from 'express';

const SECRET = process.env.GANJU_WEBHOOK_SECRET; // whsec_…
const TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 5 * 60;

const verify = (header, rawBody) => {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(
    (header ?? '').split(',').map(part => part.split('='))
  );
  const t = Number(parts.t);
  if (!parts.v1 || !Number.isInteger(t)) return false;
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - t) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS) return false;
  const expected = crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', SECRET)
    .update(`${t}.${rawBody}`)
    .digest('hex');
  const a = Buffer.from(expected, 'hex');
  const b = Buffer.from(parts.v1, 'hex');
  return a.length === b.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
};

const app = express();
app.post(
  '/hooks/orders',
  express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }),
  (req, res) => {
    const raw = req.body.toString('utf8');
    if (!verify(req.get('x-ganju-signature'), raw)) return res.sendStatus(401);
    const event = JSON.parse(raw);
    // Skip an eventId you already handled, then do the work.
    res.sendStatus(200);
  }
);
app.listen(3000);
```

Answer with a `2xx` within 10 seconds. Anything else, a redirect included, is
a failure and is retried. Each delivery is signed again with a new `t`. The URL
must be `https`, and private or local addresses are refused.

## Usage and limits

- Every run counts on the billing page's **Data** block, as a trigger run. A
  run that calls a function also counts as a custom tool call.
- On **Pro**, triggers run up to 5,000,000 times a month. Past that, they
  pause until the next billing period, and the organization's admins get an
  email. Enterprise has no such limit.
- Email triggers run up to 500 times in 24 hours per organization on Pro, and
  5,000 on Enterprise. The limit counts runs, and each run writes to up to 10
  addresses. Past it, runs are skipped and say so.
- If the organization's plan no longer includes Data, triggers pause: their
  runs are skipped.

A trigger is a rule on a table: when a row is added, changed or deleted, and a condition holds, Ganju runs one action. A new order posts to the kitchen’s group; an order that becomes ready messages the customer; every change to bookings reaches your own system as a webhook.

Triggers fire for every write, wherever it came from: the assistant on a channel, the dashboard, the CLI, the API, a function or a spreadsheet sync. A write that is undone (because a guard failed, say) fires nothing.

A time trigger fires when time passes instead, with nothing written: an order still pending 30 minutes after it was placed, a booking nobody confirmed by noon the day before.

A schedule runs on the clock, every day or every week at a set time, with no table: “every night at 9, email me today’s orders”.

Create one

Open a table on the Data page, then its Triggers tab, and click New trigger:

  1. Name and Description: optional. A name is lowercase letters, digits, _ and -, starting with a letter; left empty, one is made up.
  2. When: A row is added, A row changes, A row is deleted, or Time passes (see time triggers).
  3. Only if: optional. A column, a test (changes to, changes from, is, changes (any value)) and a value, such as status changes to ready. Advanced (JSON) takes any condition.
  4. Then: the action.
  5. Runs a minute: 60 by default, up to 600. Past it, events wait and go out later.

Each trigger shows as a card on the Triggers tab with what it does in one line, such as “status changes to ready”. From the card you can turn it on and off, Edit it, Delete it, and open Recent runs: each event it handled, with its status (Running, Waiting, Done, Failed or Skipped), its attempts and error, and Retry to send a failed one again. When events are waiting to go out, the tab says how many.

A database holds up to 50 triggers, schedules included. Dropping a table deletes its triggers. Renaming a column renames it in the triggers that use it, in their conditions and {{column}} texts. A column a trigger uses can’t be dropped until you change or delete that trigger.

You can also ask the project’s Assistant to make one (“when an order becomes ready, message the customer”): it proposes the trigger and you apply it.

Link that chat first: from your phone, write to the project’s bot, send /link, and open the link it answers with while signed in to Ganju. With more than one linked chat, pick one under Send to. Send as the template sends the WhatsApp template even inside the 24-hour window; off, a test decides between text and template the way a real run does.
  • Send an email: the test goes only to your own account’s address, whatever To says, with “[Test]” before the subject.

Click Send a test; the dialog shows what went out, and Meta’s or the channel’s refusal when there is one. You can send five tests a minute.

The API has the same: GET /trigger/test-send lists your linked chats, and POST /trigger/test-send sends one, with { table, customer, rowId?, participantId?, asTemplate? } or { table, email, rowId? }.

Deploy triggers with the CLI

List them under "triggers" in ganju.json, next to your functions, and ganju deploy publishes both:

{
  "tools": [ … ],
  "triggers": [
    { "table": "orders", "on": "insert", "function": "notify-kitchen" },
    {
      "name": "order-ready",
      "table": "orders",
      "on": "update",
      "when": { "status": { "changedTo": "ready" } },
      "function": "tell-customer"
    },
    { "table": "orders", "on": "update", "webhook": "https://example.com/hooks/orders", "rateLimit": 120 }
  ]
}
Field What it is
name Optional. Lowercase letters, digits, _ and -, starting with a letter
description Optional, up to 300 characters
table The table. Left out on a schedule
on insert, update, delete, time (with after, see time triggers) or schedule (see schedules)
when Optional. A condition
after On time: { "column", "minutes" }
rateLimit Runs a minute, 1 to 600; 60 when left out
enabled true or false. Left out, a deploy keeps it as it was
one action function, webhook, chat, email or customer; exactly one
  • Without a name, one is made from the table, the event and the action: orders-insert-notify-kitchen. In the dashboard and the API, saving a trigger without a name always creates a new one, numbered when the name is taken (orders-insert-webhook-2), so it never replaces another.
  • ganju deploy adds and updates the triggers listed and removes the ones it deployed before that aren’t listed anymore. Triggers made in the dashboard are left alone, and a name used by both is refused. All of it applies, or none.
  • Renaming a column a deployed trigger uses: run ganju data column rename, which renames it in the trigger too, then change ganju.json to the new name before the next deploy. A deploy that still names the old column is refused. ganju data schema push reads a renamed column as a drop and an add, and a drop is refused while a trigger uses the column.
  • Dropping one: take it out of the trigger in ganju.json and deploy first, then drop the column.
  • A trigger turned off in the dashboard, or by Ganju after failures, stays off through later deploys unless its entry says "enabled": true.
  • Leave "triggers" out and a deploy doesn’t touch the database’s triggers. "triggers": [] removes the ones the CLI deployed.
  • A new webhook’s signing secret is printed once.

In the dashboard, a deployed trigger shows Managed by the CLI (ganju.json). You change it in the file, but can still turn it off and on there.

From the Data API

The Data API has the same routes the dashboard uses:

Route What it does
GET /trigger Every trigger and schedule, and pending: events not yet sent. Webhook secrets are never listed
POST /trigger Save one (the shape above). A new webhook answers with its secret, once; addresses still to confirm come back as confirming. "replace": false refuses to save over a trigger of that name
PATCH /trigger/:name Turn it on or off: { "enabled": false }. Turning it on clears why Ganju turned it off
DELETE /trigger/:name Delete it
POST /trigger/deploy What ganju deploy sends: { "triggers": [...] }
GET /trigger/:name/run Its recent runs, newest first, up to 50 (?limit=)
POST /trigger/:name/run/:runId/retry Run a failed or skipped event again, with the same eventId
GET /trigger/test-send, POST /trigger/test-send Test a message

How events are delivered

  • At least once. The same event can arrive twice. Every event has an eventId, the same on every delivery and on a Retry, so a receiver can skip one it already handled. The data-orders example keeps it on the row.
  • Order is kept per row as far as possible, not across rows.
  • Retries. A failed run is tried three more times, waiting longer each time. Some failures aren’t retried, because trying again wouldn’t change them: a function that isn’t published, a customer outside WhatsApp’s window, a chain that went too deep, a webhook URL that points at a private address.
  • Turned off after 20 failures in a row. The trigger’s card says why, and the organization’s admins get an email. Turn it back on once the cause is fixed.
  • Rate. A trigger’s runs a minute count from when each run starts, so a backlog goes out at that rate too.
  • Large rows. A row over 48 KB (in UTF-8 bytes) is sent without row and previous, with truncated: true and its rowId, to read it by id.
  • Restores. Events still waiting when you restore the database are dropped, and the rows a restore brings back don’t fire triggers.

Loops and chains

  • A function a trigger runs writes as that trigger (trigger:<id>), and those writes never fire the same trigger again. notify-kitchen can mark the order it just posted without posting it twice.
  • Its writes can fire other triggers, one level deeper. A chain stops at three levels, and the run that would go deeper fails with that error.

Verify a webhook

A webhook trigger gets a secret that starts with whsec_. It is shown once, when the trigger is created (or printed once by ganju deploy). Keep it with your receiver.

Each event is a POST with a JSON body:

{
  "eventId": "…",
  "triggerId": "trg_…",
  "trigger": "orders-update-webhook",
  "table": "orders",
  "event": "update",
  "rowId": 42,
  "row": { "id": 42, "status": "ready", "total": 56000, … },
  "previous": { "id": 42, "status": "open", "total": 56000, … },
  "actor": "user:…",
  "at": "2026-11-03T15:04:05Z"
}

A time trigger’s event has "event": "time", "previous": null, "actor": null and dueAt, when the row came due. A schedule’s has "event": "schedule", an empty table, "row": null, dueAt, date (the run’s date in the database’s time zone) and, with a query, query, rows and rowCount (rowsTruncated when some were left out). A row too large to send comes with "truncated": true.

and these headers:

Header Value
content-type application/json
user-agent Ganju-Webhooks/1
x-ganju-signature t=<unix seconds>,v1=<signature>
x-ganju-event-id The eventId
x-ganju-event <table>.<event>, such as orders.update or orders.time; schedule for a schedule
x-ganju-trigger The trigger’s name

The signature is the hex HMAC-SHA256 of <t>.<raw body>, keyed with the secret. To check it, recompute it over the body exactly as it arrived, before parsing it, compare in constant time, and refuse an old t:

import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import express from 'express';

const SECRET = process.env.GANJU_WEBHOOK_SECRET; // whsec_…
const TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 5 * 60;

const verify = (header, rawBody) => {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(
    (header ?? '').split(',').map(part => part.split('='))
  );
  const t = Number(parts.t);
  if (!parts.v1 || !Number.isInteger(t)) return false;
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - t) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS) return false;
  const expected = crypto
    .createHmac('sha256', SECRET)
    .update(`${t}.${rawBody}`)
    .digest('hex');
  const a = Buffer.from(expected, 'hex');
  const b = Buffer.from(parts.v1, 'hex');
  return a.length === b.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
};

const app = express();
app.post(
  '/hooks/orders',
  express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }),
  (req, res) => {
    const raw = req.body.toString('utf8');
    if (!verify(req.get('x-ganju-signature'), raw)) return res.sendStatus(401);
    const event = JSON.parse(raw);
    // Skip an eventId you already handled, then do the work.
    res.sendStatus(200);
  }
);
app.listen(3000);

Answer with a 2xx within 10 seconds. Anything else, a redirect included, is a failure and is retried. Each delivery is signed again with a new t. The URL must be https, and private or local addresses are refused.

Usage and limits

  • Every run counts on the billing page’s Data block, as a trigger run. A run that calls a function also counts as a custom tool call.
  • On Pro, triggers run up to 5,000,000 times a month. Past that, they pause until the next billing period, and the organization’s admins get an email. Enterprise has no such limit.
  • Email triggers run up to 500 times in 24 hours per organization on Pro, and 5,000 on Enterprise. The limit counts runs, and each run writes to up to 10 addresses. Past it, runs are skipped and say so.
  • If the organization’s plan no longer includes Data, triggers pause: their runs are skipped.
Ganju is open source (Apache-2.0). Run your own instance on Cloudflare and Postgres, with your keys and your infrastructure.

Ganju is **open source under Apache-2.0**, so you can run the whole platform
yourself instead of using the hosted version. Self-hosting means your own model
keys, full control of your data, and plans you grant yourself; you just bring
the infrastructure.

This page is an overview; the repository holds the authoritative, always-current
runbook:
[README](https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju#readme),
[DEVELOPMENT.md](https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju/blob/main/docs/DEVELOPMENT.md),
and [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju/blob/main/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md).

## What it runs on

Ganju runs almost entirely on the **Cloudflare** developer platform, with
**Postgres + [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector)** for storage and
retrieval. It's an npm-workspaces + [Turborepo](https://turbo.build/) monorepo:

| App | Runtime | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `apps/api` | Cloudflare Worker | Control plane: auth, CRUD, OAuth, channel webhooks, queues, crons, the Assistant |
| `apps/mcp` | Cloudflare Worker | The MCP server every project exposes |
| `apps/data` | Cloudflare Worker | Project databases (one SQLite Durable Object per database) |
| `apps/tool-broker` | Cloudflare Worker | What customer-written functions call for connections, secrets and files |
| `apps/tool-outbound` | Cloudflare Worker | Screens every outbound request a customer's function makes |
| `apps/web` | Next.js (OpenNext → Cloudflare) | The dashboard |
| `apps/website` | Cloudflare Pages | The marketing site and these docs |
| `apps/resource-handler` | Container | Heavy work: document extraction, crawling, large sends. Built and deployed with `apps/api` |

> **Heads up:** you need a **paid** Cloudflare Workers plan. The
> `ResourceHandler` container requires it, and
> [Functions](/docs/tools/functions/) deploy into a Workers for Platforms
> dispatch namespace, which is a separate paid add-on.

## Run it locally first

You'll need Node.js 20 or newer, npm 11, Docker (for the resource-handler
container), a Cloudflare account, and a Postgres database (15+) with
`pgvector` 0.8 or newer.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju
cd ganju
npm install
cp .env.example .env      # then fill in the values
npm run migrate-dev       # generate + apply DB migrations
npm run dev               # start all apps via Turbo
```

Default local ports:

| App | Port |
|---|---|
| `apps/api` | 8080 |
| `apps/mcp` | 8081 |
| `apps/resource-handler` | 8082 |
| `apps/tool-broker` | 8083 |
| `apps/tool-outbound` | 8084 |
| `apps/data` | 8085 |
| `apps/web` | 3000 |

`apps/data` must be running for project databases to work locally. Functions
always run in the remote dispatch namespace, so `wrangler dev` must be logged in
to the Cloudflare account that owns it.

The `.env` covers:

- `DATABASE_URL` and the local Hyperdrive connection string.
- Auth and crypto secrets: `JWT_SECRET`, `CRYPTO_SECRET` (exactly 32 bytes,
  base64, from `openssl rand -base64 32`), `MCP_INTERNAL_SECRET`,
  `CUSTOM_CODE_TOKEN_SECRET`.
- `EMBEDDING_API_KEY`: a Gemini key for embeddings and the default model.
- `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`: for the [Assistant](/docs/assistant/).
- OAuth client IDs and secrets for the providers you want: Google (sign-in,
  Gmail, Drive, Calendar), GitHub (sign-in), Microsoft (Outlook, OneDrive),
  Slack.
- `BOT_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` / `BOT_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`: the client channel bots
  use to link accounts. Provision its row with
  `npx dotenv -e .env -- node scripts/provision-bot-client.mjs`.
- `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` and `CUSTOM_CODE_CF_API_TOKEN`: to publish functions.
- `EMAIL_FROM` and `ALERT_EMAIL`.
- Only if you want billing: your Polar keys.
- The `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` URLs of the API, web app, and MCP server.

## Provision Cloudflare resources

For a hosted deployment, create these in your Cloudflare account (names must
match each app's `wrangler.toml`, or update the toml to match yours):

- **Hyperdrive**: pointing at your Postgres.
- **R2 bucket**: `ganju-storage-<env>` (binding `STORAGE_BUCKET`).
- **KV namespace**: `<env>-JWKS_CACHE`, bound in `apps/mcp`.
- **Queues**: eight, each with a dead-letter queue: `ganju-index`,
  `ganju-crawl-discover`, `ganju-crawl-page`, `ganju-gdrive-discover`,
  `ganju-gdrive-file`, `ganju-onedrive-discover`, `ganju-onedrive-file`,
  `ganju-data-triggers` (suffixed `-<env>`, with a `-dlq-<env>` twin).
- **Workers for Platforms dispatch namespace**: `ganju-tools-<env>`, where
  customer functions are deployed.
- **Email Service** (`SEND_EMAIL`): onboard your sending domain under Email
  Service so mail reaches any recipient; before that it only delivers to
  verified Email Routing destinations.
- **Containers**: the `ResourceHandler` container, built from
  `apps/resource-handler/Dockerfile` during the `apps/api` deploy.
- **Durable Objects**: created by the migrations in each `wrangler.toml`:
  `ResourceHandler`, `DiscordGatewayDO`, `MessageBufferDO`, and
  `BuilderConversationDO` in `apps/api`, and `ProjectDatabase` in `apps/data`.
- **Custom domains**: `api`, `mcp`, and `app` under your zone.

The committed `wrangler.toml` files reference the hosted account's resource IDs
and domains (`ganju.ai`); replace those with **your** resource IDs and domain.

## Set secrets

`wrangler.toml` `vars` hold only non-secret config (the `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` URLs,
`NODE_ENV`, ports). Everything sensitive is set with `wrangler secret`, per app
and per environment, and only **after** that Worker's first deploy, since a
Worker must exist before it can hold a secret:

```bash
cd apps/api
wrangler secret put JWT_SECRET --env production
wrangler secret put CRYPTO_SECRET --env production
wrangler secret put MCP_INTERNAL_SECRET --env production
wrangler secret put EMBEDDING_API_KEY --env production
wrangler secret put GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET --env production
# …and the rest: see DEPLOYMENT.md for the full list per Worker
```

`apps/api`, `apps/mcp`, and `apps/tool-broker` each need their own set.
`apps/tool-outbound` and `apps/web` need none. Three secrets must be
**identical** across the Workers that share them:

| Secret | Shared by |
|---|---|
| `CRYPTO_SECRET` | api, mcp, tool-broker |
| `MCP_INTERNAL_SECRET` | api, mcp |
| `CUSTOM_CODE_TOKEN_SECRET` | api, tool-broker |

Choose `CRYPTO_SECRET` once: every stored OAuth token and API key is encrypted
under it, so rotating it later orphans them all.

## Deploy

Each Worker app ships `development` and `production` environments; the root
scripts fan out across the workspace via Turbo.

1. Provision the Cloudflare resources above.
2. Apply DB migrations against your target database (code and schema ship
   together, so migrate first):
   ```bash
   npm run migrate-prod   # generates + applies against .env.prod
   ```
3. **First deploy only:** deploy the Workers in order, because some bind to
   each other: `apps/tool-outbound` and `apps/data`, then `apps/api` (with its
   service binding to the MCP Worker temporarily commented out), then
   `apps/mcp`, then `apps/api` again with the binding restored, then
   `apps/tool-broker`, `apps/web`, and `apps/website`. DEPLOYMENT.md has the
   details.
4. Set the secrets for each Worker environment, and provision the bot OAuth
   client against the same database.
5. From then on, every deploy is:
   ```bash
   npm run migrate-prod   # if the schema moved
   npm run deploy-prod    # or deploy-dev for the development environment
   ```

There's no catalog seeding step: the shipped tool catalog is code. The curated
remote MCP servers (`mcp_server_catalog`) are the only rows you add yourself.

Under the hood each app runs `wrangler deploy --env <env>` (or
`opennextjs-cloudflare deploy` for the dashboard). With `production`, your apps
land on `{api,mcp,app}.<your-domain>`; `development` uses the `development-`
prefix.

## Check it works

- `https://api.<your-domain>/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` answers;
  MCP clients read it to discover how to sign in.
- `https://mcp.<your-domain>/health` answers.
- Sign in at `https://app.<your-domain>`, create an organization, and confirm
  the tools catalog renders.
- Publish a small function (`ganju deploy` with `GANJU_API_URL` pointing at your
  API), the only thing that exercises the dispatch namespace, the broker, and
  the outbound Worker together.

## Plans and billing on your instance

Billing is optional. Without a Polar token, checkout and the billing portal are
off, and every organization runs with the **Free** plan's limits until you grant
it a plan. As the operator you do that in the database, by setting the
organization's `subscription` row to `plan = 'PRO'` (or `'ENTERPRISE'`) and
`status = 'active'`. To sell plans yourself, set up Polar as described in
DEPLOYMENT.md.

## Observe & operate

Workers have observability enabled: stream logs with
`wrangler tail --env <env>`, watch the dead-letter queues for stuck background
jobs, and check the `error_log` table for cross-service errors. Two crons run on
`apps/api`: every 15 minutes (the error digest, emailed to `ALERT_EMAIL`) and
hourly (usage metering, the retention purge, data jobs, and alerts). For the
data model and architecture, see
[ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)
and [DATA_MODEL.md](https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju/blob/main/docs/DATA_MODEL.md)
in the repo.

Prefer not to run any of this? The [hosted version](https://app.ganju.ai)
handles all of it: start on the Free plan and
[upgrade](/docs/settings/#billing--plan) when you grow.

For the data model and architecture, see ARCHITECTURE.md and DATA_MODEL.md in the repo.

Prefer not to run any of this? The hosted version handles all of it: start on the Free plan and upgrade when you grow.

**Channels** are how you deliver your assistant to other people: clients, your
team, or individuals. Connect **Telegram**, **WhatsApp**, **Slack**, or
**Discord** and they chat with it on the app they already use. Everything you set

## Tell the bot how to answer

At the top of **Channels**, **Bot instructions** sets how your bot answers on
every channel (and in the Assistant's **Try it** chat): its language, length and
tone, or what it should always or never say. Up to 2,000 characters. Select
**Save**.

```text
Answer in two sentences at most.
Always answer in Spanish.
Call customers by their first name.
```

Facts like prices and opening hours don't go here; put them in
[Resources](/docs/getting-started/resources/) so the bot can look them up.

![The Bot instructions dialog with example instructions and the 2,000-character counter](/images/channels-bot-instructions.webp)

## Add a channel

Open **Channels** and select **Add channel**. In the **Connect channel** panel,
pick a **Platform**, choose the **Language model** (or leave **System
default**), and fill in that platform's credentials. For Telegram that's just a
**Bot token**, and Ganju registers the webhook for you.

![The Connect channel panel with Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, and Discord options and a bot token field](/images/new-channel.webp)

What each platform asks for:

| Platform | Credentials |
| --- | --- |
| Telegram | Bot token |
| Slack | Bot token, Signing secret |
| Discord | Bot token, Application ID, Public key |
| WhatsApp | Access token, Phone number ID, Verify token, App secret |

Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp then give you a URL to paste back into the
platform (**Request URL**, **Interactions Endpoint URL**, or **Callback URL**),
and the per-platform pages walk through it.

## Create a Telegram bot

For Telegram, the token comes from Telegram's own **@BotFather**. Message it,
send `/newbot`, choose a name and a username ending in `bot`, and copy the token
it gives back. Keep it secret: anyone with it can control your bot.

![The BotFather chat in Telegram walking through /newbot to create a bot and get its token](/images/new-channel-telegram.webp)

## Connect it

Paste the token into the **Bot token** field and select **Connect**.

![The Connect channel panel with a Telegram bot token entered, ready to connect](/images/telegram-token.webp)

The channel shows **Active**. Its **Overview** tab holds its settings:

- **Status**: **Receiving messages**, or **Paused** to drop incoming messages
  without disconnecting.
- **Language model**: switch the model this channel uses. Your own models come
  from [Settings → Models](/docs/settings/#models-bring-your-own).
- **Reply timing**: wait for a pause so several short messages get one answer:
  **Answer every message**, or wait 2, 5 (recommended), 10, or 30 seconds.
- **Replies per customer**: how many replies one customer gets in 24 hours, or
  **No limit**.
- **Customer memory**: **Remember customers**: the bot keeps what each customer
  tells it about themselves (private chats only) and uses it next time.
- **Activity**, with conversation and message counts, and **Remove channel** in
  the **Danger zone**.

![A Telegram channel's Overview: the bot, Receiving messages, Language model, Reply timing and Replies per customer](/images/channel-overview.webp)

## Chat with your assistant

Now anyone can message your bot. Run the `/start` prompt and it introduces
itself with the resources and tools you set up earlier.

![The Telegram bot answering /start with a project overview of its resources and tools](/images/telegram-message.webp)

Ask it to do something real (here, "send me the math book and tell me what it's
about") and it uses your **tools** and **resources** to answer and deliver the
file.

![The Telegram bot sending the mathematics PDF and describing what the book covers](/images/message-ask-book.webp)

## Monitor conversations

Back in the dashboard, each channel's **Conversations** tab shows every
exchange: the messages, the tools and resources each reply used, and the
**Sources** an answer cited. That way you can see exactly how people are using
your assistant.

![A channel's Conversations tab listing a private chat with its message count](/images/channel-conversations.webp)

## Create a prompt

2. Select **New prompt**. The **New Prompt** panel opens.

![The New Prompt panel: Title, Description, Messages with the Visual/JSON switch and Add message](/images/new-prompt-panel.webp)

## Fill it in

1. **Title**: a short name. Ganju turns it into the slash command shown just
   below it (**Slash command:**). Here, `start` becomes `/start`.
2. **Description**: what the prompt does. People and AI clients see it.
3. **Messages**: write one or more messages, switching each between **User**
   and **Assistant**. **Add message** adds another turn. Prefer raw JSON? Switch
   **Visual / JSON** at any time.
4. **Variables**: any `{{name}}` you type is detected automatically. Set each
   one's **Type**, a **Description**, and whether it's **Required** or
   **Optional**.

## Use it

Select **Create**. The prompt appears as a card with its slash command,
description, and messages, ready to run from any linked channel as `/start`.
Open a card to edit it, or delete it from there.

Add the files and knowledge your AI can search, from cloud drives, a website crawl, or direct uploads.

**Resources** are the documents and knowledge your assistant can search, so it
answers from your content instead of guessing. Add them from Google Drive,
OneDrive, a website crawl, or by uploading files directly. Each one gets a URI
and, once processed, is marked **Ready**.

> **Want the full picture?** This is the quick version. The complete
> **[Resources](/docs/resources/)** guide covers Google Drive and OneDrive
> imports, website crawls, uploads, citations, and sync.

## Where resources come from

Open **Knowledge** in the rail; it opens on the **Resources** tab. Everything is
grouped by source: **Google Drive**, **OneDrive**, **Websites**, **My folder**
(your own uploads), and **Data attachments** (files uploaded from a row on the
[Data](/docs/data/) page). The buttons at the top add to each: **Add from Google
Drive**, **Add from OneDrive**, **Add website**, and (inside a folder) **Add
files**.

![Knowledge, Resources tab: Google Drive, OneDrive, Websites and My folder, each with its Add button](/images/knowledge-resources.webp)

## Import from Google Drive or OneDrive

Choose **Add from Google Drive**. The first time, you connect your Google
account; then the picker opens. Browse **My Drive**, **Shared with me**,
**Shared drives**, or **Starred**, tick the files or folders you want, and select
**Add selected**.

![The Import from Google Drive picker with tabs for My Drive, Shared with me, Shared drives, and Starred](/images/resource-google-drive.webp)

**OneDrive** works the same way: browse **My files**, **Shared with me**,
**Recent**, or **Drives**, then add your selection.

![The Import from OneDrive picker with tabs for My files, Shared with me, Recent, and Drives](/images/resource-onedrive.webp)

## Upload a file

Open **My folder** and select **Add files**. In the **New Resource** panel:

1. Give it a **Title**. Its **URI** is generated from the title (like
   `resource://mathematics-book`); edit it if you like.
2. Pick a **Type**: **Static** (fixed content) or **Template** (dynamic, with
   variables).
3. Under **Content source**, choose **File** and attach one, or **Text** and
   paste it.

![The New Resource panel with a title, auto-generated URI, type, and an uploaded PDF](/images/resource-math-book.webp)

Once it's processed the resource shows **Ready**, with its type, size, and URI.
Turn on **Cite this resource in replies** to have your assistant reference it as
a source in answers that use it.

![A resource's details: Ready, source, type, size, URI and the "Cite this resource in replies" switch](/images/resource-details.webp)

## Crawl a website

Select **Add website**, enter a starting **URL** (same-origin links are
followed), an optional **Title** and **Description**, and set **Max pages** and
**Max depth**. Then select **Start crawl**.

![The Add Website panel with URL, title, description, and max pages and depth fields](/images/resource-webpage.webp)

When the crawl finishes, the site's pages are indexed and searchable, shown
**Ready** just like any other resource.

## Keep sources up to date

Drive, OneDrive, and website sources can be refreshed. Open the source and
select **Sync now**. Only new or changed content is re-indexed, and what was
removed at the source is removed here too. On **Pro** and **Enterprise** you can
also turn on **Sync automatically** and choose **Daily** or **Weekly**; on Free,
sync by hand.

| --- | --- | --- |
| Searchable (embedded) content | 5 MB | 1 GB included, then $2/GB on Pro |
