Resources are the documents and knowledge your assistant can search, so it answers from your content instead of guessing. Add them from Google Drive, OneDrive, a website crawl, or by uploading files directly. Each one gets a URI and, once processed, is marked Ready.

Want the full picture? This is the quick version. The complete Resources guide covers Google Drive and OneDrive imports, website crawls, uploads, citations, and sync.

Where resources come from

Open Knowledge in the rail; it opens on the Resources tab. Everything is grouped by source: Google Drive, OneDrive, Websites, My folder (your own uploads), and Data attachments (files uploaded from a row on the Data page). The buttons at the top add to each: Add from Google Drive, Add from OneDrive, Add website, and (inside a folder) Add files.

Import from Google Drive or OneDrive

Choose Add from Google Drive. The first time, you connect your Google account; then the picker opens. Browse My Drive, Shared with me, Shared drives, or Starred, tick the files or folders you want, and select Add selected.

OneDrive works the same way: browse My files, Shared with me, Recent, or Drives, then add your selection.

Upload a file

Open My folder and select Add files. In the New Resource panel:

  1. Give it a Title. Its URI is generated from the title (like resource://mathematics-book); edit it if you like.
  2. Pick a Type: Static (fixed content) or Template (dynamic, with variables).
  3. Under Content source, choose File and attach one, or Text and paste it.

Once it’s processed the resource shows Ready, with its type, size, and URI. Turn on Cite this resource in replies to have your assistant reference it as a source in answers that use it.

Crawl a website

Select Add website, enter a starting URL (same-origin links are followed), an optional Title and Description, and set Max pages and Max depth. Then select Start crawl.

When the crawl finishes, the site’s pages are indexed and searchable, shown Ready just like any other resource.

Keep sources up to date

Drive, OneDrive, and website sources can be refreshed. Open the source and select Sync now. Only new or changed content is re-indexed, and what was removed at the source is removed here too. On Pro and Enterprise you can also turn on Sync automatically and choose Daily or Weekly; on Free, sync by hand.

Limits

Free Pro / Enterprise
Searchable (embedded) content 5 MB 1 GB included, then $2/GB on Pro
File storage 30 MB Unlimited
Automatic sync None Daily or weekly

Create your Ganju account with Google or GitHub, accept an invitation, and manage your profile.
You're signed in to Ganju and looking at your organizations.

Ganju is free to start, no credit card required. There's no separate sign-up:
the first time you sign in, your account is created.

## Sign in

1. Go to [app.ganju.ai](https://app.ganju.ai).
2. Tick **I have read and accept the Terms & Conditions and the Privacy
   Policy**. The sign-in buttons stay disabled until you do.
3. Select **Sign in with Google** or **Sign in with GitHub** and approve the
   request on that site.

You land on your organizations. On your very first sign-in that's the **Create
Your Organization** form. Next step:
[create an organization & project](/docs/getting-started/organization-and-project/).

![The sign-in page: Sign in with Google, Sign in with GitHub and the Terms and Privacy checkbox](/images/sign-in.webp)

The app speaks English and Spanish. The sign-in page offers the other language
at the bottom (**¿Prefieres español?**), and the app remembers your choice.

## If you were invited

An invitation arrives by email and points to a page that says **You've been
invited**. Sign in with **the same email address the invitation was sent to**,
then select **Accept invitation** (or **Decline**).

- Signed in with a different address? The page tells you which address the
  invitation is for. Sign out and sign in with that one.
- Invitations expire after **7 days**. An expired, revoked, or already-used
  link says so; ask whoever invited you to send a new one.
- You can also accept from the **Organizations** page, under **Your
  invitations**, with **Accept** or **Decline**.

An invitation is either to a whole organization or to a single project. A
project invitation gives you that project only; the organization's card shows
**Project access**.

## Your account

Your avatar at the bottom of the rail opens a menu with **Account**,
**Settings**, **Documentation**, and **Logout**. **Account** lets you:

- Upload a profile image and change your **Name**.
- See your **Linked accounts** and **Link** or **Unlink** Google and GitHub, so
  you can sign in with either. You must keep at least one linked account.

To download your personal data or delete your account, see
[Settings → Your data](/docs/settings/#your-data) and
[Danger zone](/docs/settings/#danger-zone).

## Signing in from a terminal

Developers using the [`ganju` CLI](/docs/tools/cli/) sign in once per machine.
It opens the same sign-in in your browser:

```bash
ganju login     # sign in on this machine
ganju whoami    # who this machine is signed in as
ganju logout    # forget the stored token
```

## Troubleshooting

- **The buttons don't respond.** Tick the Terms and Privacy checkbox first.
- **I signed in and don't see my team's organization.** You signed in with a
  different account than the one invited. Sign out and sign in with the invited
  address.
- **"You don't have access to this project".** You're in the organization but
  not in that project. A project admin can add you from the project's members in
  the organization settings.

Switch on the actions your AI can take: connect an integration, point it at your own API, or let the Assistant write one.
An integration like Gmail connected, with the tools you want switched on.

**Tools** are the actions your assistant can take on your behalf, from the
built-in resource helpers to integrations like Gmail, Slack, and Google
Calendar. Open **Tools** in the rail. The page has three tabs:

| Tab | What's in it |
| --- | --- |
| **[Functions](/docs/tools/functions/)** | Custom actions written in code, by the [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) for you, or by a developer with the CLI. Pro. |
| **[HTTP Endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/)** | An API you already run, described once and turned into a named tool. No code. |
| **[Catalog](/docs/tools/catalog/)** | The integrations Ganju ships, plus remote MCP servers like GitHub and Notion. |

This page is about the **Catalog**; it's where everyone starts.

> **Want the full picture?** This is the quick version. The complete
> **[Tools](/docs/tools/)** guide documents every integration, tool by tool.

## Built-in tools

Every project starts with five **Built-in** tools already on (**List
Resources**, **Read Resource**, **Send Resource**, **Search Resources**, and
**List Prompts**), so your assistant can work with your knowledge right away.
They need no connection.

## Browse the catalog

The **Catalog** lists every integration you can add: Gmail, Outlook, Slack,
Slack Search, Google Calendar, Cal.com, Web Search, Built-in, and remote MCP
servers. Each card shows how many of its tools you've enabled (Gmail alone
offers 18). Use **Search integrations...** or the filters **All**, **On**,
**Off**, and **Needs connection** to narrow the list.

![Tools, Catalog tab: the tools-exposed bar, search, filters and the integration cards](/images/tools-catalog.webp)

## Connect an integration

1. Open an integration to see the tools it offers.
2. Select **Connect Gmail** (or **Connect** plus the integration's name) and
   sign in to that account. You only connect once for the whole integration.
   Some integrations ask for an API key instead (**Add … API key**).
3. Switch on just the tools you want; here, **Send Email**. Each tool you
   enable is available to your assistant straight away.

![Gmail connected: the Connected chip, Disconnect, and each tool with its switch](/images/tool-gmail-enabled.webp)

Back in the catalog, Gmail now shows **Connected** with your enabled count
(`1/18 tools enabled`).

## On, off, or removed

- The **switch** turns a tool off but keeps its settings and connection, and the
  row then reads **Off · settings kept**.
- **Remove** deletes a tool and its settings.
- **Disconnect** removes the whole integration's connection.

Prefer the switch. Every enabled tool's description is re-sent to the model on
every turn, so a long list costs more and makes the model's choice harder. The
counter at the top shows how many tools are exposed out of **40**. Past that,
channels stop sending the extras. Home's [Tool health](/docs/analytics/#tool-health)
lists tools no one has used in 30 days, with a **Disable** button.

## Limits

| | Free | Pro / Enterprise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tools switched on at once | 7 (built-ins included) | 40 |
| HTTP endpoints per project | 3 | Unlimited |
| Functions | None | ✓ |

## When the catalog doesn't cover it

- **Ask the [Assistant](/docs/assistant/)** (Pro). Describe what the bot should
  do; it writes the action, tests it, and turns it on with your click. The
  actions it writes appear under **Functions**, where you can read them. To add
  or change one, ask the Assistant.
- **[HTTP Endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/)**: describe one request
  against an API you already run and it becomes a named tool. No code, and it's
  on every plan.
- **Developers** write functions in a repository and ship them with the
  [`ganju` CLI](/docs/tools/cli/):

```bash
ganju init my-tools   # scaffold a project that deploys as-is
cd my-tools
ganju login
ganju link            # pick the organization and project
ganju deploy          # bundle, upload, publish
```

A version uploaded from the CLI shows in **Functions** read-only; it changes in
the repository, with `ganju deploy`.

Copy your project's MCP URL and connect it to any MCP client (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, or VS Code) so your AI works right inside the tools you already use.

Every Ganju project is a **Model Context Protocol (MCP) server**. That means any
MCP-compatible client (**Claude**, **ChatGPT**, **Cursor**, **VS Code**, and
more) can connect to it and get your project's [prompts](/docs/prompts/),
[resources](/docs/resources/), [tools](/docs/tools/), and [data](/docs/data/).
Where [channels](/docs/channels/) deliver your assistant to other people, MCP
clients wire it into your own workflow.

## Copy your MCP URL

Each project has its own **MCP URL**, shown at the top right of the project
**Home**. Click it (**Click to copy**) to copy it. That single link is
everything a client needs. It looks like:

```
https://mcp.ganju.ai/your-project-slug
```

![The project Home with the MCP URL box, its copy and edit buttons at the top right](/images/project-home.webp)

## Change the URL

Select the pencil next to the MCP URL to open **Edit MCP URL**. Change the
**Slug** (the last part of the address) and the **Preview** updates the full
**MCP URL** and a ready-to-paste **Client config**, the JSON block most MCP
clients accept. Select **Save** to apply it.

![The Edit MCP URL dialog: the slug, the full MCP URL and the client config JSON](/images/home-mcp-edit.webp)

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-company": {
      "url": "https://mcp.ganju.ai/my-company"
    }
  }
}
```

A slug is 3 to 63 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens, starting and ending
with a letter or digit. Some slugs are reserved, and each one can only be used
by one project. New projects get a unique generated slug; you can set your own
on any plan.

> Changing the slug changes the address. Clients connected to the old URL stop
> reaching the project, so reconnect them with the new one.

## Add it to your client

The steps differ slightly per client, so follow each one's own documentation;
in every case you're pasting the **MCP URL** (or the client-config JSON):

- **Claude**: Settings → **Connectors** → **Add custom connector**, then paste
  your MCP URL. See
  [Claude's custom-connector guide](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11175166-get-started-with-custom-connectors-using-remote-mcp).
- **Claude Code**: add it from a terminal:

  ```bash
  claude mcp add --transport http my-company https://mcp.ganju.ai/my-company
  ```

- **ChatGPT**: enable **Developer mode**, then Settings → **Connectors** →
  **Advanced**, and add your server URL. See
  [Developer mode and MCP apps in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12584461-developer-mode-and-mcp-apps-in-chatgpt).
- **Cursor**: Settings → **Tools & MCP** → **New MCP Server**, or drop the JSON
  in `.cursor/mcp.json`. See [Cursor's MCP docs](https://cursor.com/docs/mcp).
- **VS Code**: Command Palette → **MCP: Add Server**, or edit
  `.vscode/mcp.json`. See
  [Add MCP servers in VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers).

## Sign in from the client

The first time a client connects, it opens a Ganju sign-in in your browser. Sign
in with your Ganju account and approve the connection. From then on, the client
acts as you:

- **Only project members can connect.** An account that isn't a member of the
  project is refused, even if it's in the organization. Add people under
  [Settings → Projects → Members](/docs/settings/#projects).
- The client sees the project's prompts, resources, and the tools that are
  turned on. With [Data](/docs/data/), a signed-in person works on every table,
  and an organization member also gets the database's admin tools.
- Removing someone from the project stops their client on its next request.

Once connected, ask the client to use your tools or search your resources, and it
routes through your Ganju project securely.

## Approving actions

Two safeguards apply to tools that send, change, or delete something:

- **Confirm sensitive actions** (an organization setting, off by default): the
  first call comes back *not run yet*, the assistant asks you in its chat, and
  runs it on a second call. See
  [Settings → Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions).
- **After outside content** (always on): once the session has read outside
  content (an email, a web page, another server's answer), that content could
  have been written to steer the assistant. A sensitive action then needs your
  own yes, outside the chat. The assistant gives you a link to a dashboard page,
  **An assistant wants to take an action**, showing the action and **With these
  details**. Select **Approve** or **Deny**, then tell the assistant. An approval
  runs once, with exactly those details, and requests expire 10 minutes after
  the assistant makes them. Only the person signed in to that client's
  connection can answer.

Read-only tools (searching, listing, reading) run straight away in both
cases.

## Watching and billing

**Home** charts all activity across channels and MCP clients together (a client
like `claude-code` shows up right next to your Telegram channel), and
[Tool health](/docs/analytics/#tool-health) lists every call a client made.

An MCP client runs its own model, so its conversations aren't **assistant
replies**, so they don't use your reply allowance. Calls to
[functions](/docs/tools/functions/) you wrote do count as **custom tool calls**,
the same as from a channel. See
[Settings → Billing & plan](/docs/settings/#billing--plan).

## Troubleshooting

- **"You do not have access".** The account you signed in with isn't a member of
  this project. Sign in with another account, or ask a project member to add
  you.
- **The client can't connect after I changed the slug.** It's still using the
  old URL. Remove the server from the client and add the new one.
- **A tool is missing in the client.** It's turned off on the **Tools** page, or
  the client cached an older tool list. Reconnect or restart the client.
- **An action says it needs approval and there's no link.** The connection has
  no signed-in user (for example, a machine token), so there's nobody to
  approve; such calls don't run after outside content.

  • Confirm sensitive actions (an organization setting, off by default): the first call comes back not run yet, the assistant asks you in its chat, and runs it on a second call. See Settings → Confirm sensitive actions.
  • After outside content (always on): once the session has read outside content (an email, a web page, another server’s answer), that content could have been written to steer the assistant. A sensitive action then needs your own yes, outside the chat. The assistant gives you a link to a dashboard page, An assistant wants to take an action, showing the action and With these details. Select Approve or Deny, then tell the assistant. An approval runs once, with exactly those details, and requests expire 10 minutes after the assistant makes them. Only the person signed in to that client’s connection can answer.

Read-only tools (searching, listing, reading) run straight away in both cases.

Watching and billing

Home charts all activity across channels and MCP clients together (a client like claude-code shows up right next to your Telegram channel), and Tool health lists every call a client made.

An MCP client runs its own model, so its conversations aren’t assistant replies, so they don’t use your reply allowance. Calls to functions you wrote do count as custom tool calls, the same as from a channel. See Settings → Billing & plan.

Troubleshooting

  • “You do not have access”. The account you signed in with isn’t a member of this project. Sign in with another account, or ask a project member to add you.
  • The client can’t connect after I changed the slug. It’s still using the old URL. Remove the server from the client and add the new one.
  • A tool is missing in the client. It’s turned off on the Tools page, or the client cached an older tool list. Reconnect or restart the client.
  • An action says it needs approval and there’s no link. The connection has no signed-in user (for example, a machine token), so there’s nobody to approve; such calls don’t run after outside content.
How Ganju is structured: an organization holds your team, billing, and plan; each project inside it is a self-contained workspace for one assistant.

Ganju has two levels. Your **organization** represents your team or company:
it's where members, billing, your [plan](/docs/settings/), and your own language
models live. Inside it, each **project** is a self-contained workspace for one
assistant, with its own [knowledge](/docs/resources/), [prompts](/docs/prompts/),
[data](/docs/data/), [tools](/docs/tools/), [channels](/docs/channels/), and
[MCP URL](/docs/mcp/). One organization can hold many projects.

## What lives where

| Organization | Project |
| --- | --- |
| Plan, billing, and usage | Resources and prompts (**Knowledge**) |
| Members (Owner and admins) | Its own member list |
| Language models you bring (**Models**) | Data (tables, triggers, schedules) |
| **Confirm sensitive actions** (applies to every project) | Tools: catalog connections, HTTP endpoints, functions |
| Assistant credits (shared by all projects) | Channels and their **Bot instructions** |
| | MCP URL, activity, and tool health |
| | Access tokens for the CLI |

## Why two levels

- **One workspace per assistant.** Give each client, product, or use case its
  own project, so their knowledge, data, and tools stay completely separate.
- **Shared team and billing.** Members and the plan sit at the organization
  level, so everything inside is covered by one subscription and one member
  list.
- **Clean separation, one account.** Run a Free organization for personal
  projects and a Pro one for your company, side by side, from the same login.

## Switch between them

The **Organizations & Projects** switcher (the grid icon at the top of the left
rail) is how you move around. Pick an organization on the left (each shows its
member count) to see its projects on the right, then open one. At the bottom:
**Manage organizations** and **New project**.

![The Organizations & Projects switcher: organizations on the left, their projects on the right, Manage organizations and New project](/images/org-project-switcher.webp)

## Create a project

1. Select **New project** in the switcher. The **Create a new project** dialog
   shows which organization it goes into (**In …**).
2. Enter a **Name** (at least 3 characters) and, optionally, a **Description**.
3. Select **Create**.

You land on the new project's Home, which starts with the five built-in tools.
On Pro and Enterprise it offers to **Open the Assistant**.

![The Create a new project dialog: Name and Description](/images/new-project-dialog.webp)

**Free** organizations have **one project**. Creating a second one asks you to
upgrade; Pro and Enterprise have no project limit.

## Manage organizations

**Manage organizations** opens the **Organizations** page, listing every
organization you belong to. Each card shows your badges (**Owner** if you
created it, and its plan: **Free**, **Pro**, or **Enterprise**), its project and
member counts, and when it was created, with **Invite** and **Settings**
actions. If you were added to just one project in an organization, its card
reads **Project access** instead and says how many projects you can open.

Above the list, **Your invitations** shows invitations waiting for you, with
**Accept** and **Decline**.

![The Organizations page: one card per organization with its role and plan, counts, and Invite and Settings](/images/new-org.webp)

### Create another organization

Select **New organization**. The **Create a new organization** dialog asks for
the organization **Name** and its first project's **Project name** and
**Project description**. Every organization starts with one project.

You can own **one Free organization**. To create more, at least one
organization you own must be on a paid plan: upgrade one to Pro and you can add
others (each new one starts on Free with its own billing).

## Who can do what

Organization membership and project membership are separate:

- **Organization members** see the organization's full **Settings**: rename
  it, billing, members, projects, models. The person who creates an
  organization is its **Owner**; everyone invited to it joins as an **Admin**.
  Only the Owner can remove the organization.
- **Project members** can open that project. Whoever creates a project is a
  member of it; anyone else is added from **Settings → Projects → Members**, or
  by an invitation to that project.

So someone can be in a project without being in the organization (their card
on **Organizations** reads **Project access**, and Settings shows them only the
projects they're in), and an organization member who opens a project they
aren't in sees **You don't have access to this project**, with a link to the
organization settings where a project member can add them.

## From a terminal

The [`ganju` CLI](/docs/tools/cli/) works against one project at a time. Link a
folder to an organization and project by name or id:

```bash
ganju link                                                # choose from a list
ganju link --organization "Acme" --project "Support bot"  # no prompts
ganju link --status                                       # what this folder points at
```

Build reusable, multi-turn prompt templates with typed variables. Each becomes a slash command in your linked chat channels and a prompt in any MCP client.

**Prompts** are reusable message templates your project exposes through its MCP
server. In any linked chat channel, each prompt becomes a **slash command** people
can run by name, so a common request turns into a one-word shortcut. A prompt can
be a single message or a full multi-turn exchange, and any `{{variable}}` you use
is filled in when the prompt runs.

## Why use prompts

- **Turn repeat work into one command.** Capture a request you send again and
  again once, then run it as `/command`, with no re-typing, no forgetting the details.
- **Consistent results every time.** Everyone triggers the exact same wording and
  structure, so your AI answers the same way no matter who asks.
- **Share expertise with your whole team.** A well-crafted prompt written once is
  instantly available to every teammate in the channel, with no prompt-engineering
  skill required to use it.
- **Guide the model with typed inputs.** Each variable has a type, a description
  and a required flag, so MCP clients know exactly what to ask for.
- **Steer the conversation.** Multi-turn User/Assistant templates set the tone and
  give the model examples to follow, producing sharper, more predictable replies.
- **Edit without redeploying.** Update a prompt in the dashboard and the new
  version is live in every linked channel and MCP client right away.

## Where prompts live

Prompts sit next to your resources. Open **Knowledge** in the project's sidebar
and pick the **Prompts** tab (the **Resources** tab is the other one). The page
lists every prompt as a card with its title, its slash command, its description
and the date it last changed. Until you create one, it shows **No prompts yet**
with a **New prompt** button.

![Knowledge, Prompts tab: a prompt card with its /start command and the New prompt button](/images/knowledge-prompts-tab.webp)

## Create a prompt

Select **New prompt**. The **New Prompt** panel opens on the right with
**Title**, **Description** and **Messages**.

![The New Prompt panel: Title, Description, Messages with the Visual/JSON switch and Add message](/images/new-prompt-panel.webp)

## Name it and write a message

Give the prompt a **Title**. Ganju turns it into the slash command shown right
under it, as **Slash command:** in lowercase, with every run of spaces or symbols
replaced by `_`. "Summarize Article" becomes `/summarize_article`; "test"
becomes `/test`. Two prompts in a project can't share the same command: Ganju
refuses the second one with "A prompt with this command name already exists".

Add a short **Description** so teammates know what it does (Telegram and
Discord also show it next to the command in their menus), then write your first
message.

Drop `{{variables}}` anywhere you want a value supplied at run time. In this
example the user message is `hi user {{name}} your age is {{age}}`, so `name` and
`age` become inputs. A variable name uses letters, digits and underscores.

![The New Prompt panel with the title "test", slash command /test, a description, and a user message containing {{name}} and {{age}}](/images/new-prompt-1.webp)

## Configure the variables

Ganju **auto-detects** every `{{variable}}` in your messages and lists them under
**Variables**. Each new one starts as a required String. For each one you can:

- set the **Type**: **String**, **Number** or **Boolean**;
- add a **Description** to tell whoever runs the prompt what to put there;
- tick or untick **Required**.

Here `{{name}}` is a required String ("user's name") and `{{age}}` a required
Number ("user's age").

![The Variables section listing {{name}} as a required String and {{age}} as a required Number, each with a type and description](/images/new-prompt-2.webp)

Every `{{variable}}` in a message must be listed in Variables; Ganju won't save a
prompt that uses one it doesn't know. When the prompt runs, a variable with no
value is left empty in the text.

## Add more messages

Real prompts are often a conversation, not a single line. Select **Add message**
to append another turn, and switch each message between **User** and **Assistant**
to shape the exchange. This second message is an Assistant turn,
`this is a new {{message}}`.

![The Messages section with two messages: a User message and an Assistant message containing {{message}}](/images/new-prompt-3.webp)

New variables you introduce are picked up automatically: `{{message}}` now
appears alongside `{{name}}` and `{{age}}` in the Variables list, ready to type
and describe.

![The Variables section now showing {{name}}, {{age}}, and {{message}}, each configurable](/images/new-prompt-4.webp)

A prompt needs at least one message. If the last message is an Assistant turn
(a canned greeting, say), the channel bot still adds the person's own text after
it, so the model always has something to answer.

## Edit as JSON

Prefer to work with raw structure? Switch **Visual / JSON** at any time to edit
the messages as an array of `{ role, content }` objects, where `role` is `user`
or `assistant`. It's the fastest way to paste in a template you already have,
and it stays in sync with the visual editor.

![The Messages editor in JSON mode showing an array of role/content objects](/images/new-prompt-5.webp)

```json
[
  { "role": "user", "content": "Summarize this article in three bullets: {{article}}" },
  { "role": "assistant", "content": "Sure, here are the key points:" }
]
```

## Save, edit and delete

Select **Create** and the prompt is saved as a card. Select a card to see its
description and messages; from there you can edit it (the panel becomes **Edit
Prompt**) or delete it. Deleting asks you to confirm and can't be undone.

Every change reaches your channels on its own: Ganju refreshes the command menu
of your Telegram and Discord bots whenever a prompt is added, renamed or
removed.

## Run a prompt from a channel

In a linked channel, type the command, then any text you want to pass:

```
/summarize_article https://example.com/news/launch
```

- The text after the command goes into the prompt's **first variable**. Other
  variables stay empty, so put the one people will type first.
- The prompt's messages, with the variable filled in, replace what the person
  typed, and the bot answers them as usual, with your resources, tools and
  [bot instructions](/docs/channels/#tell-your-bot-how-to-answer).
- A command answers right away, without waiting for a pause in the conversation.
- If no prompt has that name, or the prompt can't be built (for example a
  required variable got no value), the message is answered like any other.

How people find the commands depends on the app:

| Channel | How a prompt shows up |
| --- | --- |
| [Telegram](/docs/channels/telegram/) | In the bot's **/** command menu, with the description. In groups, `/command@yourbot` works too. |
| [Discord](/docs/channels/discord/) | As a native slash command with one optional `text` option. Needs the Interactions Endpoint URL. |
| [Slack](/docs/channels/slack/) | Create a Slack slash command with the same name pointing at Ganju's Request URL. |
| [WhatsApp](/docs/channels/whatsapp/) | No menu: people type `/command` at the start of a message. |

Telegram and Discord list at most 100 commands, and a command name there is cut
to 32 characters and must start with a letter. The name `link` is reserved for
the `/link` command and is never used for a prompt.

Prompts that come from an MCP server you added in [Tools](/docs/tools/) are
commands too, named after their title.

## Use prompts from an MCP client

Your project is also an MCP server, so every prompt is available in
[MCP clients](/docs/mcp/) like Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor under its command name,
with its variables as arguments (descriptions and required flags included). The
client asks for the values and inserts the result into the chat.

## Let the assistant write them

The project [assistant](/docs/assistant/) can list, create, edit and remove
prompts for you: describe the command you want ("a /menu command that lists
today's specials") and it proposes the prompt for you to approve.

## Plan limits

The **Free** plan holds up to **3 prompts** per project. **Pro** and
**Enterprise** have no limit. See [Settings](/docs/settings/) for plans.

## Troubleshooting

- **"A prompt with this command name already exists".** Another prompt's title
  gives the same command (case and punctuation don't count). Change the title.
- **The command doesn't show in Telegram's menu.** Titles that don't start with a
  letter are left out of the menu, and Telegram can take a moment to refresh it.
  Typing the command still works.
- **Discord shows no slash commands.** Set the Interactions Endpoint URL and
  invite the bot with the `applications.commands` scope; see
  [Discord](/docs/channels/discord/).
- **Slack says the command isn't valid.** Slack only accepts slash commands
  you've created in the Slack app; see [Slack](/docs/channels/slack/).

Give your AI knowledge to search: import from Google Drive or OneDrive, upload files or paste text, crawl a website, keep it all in sync, and cite your sources.

**Resources** are the documents and knowledge your assistant can search, so it
answers from your own content instead of guessing. Add them from Google Drive,
OneDrive, a website crawl, or by uploading files and pasting text. Each resource
gets a URI (like `resource://price-list`) and, once processed, is marked
**Ready** and becomes searchable by your bot on every channel and by any MCP
client.

## Why add resources

- **Grounded, accurate answers.** Your AI replies from your actual documents, not
  from general training: fewer made-up answers, more citations you can trust.
- **One knowledge base, every channel.** Add a file once and it's searchable from
  every linked channel and MCP client at the same time.
- **Bring what you already have.** Pull straight from Google Drive or OneDrive,
  upload files, or crawl a whole website, with no reformatting or copy-paste.
- **Always current.** Sync a drive or a website and only what changed is indexed
  again; on Pro it happens on its own, daily or weekly.
- **Show your sources.** With citations on, the bot lists the exact resource
  behind each answer, with a link to the page or file.

## Where resources live

Open **Knowledge** in the project's sidebar. It has two tabs: **Resources** and
[Prompts](/docs/prompts/). The Resources tab has two views, switched at the top
right:

- **Sources** groups everything by where it came from, one card per source with
  its count and an add button: **Google Drive**, **OneDrive**, **Websites**,
  **My folder** (your uploads and pasted text) and, once there are some, **Data
  attachments** (files uploaded from a row on the [Data](/docs/data/) page).
- **All resources** lists every resource in one place.

Inside a source, or in All resources, a **Search** box filters by title, URI or
description, and **Back** returns to the cards.

![Knowledge, Resources tab, Sources view: Google Drive, OneDrive, Websites and My folder](/images/knowledge-resources.webp)

## Upload a file or paste text

Open **My folder** and select **Add files**. The **New Resource** panel asks for:

- **Title**: a readable name (3 to 200 characters). Picking a file fills it
  with the file's name.
- **URI**: generated from the title (like `resource://price-list`); edit it if
  you like. Each URI must be unique in the project.
- **Type**: **Static** (fixed content) for a normal document, or **Template**
  (dynamic with variables) for content with placeholders like `{userId}` that an
  MCP client fills in.
- **Description**: what the resource is about (up to 1,000 characters). It's
  indexed too, so a good description helps the bot find it.
- **Content source**: **File** to upload one, or **Text** to paste or write
  content directly, with its **MIME Type** (plain text, CSV, HTML, JSON, YAML,
  code and other text formats) and **Encoding**.
- **Advanced options**: the MCP annotations clients can read: **Audience**,
  **Priority (0 to 1)** and **Icons**.

![The New Resource panel: Title, URI, Type, Description, File or Text, and Advanced options](/images/resource-new-file.webp)

Select **Create**. The resource shows **Indexing** while Ganju reads it, then
**Ready** (or **Failed**, if the file couldn't be read).

### File types and sizes

One file can be up to **500 MB**. What Ganju **reads and makes searchable**:

| Kind | Formats |
| --- | --- |
| Documents | PDF, Word (`.doc`, `.docx`), PowerPoint (`.pptx`) |

## Troubleshooting

- **"Unsupported mime type".** The browser reported a file type Ganju doesn't
  store. Save it as one of the formats above (PDF is the safest).
- **A resource shows Failed.** The file couldn't be read (a damaged or
  password-protected file, for example). Export it again and upload the new copy
  (edit the resource and replace the file).
- **A website crawl found few pages.** Raise **Max depth** or **Max pages**,
  and check that the links stay on the same domain as the starting URL
  (`www.example.com` and `example.com` are different origins).
- **"Resource URI must be unique".** Another resource uses that URI or URL.
  Change the URI, or open the existing website instead of adding it again.
- **"Connect Google Drive to import files".** The Google or Microsoft session
  expired. Select **Add from Google Drive** (or OneDrive) again to reconnect.

### Confirm sensitive actions

Off by default. Turn it on (**Confirmation is on**) and the assistant asks the
person before any action that reaches someone else or can't be undone, and runs
it only on a yes. It applies to every project in the organization.

- **In channels** (Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack, Discord), the bot holds the call
  and asks in the chat. Under its question it lists exactly what a yes will
  run (the tool and each argument), written by the platform, not the model.
  Only the person who was asked can answer. A yes within 30 minutes runs those
  stored calls; anything else, including "yes, but change the time", drops
  them. Telegram private chats, Discord and WhatsApp offer **Yes / No** buttons;
  elsewhere the answer is typed.
- **In MCP clients** (Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT), the first call comes back *not
  run yet* with a one-time token. The assistant asks in its own chat and, on a
  yes, calls again with the token. It only works for those exact arguments,
  once, within 10 minutes.

**What counts as sensitive** comes from each tool's
[MCP annotations](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools#tool-annotations):
anything not marked read-only (`readOnlyHint: true`) or safe to undo
(`destructiveHint: false`) is confirmed.

- **Built-in tools** are already marked. Searching, listing and reading run
  straight away. Sending or forwarding email, posting to Slack, creating,
  changing or deleting calendar events and bookings, and deleting mail or
  drafts are confirmed.
- **[HTTP endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/)**: choose **What it does** in
  the endpoint dialog. Left unset, a `GET` counts as a read and any other
  method is confirmed.
- **[Functions](/docs/tools/functions/)**: each function declares its
  `annotations`, and developers set them in `ganju.json`. The
  [order desk example](/docs/tools/examples/#order-desk) shows one tool of
  each kind.
- **Connected MCP servers** use the annotations the remote server declares, and
  you can mark which of their tools only read.

A tool that declares nothing is treated as one that may change things, so it's
confirmed on every call, lookups included. `ganju build` warns about it.

What it doesn't do: an MCP client's assistant is told to ask, but the server
never sees the person's words, only the second call. It stops a sensitive
action from happening in one step, not an assistant set on skipping the
question.

**After outside content, whatever this setting says.** Once an MCP client's
session has read outside content (an email, a web page, another server's
answer), a sensitive action needs the signed-in person's own approval in the
dashboard. See [MCP clients → Approving actions](/docs/mcp/#approving-actions).

### How the message allowance really works

The one number to understand is **assistant replies**. Only your assistant's
_replies_ count; incoming user messages are always free.

Every plan includes an allowance of replies that run on **Ganju's shared model**.
Because Ganju pays for that inference, the shared model is an _allowance_, not
unlimited:

- **Free**: 100 replies a month on the shared model. When you hit the cap the
  assistant pauses until the next cycle, or you upgrade. Free can't bring its
  own model key.
- **Pro**: 3,000 replies a month included, of which up to **1,000 may run on
  the shared model**. Past those 1,000, shared replies keep working and bill at
  the higher shared rate below. Adding your own provider key in
  [Models](#models-bring-your-own) moves them to the much cheaper own-key rate,
  which is what most people do once they're sending real volume. The billing
  page links straight to it (**connect your own model**).

### Overage (Pro)

Pro adds nothing to your bill until you go past the included amounts:

- **Extra replies on your own model key**: $2 per 1,000. This is a **platform
  fee** for running the tools and compute of each turn, _not_ a resale of model
  tokens (you pay your provider directly via your key).
- **Extra replies on Ganju's model**: $15 per 1,000 beyond the first 1,000.
  Higher because Ganju is buying the inference for you, so this rate covers a
  real cost rather than just the platform work.
- **Extra embedded content (RAG)**: $2 per GB beyond the included 1 GB.
  Searchable content is stored with a search index several times its own size,
  which is why this costs more per GB than plain file storage (which is free).
- **Extra calls to tools you wrote**: $5 per million beyond the included
  1,000,000. Only your own code counts here; calls to the integrations Ganju
  ships, and to remote MCP servers you connect, are bundled.
- **Extra [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) credits**: $2 per 100 beyond the
  included 1,000, up to the limit you set under **Extra credits a month**.
- **Custom domain**: $15 / mo add-on.

### If a payment fails or you cancel

While a subscription is active, trialing, or past due, its paid features keep
working. Once it's canceled or unpaid, the organization falls back to the Free
plan's limits. Project databases are kept, read-only.

> Want more for free? Ganju is Apache-2.0, so you can
> [self-host](/docs/deploy/) and run on your own keys.

### Access tokens

A token acts as you, on that project and nothing else: for a CI job, a
container, or a server reached over SSH.

1. Under the project, open **Access tokens**.
2. Fill in **What is it for** (e.g. "GitHub Actions deploy"). It's the only thing
   anyone will have to go on when deciding whether revoking it breaks a deploy.
3. Pick **Expires**: **In 30 days**, **In 90 days**, **In a year**, or **Never**.
4. Select **Create token**, copy the value, and select **I have copied it**.
   It's shown **once**; Ganju keeps only a hash.

Set it as `GANJU_API_TOKEN` wherever the CLI runs; `ganju deploy` works with it
unchanged. Each token shows when it was last used and when it expires;
**Revoke token** stops it immediately. A token whose owner was deleted is marked
**Inactive** and no longer works, so revoke it and create a new one.

![A project's Access tokens: "What is it for", Expires and Create token](/images/settings-access-tokens.webp)

The same from a terminal, in a folder linked to the project:

```bash
ganju token create "GitHub Actions" --expires 90   # days, or "never"
ganju token list
ganju token revoke "GitHub Actions"
```

A token can't create other tokens; run `ganju token create` from a browser
login (`ganju login`).

## Models: bring your own

By default your channels use the **System default** model. Under **Models**
you can bring your own (Pro and Enterprise; on Free this section explains it's a
Pro feature). Select **Add model**, then fill in:

- **Display name**: a label to recognize it by (e.g. "Production Gemini").
- **Model**: pick from the catalog: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro,
  GPT-5.4 mini, GPT-5.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, or
  **Custom (OpenAI-compatible)** for any service that speaks the OpenAI
  chat-completions protocol (a gateway, an aggregator, or your own server). A
  custom model also needs its **Model ID** (e.g. `anthropic/claude-opus-5`).

Confirm sensitive actions

Off by default. Turn it on (Confirmation is on) and the assistant asks the person before any action that reaches someone else or can’t be undone, and runs it only on a yes. It applies to every project in the organization.

  • In channels (Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack, Discord), the bot holds the call and asks in the chat. Under its question it lists exactly what a yes will run (the tool and each argument), written by the platform, not the model. Only the person who was asked can answer. A yes within 30 minutes runs those stored calls; anything else, including “yes, but change the time”, drops them. Telegram private chats, Discord and WhatsApp offer Yes / No buttons; elsewhere the answer is typed.
  • In MCP clients (Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT), the first call comes back not run yet with a one-time token. The assistant asks in its own chat and, on a yes, calls again with the token. It only works for those exact arguments, once, within 10 minutes.

What counts as sensitive comes from each tool’s MCP annotations: anything not marked read-only (readOnlyHint: true) or safe to undo (destructiveHint: false) is confirmed.

  • Built-in tools are already marked. Searching, listing and reading run straight away. Sending or forwarding email, posting to Slack, creating, changing or deleting calendar events and bookings, and deleting mail or drafts are confirmed.
  • HTTP endpoints: choose What it does in the endpoint dialog. Left unset, a GET counts as a read and any other method is confirmed.
  • Functions: each function declares its annotations, and developers set them in ganju.json. The order desk example shows one tool of each kind.
  • Connected MCP servers use the annotations the remote server declares, and you can mark which of their tools only read.

A tool that declares nothing is treated as one that may change things, so it’s confirmed on every call, lookups included. ganju build warns about it.

What it doesn’t do: an MCP client’s assistant is told to ask, but the server never sees the person’s words, only the second call. It stops a sensitive action from happening in one step, not an assistant set on skipping the question.

After outside content, whatever this setting says. Once an MCP client’s session has read outside content (an email, a web page, another server’s answer), a sensitive action needs the signed-in person’s own approval in the dashboard. See MCP clients → Approving actions.

How the message allowance really works

The one number to understand is assistant replies. Only your assistant’s replies count; incoming user messages are always free.

Every plan includes an allowance of replies that run on Ganju’s shared model. Because Ganju pays for that inference, the shared model is an allowance, not unlimited:

  • Free: 100 replies a month on the shared model. When you hit the cap the assistant pauses until the next cycle, or you upgrade. Free can’t bring its own model key.
  • Pro: 3,000 replies a month included, of which up to 1,000 may run on the shared model. Past those 1,000, shared replies keep working and bill at the higher shared rate below. Adding your own provider key in Models moves them to the much cheaper own-key rate, which is what most people do once they’re sending real volume. The billing page links straight to it (connect your own model).

Overage (Pro)

Pro adds nothing to your bill until you go past the included amounts:

  • Extra replies on your own model key: $2 per 1,000. This is a platform fee for running the tools and compute of each turn, not a resale of model tokens (you pay your provider directly via your key).
  • Extra replies on Ganju’s model: $15 per 1,000 beyond the first 1,000. Higher because Ganju is buying the inference for you, so this rate covers a real cost rather than just the platform work.
  • Extra embedded content (RAG): $2 per GB beyond the included 1 GB. Searchable content is stored with a search index several times its own size, which is why this costs more per GB than plain file storage (which is free).
  • Extra calls to tools you wrote: $5 per million beyond the included 1,000,000. Only your own code counts here; calls to the integrations Ganju ships, and to remote MCP servers you connect, are bundled.
  • Extra Assistant credits: $2 per 100 beyond the included 1,000, up to the limit you set under Extra credits a month.
  • Custom domain: $15 / mo add-on.

While a subscription is active, trialing, or past due, its paid features keep working. Once it’s canceled or unpaid, the organization falls back to the Free plan’s limits. Project databases are kept, read-only.

Give your bot the ability to take action: integrations like Gmail, Outlook, Slack and Calendar, your own HTTP APIs, and functions the Assistant or your developer writes.

**Tools** are the actions your bot can take. Where
[resources](/docs/resources/) let it *read* your knowledge, tools let it *do*
things: send an email, post to Slack, book a meeting, search the live web,
check your stock, or call your own API. Every project ships with a set of
built-in tools, and you add more whenever you need them.

## Three kinds of tool

The **Tools** page has three tabs, one per kind:

| Tab | What it is | Who makes it | Plan |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **[Functions](/docs/tools/functions/)** | Tools in code: several steps, logic, your database, a key combined with a computation. | The [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) writes them; a developer can deploy them with the [CLI](/docs/tools/cli/). The tab shows them read-only. | Pro and Enterprise |
| **[HTTP Endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/)** | One request against an API you already run, described in a form. No code. | You, in the form, or the Assistant. | All plans |
| **[Catalog](/docs/tools/catalog/)** | The integrations we ship and maintain: connect an account, switch on the tools you want. | You, or the Assistant. | All plans |

Start at the catalog. If your case is covered there, connecting an account is
the whole job. If it isn't, an HTTP endpoint is the shortest path to your own
API, and a function is what you reach for when one request isn't enough. You
don't have to choose yourself: tell the [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) what the
bot should do, and it picks the simplest of these that works.

![Tools, Catalog tab: the tools-exposed bar, search, filters and the integration cards](/images/tools-catalog.webp)

## Why use tools

- **Go from answering to acting.** Your bot doesn't just reply: it books the
  meeting, sends the follow-up, and saves the order.
- **Connect once, reuse everywhere.** Authorize an integration once, and every
  enabled tool works across all your channels and MCP clients.
- **Enable only what you need.** Turn tools on one by one, so the bot can do
  exactly what you allow and nothing more.
- **Bring your own API.** Add an HTTP endpoint or connect a vendor's remote
  MCP server to reach services we don't ship.

## How a tool works

Under the hood, your project is an **MCP server**, and a tool is a function
that server exposes to any connected AI. The flow is always the same:

1. **You enable a tool.** It's added to the bot's toolset and described to the
   model: its name, what it does, and the inputs it expects.
2. **You connect the integration once.** Tools that touch an outside account
   (Gmail, Slack, Calendar…) need access. You authorize it once, with OAuth or
   an API key, and Ganju stores the credential encrypted and refreshes it.
   Built-in tools need no connection.
3. **The model decides to call it.** When someone asks something in a channel
   or client, the model reads the available tools and, if one fits, calls it
   with the right arguments.
4. **Ganju runs it and returns the result.** The call runs with your stored
   credentials, and the result goes back to the model to finish the reply.
   Every call is recorded toward your usage.

When your organization turns on
[Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions), a
channel bot asks the person before a tool sends, books, deletes or changes
something, and runs it only on a yes.

## Default tools

Every project starts with five **built-in** tools already installed, so your
bot can work with your [resources](/docs/resources/) and
[prompts](/docs/prompts/) from day one, with no connection:

- **List Resources**: list every resource available to the bot.
- **Read Resource**: read the contents of a stored resource.
- **Send Resource**: deliver a resource to the person as a chat attachment.
- **Search Resources**: find the resources most relevant to a question, by
  meaning.
- **List Prompts**: list the prompts and commands the bot offers, and how to
  run them on the current channel.

Once the project has a [database](/docs/data/), the bot also gets
[data tools](/docs/data/#the-assistants-data-tools) to read and change the
tables you allow it to.

## Turning tools on and off

Every tool has a switch and a remove button, and they do different things.
**Off** stops offering the tool while keeping its settings and connection;
**Remove** deletes it with its settings. Only tools that are on count toward
the limit, so you can keep more configured than you expose at once:

- **Free**: up to 7 tools on at once.
- **Pro and Enterprise**: up to 40 on at once, the most a channel sends to the
  model.

Each tool counts as one, including each function and each tool of a remote MCP
server, and a function only triggers run doesn't count.

Keep the list short on purpose. Every enabled tool's description is sent to the
model on every turn, so a long list costs tokens and makes the model's choice
harder. The Catalog tab shows how many you expose.

## Available tools

Each integration has its own page with what it does, how to connect it, and
every tool it offers:

- **[Built-in](/docs/tools/built-in/)**: the five core resource and prompt
  tools every project ships with.
- **[Gmail](/docs/tools/gmail/)**: send, read, search and manage email (18
  tools).
- **[Outlook](/docs/tools/outlook/)**: Microsoft 365 mail (18 tools).
- **[Slack](/docs/tools/slack/)**: post messages, browse channels and upload
  files.
- **[Slack Search](/docs/tools/slack-search/)**: workspace-wide message search
  (a separate connection).
- **[Google Calendar](/docs/tools/google-calendar/)**: create and manage events
  and find open time.
- **[Cal.com](/docs/tools/calcom/)**: check availability and book or cancel
  meetings.
- **[Web Search](/docs/tools/web-search/)**: search the live web and extract
  page content.
- **[GitHub](/docs/tools/github/)**: GitHub's official remote MCP server for
  repos, issues and pull requests.
- **[Notion](/docs/tools/notion/)**: Notion's official remote MCP server to
  search and update pages and databases.
- **[Greeting](/docs/tools/greeting/)**: a tiny demo tool for testing a new
  server.

And the two you build:

- **[HTTP Endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/)**: your own APIs as named
  tools, with no code.
- **[Functions](/docs/tools/functions/)**: tools in code, written by the
  [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) or deployed with the
  **[`ganju` CLI](/docs/tools/cli/)**.

Install the ganju-cli skill so Claude Code and other coding agents can write, test, deploy and debug your Ganju functions with the CLI, and know which steps to leave to you.

The **ganju-cli skill** teaches an AI coding agent, such as Claude Code, how to
build [Functions](/docs/tools/functions/) with the [`ganju` CLI](/docs/tools/cli/).
With it installed you can say *"add a tool that looks up an order in our
Shopify store"* and the agent writes the `ganju.json` entry and the handler,
builds it, tests it, and tells you exactly what's left for you to do.

A skill is a folder of instructions the agent loads only when it's relevant,
so it costs nothing in conversations that aren't about Ganju. It follows the
open [Agent Skills](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview)
format.

## Install it

**For yourself, in every project (Claude Code):**

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju.git /tmp/ganju
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -r /tmp/ganju/skills/ganju-cli ~/.claude/skills/
```

**For your team, in one repository:** copy the folder to
`.claude/skills/ganju-cli` inside the repository that holds your tools and
commit it. Everyone who opens that repository with Claude Code gets it.

**In the Claude apps:** zip the `ganju-cli` folder and upload it as a custom
skill in Claude's settings.

To update, copy the folder again. The skill is plain Markdown, so you can read
exactly what it tells the agent in
[`skills/ganju-cli`](https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju/tree/main/skills/ganju-cli).

## When it's used

The agent loads the skill on its own when the conversation is about Ganju
tools, for example:

- the folder has a `ganju.json`, or the code imports `@ganju/sdk`;
- you mention a `ganju` command: `deploy`, `test`, `logs`, `secret`, …;
- you ask to add a tool to your Ganju assistant, bot or MCP server;
- you ask why a Ganju tool call failed.

## What it teaches

| Area | What the agent learns |
| --- | --- |
| **The workflow** | `init` → `link` → `build` → `test` → `deploy` → `logs`, and when each one is safe to run |
| **`ganju.json`** | Tool declarations, the supported JSON Schema subset, reserved names, `connections`, `allowedHosts`, `timeoutMs`, `resourceAccess` |
| **Handlers** | `defineTool`, the Worker runtime (no Node APIs), and error messages the model can act on |

The five core tools every project ships with: how your assistant lists, searches, reads, and delivers your resources and prompts.

Every project starts with five **built-in** tools already on. They're the core
that lets your assistant work with your [resources](/docs/resources/) and
[prompts](/docs/prompts/) from day one, no connection or API key required. This
is what makes a Ganju assistant answer from *your* content instead of guessing.

You'll find them on the **Built-in** card of the
[Catalog](/docs/tools/catalog/) tab, each with its own switch.

![The Built-in integration with its five tools switched on](/images/tools-catalog-builtin.webp)

## Tools

The name in parentheses is the tool name MCP clients and logs show.

- **Search Resources** (`search-resources`): the workhorse. It searches every
  resource on the server for the passages most relevant to a `query`, **by
  meaning and by exact words**, so it finds paraphrases as well as literal IDs,
  codes, SKUs and names. Returns the top excerpts (`limit`: default 5, max 20),
  most relevant first, each with its URI, title, score and text, plus, when
  known, a link to the original (`source`: the web page, or the file in Google
  Drive or OneDrive), the `page`, the `section` (heading path, sheet or slide)
  and when it was last updated. The assistant is told to run it before
  answering anything about your data and to cite what it uses.
- **List Resources** (`list-resources`): lists the resources on the server a
  page at a time, as `{uri, title, description, mimeType}`, with a total and a
  cursor for the next page (`limit`: default 100, max 500). Use it to browse the
  inventory and pick a URI; Search Resources is for finding content that
  matches a question.
- **Read Resource** (`read-resource`): fetches the text of one resource by
  `uri` so the assistant can quote, summarize or reason about it. Returns plain
  text or JSON. Binary files (PDFs, images, audio, video, archives) aren't
  inlined; those are delivered with Send Resource, and their text is reachable
  through Search Resources.
- **Send Resource** (`send-resource`): delivers a resource (`uri`) to the
  person as an attachment in the channel: a preview, player or download link
  rather than raw text. Use it when someone asks to see, receive or download a
  file. An optional `caption` adds a short message alongside it.
- **List Prompts** (`list-prompts`): lists every [prompt](/docs/prompts/) and
  command the server exposes (the ones you created and the ones from a
  connected remote MCP server) with the exact slash command (for example
  `/summarize`) and arguments to run each on the current channel.

None of them reach anyone outside the conversation or change your data, so
none is held for [Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions).

## How they fit together

A typical answer chains them: **Search Resources** finds the relevant excerpts,
then the assistant either cites those directly, calls **Read Resource** to pull
a full document, or **Send Resource** to hand the person the file. **List
Resources** and **List Prompts** are for discovery, showing what's available
and how to use it.

## Keep them on

The built-in tools count toward your tool limit (on Free, 5 of the 7), but
they're the last thing to cut. You can turn one off or remove it like any other
row, and the assistant then loses that ability: without Search Resources it
answers blind. When a channel has more than 40 tools, these five are the ones
always kept.

If the project has a [database](/docs/data/), the assistant also gets three data
tools for it. They aren't in the catalog; see
[the assistant's data tools](/docs/data/#the-assistants-data-tools).

Next, add capabilities beyond your own content: see [Gmail](/docs/tools/gmail/),
[Slack](/docs/tools/slack/), or [Web Search](/docs/tools/web-search/).

Check availability and book or cancel meetings on a connected Cal.com account.

The **Cal.com** integration lets your assistant schedule through a Cal.com
account: finding a bookable meeting type, checking open slots, and creating or
cancelling bookings. It offers **4 tools**. Cal.com applies your availability,
buffers and booking rules, so a booking made by the assistant follows the same
rules as one made on your booking page.

## Connect it

Cal.com uses an **API key**, so there's no sign-in step.

1. In Cal.com, create an API key (in your Cal.com settings, under the developer
   / API keys section) and copy it.
2. In Ganju, open **Tools → Catalog**, select the **Cal.com** card and choose
   **Add Cal.com API key**.
3. Paste the key and **Save**. We check it with Cal.com before storing it; it's
   encrypted and never shown again.
4. Turn on the tools you want, then pick the defaults below.

To swap the key later, use **Update API key**; **Disconnect** removes it.

![The API key dialog for an integration, with Cancel and Save](/images/tools-api-key-dialog.webp)

## Integration defaults

With the key saved and at least one Cal.com tool on, the group header shows two
settings for every Cal.com tool (a tool you turn on later inherits them):

- **Default event type**: the meeting type bookings are made against, e.g.
  "30 Min Meeting (30 min)", unless a call names another.
- **Default time zone**: used to look up availability and as the attendee's
  booking time zone when the conversation doesn't reveal theirs. Without one,
  the zone on your Cal.com profile is used.

![Cal.com connected: Update API key, Disconnect, Default event type, Default time zone and the tools](/images/tools-calcom-defaults.webp)

## Tools

The names in parentheses are what MCP clients and logs show.

- **List Event Types** (`calcom-list-event-types`): lists the bookable meeting
  types on the account with each one's ID, title, duration and slug.
- **List Available Slots** (`calcom-list-available-slots`): finds open start
  times between `start` and `end` (ISO 8601, UTC). Optional `eventTypeId` and
  `timeZone` (IANA) for the returned times.
- **Create Booking** (`calcom-create-booking`): books a `start` (one of the
  times List Available Slots returned) for an attendee's `name` and `email`.
  Optional `attendeeTimeZone` (the zone their confirmation and reminders use,
  which the assistant passes whenever it knows where they are), `notes`, and
  `eventTypeId`. In a channel conversation, the name and email come from the
  person. Returns the booking UID and status.
- **Cancel Booking** (`calcom-cancel-booking`): cancels a booking by
  `bookingUid`, with an optional `reason` shown to the attendee, who is
  notified.

The typical flow is **List Available Slots → Create Booking**.

## Sensitive actions

With [Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions) on,
the assistant asks before **Create Booking** and **Cancel Booking**. The two
listing tools run without asking.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Invalid Cal.com API key (or Cal.com could not be reached)".** The key was
  refused when saving. Copy it again from Cal.com, with no spaces.
- **"Could not load event types. Check the API key and try again."** The key
  stopped working; use **Update API key**.
- **"Error: no event type".** Pick a **Default event type**, or ask the
  assistant to use a specific one.
- **"Cal.com is not connected".** The key was removed. Add it again from the card.

The API key is only used by these tools; [functions](/docs/tools/functions/)
can't borrow it. To call Cal.com from your own code, store a key as a function
secret.

Managing a Google Calendar directly instead? See
[Google Calendar](/docs/tools/google-calendar/).

The integrations we ship: connect an account once, switch on the tools you want, and turn them off again without losing the setup.

The **Catalog** is everything we ship and maintain: Gmail, Outlook, Slack,
Google Calendar, Cal.com, web search, and the official remote MCP servers of
GitHub and Notion. If your case is covered here you never have to write code
for it: connect an account once and switch on the tools you want.

The **Tools** page of a project has three tabs: **Functions** (your own code),
**HTTP Endpoints** (one request against your API) and **Catalog**. This page is
about the last one.

![Tools, Catalog tab: the tools-exposed bar, search, filters and the integration cards](/images/tools-catalog.webp)

## The grid

Each integration is a card with its icon, a one-line description and how many
of its tools are on (**5/18 tools enabled**). A card whose account is linked
shows a **Connected** chip; one whose sign-in has lapsed shows **Expired**.

Above the grid:

- **The tool budget**: how many tools this project exposes, out of 40 (**12 of
  40 tools exposed**). Each one is re-sent to the model on every turn; the bar
  warns you as you get close.
- **Search integrations...**: matches card names, descriptions and the names of
  the tools inside them, so searching "draft" finds Gmail and Outlook.
- **Filters**: **All**, **On** (at least one tool enabled), **Off** (nothing
  enabled) and **Needs connection** (integrations that need an account you
  haven't linked yet, and remote MCP servers you haven't connected).

Opening a card shows every tool in the group, each with its description, a
**Scopes** chip (hover it to see the permission the tool needs) and its own
switch. **Back to catalog** returns to the grid.

Some cards are not integrations with an account:

- **Built-in**: the five resource and prompt tools every project starts with.
  No connection needed. See [Built-in](/docs/tools/built-in/).
- **Greeting**: a one-tool smoke test for confirming a new server responds. See
  [Greeting](/docs/tools/greeting/).
- **GitHub** and **Notion**: remote MCP servers run by the vendor. Connecting
  one brings the tools *their* server offers. They open a dialog instead of a
  tool list; see [GitHub](/docs/tools/github/) and
  [Notion](/docs/tools/notion/).

## Connect once, enable per tool

Most integrations need a one-time connection, and **one connection serves the
whole group**: connect Gmail once and all 18 of its tools can use it. Until
you connect, the group shows a banner (*Connect Gmail to enable these tools. You
only need to connect once for the whole integration.*) and its switches are
greyed out.

There are two kinds of connection:

| Kind | Integrations | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sign in (OAuth)** | Gmail, Outlook, Slack, Slack Search, Google Calendar | Select **Connect Gmail** (or the integration's name). You're sent to the provider to approve, then brought back to the Tools page with *Connected Gmail. Toggle the tools you want to enable below.* |
| **API key** | Cal.com, Web Search (Tavily) | Select **Add Cal.com API key**, paste the key and **Save**. We check the key with the vendor before storing it, so a wrong key is refused on the spot. |

Credentials are encrypted at rest, never shown again, and OAuth tokens are
refreshed for you. Once connected, the group header offers **Disconnect** (and
**Update API key** for key-based integrations).

![Outlook before connecting: Connect Outlook, the banner and the tools greyed out](/images/tools-catalog-not-connected.webp)

### When a tool needs more permissions

Connecting asks for every permission the integration's tools use, so normally
you approve once and you're done. If a connection was made before a tool needed
a permission it doesn't have, turning that tool on opens **Additional
permissions required**: **Grant permissions** sends you back to the provider to
add the missing scope on top of your existing connection.

## The tool budget

Every enabled tool's schema is re-sent to the model on **every** call, so tool
count is a direct cost, and models choose worse past a few dozen options. We
measured it on our own traffic: an assistant with 5 tools averages ~1,100 input
tokens per turn, one with 12 averages ~13,100. A shorter tool list is a cheaper,
sharper assistant. Turn on the tools you need, not the whole group.

The limits that apply:

- **Free:** 7 tools turned on per project. The five built-in tools count toward
  it.
- **Pro and Enterprise:** no plan limit, but a project can have at most **40**
  tools turned on.
- Each tool you allow from a remote MCP server counts as one, and a project
  with a [database](/docs/data/) adds its three data tools to the count.

Past the limit, turning one more on is refused with a message saying how many
are on; turn something off or upgrade. Channels also never send more than 40
tools to the model, and the built-in resource tools are always kept first, so
your assistant never loses the ability to read your knowledge.

## Off and Remove are different things

Every enabled or previously enabled row has both, because they answer different
questions:

| | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Off** (switch) | The tool stops being exposed. Its configuration, its credential and its settings survive, and it stops counting toward your tool limit. The row is marked **Off · settings kept**. |
| **Remove** (trash) | The row is deleted, and the settings go with it. The confirmation reminds you to turn it off instead if you only want it gone from the server. |

Turning a tool off frees a slot, so on Free you can rotate through more tools
than your plan exposes at once. Turning one back on re-checks the limit.

**Disconnect** is a third thing: it revokes the stored credential for the whole
integration. Every enabled tool in the group stops working immediately, but
your installed tools stay listed, so reconnecting brings them back as they were.

For a **remote MCP server**, the on/off switch (**Exposed**) lives in its dialog
and **Disconnect** removes it.

## Sensitive actions

Every catalog tool is labelled with what it does to the world: read-only,
changes that can be undone (drafts, labels, moving mail), or actions that reach
someone else or can't be taken back (sending, posting, booking, deleting).
When your organization turns on
[Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions), the
assistant asks before running a tool of the last kind. Each integration page
lists which of its tools those are.

## Connections are shared

A connected account belongs to the project's assistant, not to one tool. The
same Gmail connection is available to:

- every Gmail tool in the catalog;
- an [HTTP endpoint](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/) using **Connected account**
  authentication, instead of holding a second copy of the credential;
- a [function](/docs/tools/functions/), through `ctx.connection('google-gmail')`,
  but only if the provider is listed in that function's connections (the
  **Connections** section of Function settings, or `"connections"` in
  `ganju.json` when you deploy with the [CLI](/docs/tools/cli/)). Your code never
  receives the refresh token, only a short-lived access token.

The connection names are `google-gmail`, `microsoft-outlook`, `slack`,
`slack-user` (Slack Search) and `google-calendar`. API keys (Cal.com, Tavily)
are not connections: only the catalog tools use them.

Disconnecting an integration affects all three.

## With the assistant

On paid plans, the [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) can work with the catalog for
you: it looks up what the catalog offers, and proposes adding a catalog tool,
turning tools on or off, or removing them, as a change you approve, with
undo. When a tool needs an account, it shows you a card to connect it; it never
asks for a password or a token. API keys (Cal.com, Web Search) and remote MCP
servers that need a sign-in or a token are added by you on the Tools page.

The `ganju` CLI doesn't manage catalog tools; it deploys functions, which can
use the same connections.
