## Troubleshooting

- **The switches are greyed out.** The integration isn't connected yet. Use
  **Connect** or **Add API key** in the group header.
- **The card says Expired.** The provider stopped accepting the stored sign-in
  (password changed, access revoked). Open the card and connect again; your
  tools and settings are kept.
- **A tool answers "credential not connected" or "not connected".** Someone
  disconnected the integration. Connect it again from its card.
- **Turning a tool on is refused.** You're at your tool limit. Turn off a tool
  you don't need, or upgrade.
- **The bot ignores a tool it has.** Check it's on (not **Off · settings kept**)
  and that its description fits the request, and remember a channel sends at
  most 40 tools.

## Not here?

Two escape hatches, in order of effort:

- **[HTTP Endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/)**: one request against an API
  you already run, described in a form. Available on every plan.
- **[Functions](/docs/tools/functions/)**: your own code, when you need logic
  rather than a single call.

The Catalog is everything we ship and maintain: Gmail, Outlook, Slack, Google Calendar, Cal.com, web search, and the official remote MCP servers of GitHub and Notion. If your case is covered here you never have to write code for it: connect an account once and switch on the tools you want.

The Tools page of a project has three tabs: Functions (your own code), HTTP Endpoints (one request against your API) and Catalog. This page is about the last one.

The grid

Each integration is a card with its icon, a one-line description and how many of its tools are on (5/18 tools enabled). A card whose account is linked shows a Connected chip; one whose sign-in has lapsed shows Expired.

Above the grid:

  • The tool budget: how many tools this project exposes, out of 40 (12 of 40 tools exposed). Each one is re-sent to the model on every turn; the bar warns you as you get close.
  • Search integrations…: matches card names, descriptions and the names of the tools inside them, so searching “draft” finds Gmail and Outlook.
  • Filters: All, On (at least one tool enabled), Off (nothing enabled) and Needs connection (integrations that need an account you haven’t linked yet, and remote MCP servers you haven’t connected).

Opening a card shows every tool in the group, each with its description, a Scopes chip (hover it to see the permission the tool needs) and its own switch. Back to catalog returns to the grid.

Some cards are not integrations with an account:

  • Built-in: the five resource and prompt tools every project starts with. No connection needed. See Built-in.
  • Greeting: a one-tool smoke test for confirming a new server responds. See Greeting.
  • GitHub and Notion: remote MCP servers run by the vendor. Connecting one brings the tools their server offers. They open a dialog instead of a tool list; see GitHub and Notion.

Connect once, enable per tool

Most integrations need a one-time connection, and one connection serves the whole group: connect Gmail once and all 18 of its tools can use it. Until you connect, the group shows a banner (Connect Gmail to enable these tools. You only need to connect once for the whole integration.) and its switches are greyed out.

There are two kinds of connection:

Kind Integrations How
Sign in (OAuth) Gmail, Outlook, Slack, Slack Search, Google Calendar Select Connect Gmail (or the integration’s name). You’re sent to the provider to approve, then brought back to the Tools page with Connected Gmail. Toggle the tools you want to enable below.
API key Cal.com, Web Search (Tavily) Select Add Cal.com API key, paste the key and Save. We check the key with the vendor before storing it, so a wrong key is refused on the spot.

Credentials are encrypted at rest, never shown again, and OAuth tokens are refreshed for you. Once connected, the group header offers Disconnect (and Update API key for key-based integrations).

When a tool needs more permissions

Connecting asks for every permission the integration’s tools use, so normally you approve once and you’re done. If a connection was made before a tool needed a permission it doesn’t have, turning that tool on opens Additional permissions required: Grant permissions sends you back to the provider to add the missing scope on top of your existing connection.

The tool budget

Every enabled tool’s schema is re-sent to the model on every call, so tool count is a direct cost, and models choose worse past a few dozen options. We measured it on our own traffic: an assistant with 5 tools averages ~1,100 input tokens per turn, one with 12 averages ~13,100. A shorter tool list is a cheaper, sharper assistant. Turn on the tools you need, not the whole group.

The limits that apply:

  • Free: 7 tools turned on per project. The five built-in tools count toward it.
  • Pro and Enterprise: no plan limit, but a project can have at most 40 tools turned on.
  • Each tool you allow from a remote MCP server counts as one, and a project with a database adds its three data tools to the count.

Past the limit, turning one more on is refused with a message saying how many are on; turn something off or upgrade. Channels also never send more than 40 tools to the model, and the built-in resource tools are always kept first, so your assistant never loses the ability to read your knowledge.

Off and Remove are different things

Every enabled or previously enabled row has both, because they answer different questions:

What happens
Off (switch) The tool stops being exposed. Its configuration, its credential and its settings survive, and it stops counting toward your tool limit. The row is marked Off · settings kept.
Remove (trash) The row is deleted, and the settings go with it. The confirmation reminds you to turn it off instead if you only want it gone from the server.

Turning a tool off frees a slot, so on Free you can rotate through more tools than your plan exposes at once. Turning one back on re-checks the limit.

Disconnect is a third thing: it revokes the stored credential for the whole integration. Every enabled tool in the group stops working immediately, but your installed tools stay listed, so reconnecting brings them back as they were.

For a remote MCP server, the on/off switch (Exposed) lives in its dialog and Disconnect removes it.

Sensitive actions

Every catalog tool is labelled with what it does to the world: read-only, changes that can be undone (drafts, labels, moving mail), or actions that reach someone else or can’t be taken back (sending, posting, booking, deleting). When your organization turns on Confirm sensitive actions, the assistant asks before running a tool of the last kind. Each integration page lists which of its tools those are.

Connections are shared

A connected account belongs to the project’s assistant, not to one tool. The same Gmail connection is available to:

  • every Gmail tool in the catalog;
  • an HTTP endpoint using Connected account authentication, instead of holding a second copy of the credential;
  • a function, through ctx.connection('google-gmail'), but only if the provider is listed in that function’s connections (the Connections section of Function settings, or "connections" in ganju.json when you deploy with the CLI). Your code never receives the refresh token, only a short-lived access token.

The connection names are google-gmail, microsoft-outlook, slack, slack-user (Slack Search) and google-calendar. API keys (Cal.com, Tavily) are not connections: only the catalog tools use them.

Disconnecting an integration affects all three.

With the assistant

On paid plans, the Assistant can work with the catalog for you: it looks up what the catalog offers, and proposes adding a catalog tool, turning tools on or off, or removing them, as a change you approve, with undo. When a tool needs an account, it shows you a card to connect it; it never asks for a password or a token. API keys (Cal.com, Web Search) and remote MCP servers that need a sign-in or a token are added by you on the Tools page.

The ganju CLI doesn’t manage catalog tools; it deploys functions, which can use the same connections.

The ganju command line: write, deploy, test and debug your project's functions from a terminal, manage its database, and ship from CI.

`ganju` is the command line for developers. It writes, tests and deploys a
project's [functions](/docs/tools/functions/) (the actions your bot runs),
manages the project's [database](/docs/data/), and runs the same way in CI. It
is a client of the same endpoints the app uses, so a deploy from the CLI and a
change made by the [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) land in the same place.

Inside the app, the project's owner builds by talking to the Assistant and
reads the code on the **Tools** page; nobody edits code in the browser. Reach
for the CLI when the functions belong in a repository, in code review and in a
pipeline.

```bash
npm install -g @ganju/cli
```

Node 20 or newer. The package is `@ganju/cli`, and the binary is `ganju`. To run
it without installing, use `npx @ganju/cli <command>`. Functions and Data need
the organization to be on **Pro** or **Enterprise**.

## Your first deploy

```bash
ganju init my-tools     # scaffold a project that deploys as-is
cd my-tools
ganju login             # opens your browser, signs in on this machine
ganju link              # pick the organization and project this deploys to
ganju deploy            # bundle, upload, publish
```

`ganju init` writes a working tool rather than an empty file: a `ganju.json`
with one `lookup-order` tool declared, and `src/lookupOrder.js` implementing it.
The next command succeeds, and you edit from something that ran.

`ganju deploy` prints each step, and ends with the tools now live:

```
› bundling 1 tool
  1.1 KB (from 1.6 KB) · 1 entry, router generated
› creating a draft version
› uploading v1
› uploading the source (2 files, 1.9 KB)
› publishing
✓ v1 is live on my-tools — 1 tool
  lookup-order
```

## Every command

Run `ganju help` (or `ganju <command> --help`) for the list in your terminal,
and `ganju --version` for the version you have.

### Getting started

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ganju init [dir]` | Scaffold `ganju.json` and a handler in `dir` (default: the current folder). Refuses if that folder already has a `ganju.json`, and keeps an existing handler rather than overwriting it. |
| `ganju login` | Sign in on this machine, in your browser. |
| `ganju logout` | Delete the stored token for this API. Nothing you deployed changes. |
| `ganju whoami` | Who this machine is signed in as, and against which API. |
| `ganju link` | Pick the organization and project, and write them into `ganju.json`. Creates `ganju.json` when there is none, so a folder that only uses `ganju data` needs no `init`. |
| `ganju link --status` | Show what `ganju.json` is linked to, without changing it. |

### Working on functions

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ganju build` | Lint the tools, bundle and minify them to `.ganju/bundle.js`, and report the size. |
| `ganju deploy` | Build, upload and publish. Also deploys the `triggers` in `ganju.json`, if it has any. |
| `ganju test <tool>` | Run one tool once, without publishing it. |
| `ganju logs` | Recent calls and their `ctx.log` output. |

### Managing what is live

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ganju versions` | Every version, which is published, and which one is live. |
| `ganju rollback <version>` | Put a previously live version back. |
| `ganju secret set\|list\|rm` | The values `ctx.secret()` reads. |
| `ganju token create\|list\|revoke` | Durable tokens for CI, scoped to this project. |

| --- | --- |
| `ganju channel templates` | The WhatsApp message templates of the project's channels, with Meta's status. |
| `ganju data …` | The project's database: tables, rows, imports, exports, saved queries, schema as code and restore. See [Project data](#project-data). |

## `ganju.json`

One file describes the project: the tools it exposes, the rules the code runs
under, and optionally the database triggers it deploys. It travels with the
deploy, so the code and the permissions it needs are reviewed in the same pull
request.

```jsonc
{
  "artifact": "acme-support",  // written by `ganju link`
  "organizationId": "…",       // written by `ganju link`
  "projectId": "…",            // written by `ganju link`
  "uploadSource": true,        // the default: send the readable source too

  // How the code may run. One set of rules for the whole project.
  "connections": ["google-gmail"],
  "allowedHosts": ["api.acme.com"],
  "timeoutMs": 10000,
  "resourceAccess": "own",

  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "lookup-order",
      "title": "Look up order",
      "description": "Find an order by its id. Use when the customer gives an order number.",
      "entry": "src/lookupOrder.js",
      "input": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "orderId": { "type": "string", "description": "The order number the customer gave." }
        },
        "required": ["orderId"]
      },
      "output": { "type": "object", "properties": { "status": { "type": "string" } } },
      "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true },
      "data": { "access": "read", "tables": ["orders"] }
    }
  ]
}
```

### Project settings

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `artifact`, `organizationId`, `projectId` | Where this deploys. Written by `ganju link`; none of them is secret, so commit them. |
| `apiUrl` | Which Ganju deployment to talk to. Default `https://api.ganju.ai`. `GANJU_API_URL` overrides it. |
| `main` | Your own router, for projects whose tools don't name an `entry`. Default `src/index.ts`. |
| `connections` | The connected accounts the code may ask a token for, and send files as, e.g. `google-gmail`, `google-calendar`. Anything else is refused when the tool runs. |
| `allowedHosts` | The hosts `fetch` may reach. An entry allows its subdomains too. **Empty or left out means any public host**. Private and loopback addresses are always blocked. |
| `timeoutMs` | How long one call may take. Default 10,000, at most 30,000. |
| `resourceAccess` | How far `ctx.resources.create` and `.delete` reach: `"own"` (the default, only what the tools wrote) or `"all"`. |
| `uploadSource` | Whether `deploy` uploads the readable source beside the bundle. On unless `false`. |
| `tools` | The tools, below. At least one. |
| `triggers` | Database triggers to deploy with the functions. Left out, `deploy` doesn't touch the database's triggers; `[]` removes the ones it deployed. See [Triggers](#triggers). |

Only the keys you write are sent; the server applies its own defaults for the
rest. The four keys `connections`, `allowedHosts`, `timeoutMs` and
`resourceAccess` are the same settings the **Settings** dialog on the
**Tools** page shows, so a change in either place shows in the other.

### Each tool

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | What the model calls, e.g. `lookup-order`. Letters, digits, `_` or `-`, up to 64 characters. |
| `title` | The readable label. |
| `description` | How the model decides whether to call it. Say **when** to use it, not only what it does. |
| `entry` | The file whose default export handles this tool. Give it on every tool, or on none. |
| `input` | JSON Schema of the arguments. Each property is offered to the model. |
| `output` | Optional JSON Schema. Declare one and the tool must return a matching object; MCP clients get structured output instead of text. |
| `annotations` | `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint`. |
| `data` | What the tool may do with the project's database through `ctx.data`: `{ "access": "read" \| "write", "tables": [...] }`. Left out, everything. |
| `expose` | `false` deploys the tool for triggers only: the bot never sees it, and it doesn't count toward the project's tools. |
| `channels` | `true` lets the tool message customers and chats through `ctx.channels`. Left out, those calls are refused. |

`annotations` are the [MCP tool annotations](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools#tool-annotations).
They reach MCP clients as hints, and they decide what a channel bot confirms
when the organization turns on
[Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions): a tool
that declares neither `readOnlyHint: true` nor `destructiveHint: false` is asked
about before it runs. Mark lookups read-only; leave anything that sends,
charges or deletes as `destructiveHint: true`.

`data`, `expose` and `channels` are explained in
[Data from functions](/docs/data/functions/).

**Secrets are not in this file, and must not be.** A value committed beside
your source is exactly what secrets exist to avoid. Send them once with
[`ganju secret set`](#secrets).

## Two ways to write the router

Give every tool an **`entry`** and the map from tool name to handler is
generated from `ganju.json`, so the tool name is written in exactly one place:

```js
// src/lookupOrder.js
import { defineTool } from '@ganju/sdk';

export default defineTool(async (input, ctx) => {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.acme.com/orders/${input.orderId}`, {
    headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${await ctx.secret('ACME_KEY')}` }
  });
  return { status: (await res.json()).status };
});
```

Or give **none** of them one and write the map yourself, in the file named by
`main` (default `src/index.ts`). This is the shape of the functions the
Assistant writes, so it's also what you have if you move them into a
repository:

```js
import { createHandler, defineTool } from '@ganju/sdk';

export default createHandler({
  'lookup-order': defineTool(async (input, ctx) => ({ status: 'shipped' }))
});
```

**A mix of the two is refused rather than resolved**, because either reading
silently drops half of what you wrote.

## What the build does

`esbuild` bundles the project to one ES module, because a deployed script is a
single module, and bundling is what lets you split code across files and use
npm packages.

**`@ganju/sdk` is not bundled.** It's rewritten to `./ganju-sdk.js`, the module
the platform attaches beside every upload, so your bundle never carries a copy
that could drift from the platform it talks to.

TypeScript works. Types are **stripped, not checked**, so run `tsc --noEmit`
yourself if you want them enforced. A bundle is capped at 3 MB.

```bash
ganju build              # lint, bundle, minify, report the size
ganju build --no-minify  # keep .ganju/bundle.js readable
ganju build --strict     # fail on any lint warning (useful in CI)
```

`deploy` bundles on its own from the current source; it never reads a
`.ganju/bundle.js` you built earlier.

## The tool linter

Before it bundles, `ganju build` checks how each tool reads to a model, the
things that make a model pick the wrong tool or guess at its arguments. It
warns about:

- a **missing or very short description**, or one that never says **when** to
  use the tool;
- **no `annotations`**: the tool is then treated as one that may change things,
  and confirmed before every call when the organization confirms sensitive
  actions, lookups included;
- **input properties with no description**;
- an input property named **`confirmation`**, which the platform keeps for
  itself;
- **two tools that look alike** in name or description.

Warnings never stop a build. `--strict` makes them fail it.

`ganju deploy` prints the same checks, run by the API against the whole
server, so they also cover overlap with the project's other tools and warn
when more than 25 are enabled.

## Deploying

```bash
ganju deploy             # build, upload, publish
ganju deploy --draft     # upload a version, publish nothing
ganju deploy --force     # don't stop for a live version made in the app
```

A deploy is three steps: a draft version is created from `ganju.json`, the
bundle (and the readable source) is attached to it, and the draft is
published. A deploy that dies partway leaves a draft behind. That's
intended: `ganju versions` shows it, and the next deploy makes a new one
rather than resuming a draft whose bundle never arrived.

**A deploy replaces every function of the project** with the ones in the
folder. A function that isn't in `ganju.json` stops existing on the server.

### Deploying over changes made in the app

The project's owner may have changed the functions through the
[Assistant](/docs/assistant/) since your last deploy. When the live version was
made in the app, `ganju deploy` stops before publishing:

```
! The live version, v14, was made in the app. Deploying replaces it with this folder's code.
  These functions would stop working: check-stock
  Copy any changes made in the app that you want to keep into this project first.
Replace it? [y/N]
```

It names the functions your folder doesn't have, which would stop working. In a
terminal it asks; in a script, where there is nobody to ask, it stops, and
`--force` deploys anyway. `--draft` is never stopped, since a draft replaces
nothing.

### Your source in the app

Beside the bundle, `ganju deploy` uploads the project's **readable source**, so
the **Tools** page shows your real files instead of minified code, and so the
project's Assistant can read them. It is only shown, never run: the bundle is
what runs.

The files are what git would commit: tracked files, plus untracked ones that
aren't ignored. Outside a git repository, your `.gitignore` files are read
instead. Some things never go, whatever the ignore rules say: `node_modules`,
`.ganju`, `.git`, `.env*` files, lockfiles and binary files. A file over
256 KB is left out and named in the output; a project over 2 MB or 500 files
sends no source at all, with a warning. A failed source upload never fails the
deploy. Set `"uploadSource": false` to send only the bundle.

Because your source is there, the Assistant doesn't replace code you deploy.
When the owner asks it for a code change, it writes a patch for you instead,
which they pass on as **A change for your developer**. Apply it, then deploy as
usual.

## Testing

```bash
ganju test lookup-order --input '{"orderId":"A-1029"}'
ganju test lookup-order --input-file ./fixtures/order.json
ganju test lookup-order --version active    # what is live now
ganju test lookup-order --version latest    # the newest version
ganju test lookup-order --version 12        # one version, by number
ganju test lookup-order --input '{"orderId":"A-1029"}' --json
```

The version runs on a preview script nothing else calls, once, against **real**
connections, secrets and egress rules, and the preview is deleted afterwards.
Your live version keeps serving clients throughout. A tool that sends an email
or writes a row does it for real, so point tests at yourself or at test data.

Without `--version`, `test` bundles the folder and uploads it as a new draft
first (it prints `saved as draft vN — not published`). With `--version`, it
uploads nothing.

The input is checked against the tool's input schema before the run, and the
result against its output schema after, because those are the two ways a real
call fails. You get the tool's `ctx.log` lines, then the output or the error,
and how long it took. A failed run exits with code 1. Test runs count toward
your monthly tool calls.

## Logs

```bash
ganju logs                       # the last 20 calls
ganju logs --tool lookup-order   # only this one
ganju logs --limit 100
ganju logs --follow              # keep watching; ctrl-c to stop
ganju logs --json
```

Each entry is one completed call: when, the tool, how long it took, the
`ctx.log` lines it produced, and the error if there was one. Logs travel back
with the result, which is why a `ctx.log` costs nothing extra and why a call
arrives as one whole entry. `--follow` polls every few seconds, since a call
appears only when it finishes; it can't be combined with `--json`.

## Versions and rollback

```bash
ganju versions
ganju versions --json
ganju rollback 12
```

```
   VERSION  STATUS     TOOLS  SOURCE           CREATED
●  v14      live       3      editor           2026-11-12 21:04:10
   v13      published  2      bundle + source  2026-11-10 15:22:41
   v12      draft      2      bundle + source  2026-11-10 15:20:03
```

`SOURCE` says where a version came from: `editor` is a version made in the app
(by the Assistant), `bundle` one uploaded by the CLI, and `+ source` means its
readable source was uploaded too. Times are UTC. A version that failed to
publish is listed with its error under the table.

**Published** and **live** are not the same thing: every version that has ever
been live is published, and exactly one is the project's live version.
`ganju rollback` takes a version number (or id) that has been live before, and
moves the live pointer back to it.

A version is the unit of both code and contract. The tool names your clients
see come from that version, not from the running script, so rolling back
brings the schemas back with the code.

## Secrets

```bash
GANJU_SECRET_VALUE=sk_live_… ganju secret set ACME_KEY
ganju secret list
ganju secret rm ACME_KEY
```

These are the values `ctx.secret('ACME_KEY')` reads. Three things to know:

- **`set` replaces rather than adds.** Setting an existing name deletes the old
  value first.
- **`list` never prints a value.** It shows names and when each was set. To
  change a value, set it again.
- **A secret is live from the next call**, with no deploy.

`ganju secret set NAME VALUE` works too, but puts the value in your shell
history. To keep it out, read it without echoing:

```bash
read -s GANJU_SECRET_VALUE && export GANJU_SECRET_VALUE
ganju secret set ACME_KEY
unset GANJU_SECRET_VALUE
```

`ls` works for `list`, and `remove` or `delete` for `rm`. Secrets can also be
added and removed in the **Settings** dialog of the **Tools** page.

## Triggers

`ganju.json` can carry the project's database triggers, deployed by
`ganju deploy` right after the functions, so a trigger can name a function
the same deploy added:

```jsonc
"triggers": [
  { "table": "orders", "on": "insert", "function": "notify-kitchen" },
  {
    "table": "orders",
    "on": "update",
    "when": { "status": { "changedTo": "ready" } },
    "function": "tell-customer"
  },
  {
    "name": "nightly-orders",
    "on": "schedule",
    "every": "day",
    "at": "21:00",
    "query": "todays_orders",
    "email": { "to": "owner@example.com", "subject": "Today's orders", "text": "{{count}} orders on {{date}}" }
  }
]
```

`deploy` lists each trigger it deployed, the ones it removed, and the signing
secret of a new webhook trigger, shown once. The rules for conditions, time
triggers and actions are in
[Triggers](/docs/data/triggers/#deploy-triggers-with-the-cli), and schedules
have their own page, [Schedules](/docs/data/schedules/).

## WhatsApp templates

```bash
ganju channel templates
ganju channel templates --json
```

Lists the message templates of each WhatsApp channel in the project, as Ganju
last synced them from Meta: name, language, category, status (with Meta's
reason when rejected), and the variables. It only reads: templates are created
in the channel's **Message templates** tab in the app, where they are checked
before going to Meta for review. A function sends an approved one with
`ctx.channels.send`.

## Project data

`ganju data` manages the project's [database](/docs/data/) from a terminal.
Every command calls the [Data API](/docs/data-api/) the app uses, so a row
written here follows the same rules and is recorded under your login or
token. Run `ganju data help` for the list in your terminal.

### Database

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ganju data create [--name <name>]` | Create the project's database. `--replace --yes` gives up restoring a deleted one and starts a new one. |
| `ganju data info` | Status, size, tables and open index suggestions. `status` works too. |
| `ganju data drop --yes --confirm <name>` | Delete the database. It can be restored for 7 days. |
| `ganju data restore` | Undo a delete. |
| `ganju data restore --at <ISO time> --yes` | Put the database back to a point in time, e.g. `2026-10-30T09:15:00-05:00`. |
| `ganju data restore --bookmark <b> --yes` | Put it back to a bookmark (a drop prints the one that undoes it). |
| `ganju data checkpoint` | Take a bookmark of right now. Prints it alone, so `B=$(ganju data checkpoint)` works. |
| `ganju data time-zone [<zone>]` | Show or set the zone datetimes come back in and schedules run in, e.g. `America/Bogota`. `--clear` goes back to UTC. |
| `ganju data export [--format jsonl\|csv] [--out <dir>]` | Download every table (default JSONL) and the schema. |
| `ganju data changes` | The schema change log. `log` works too. |
| `ganju data copy [status\|wait\|dismiss]` | A table copy running in the background, after a column change. |
| `ganju data index add\|dismiss <id>` | Act on an index suggestion from `info`. |

### Tables and columns

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ganju data tables` | The tables and their columns, what the bot may do with each, and which are synced from a spreadsheet. |
| `ganju data table create <name> --schema <file>` | Create a table from a schema file. |
| `ganju data table rename <name> <new-name>` | Rename a table. |
| `ganju data table rm <name> --yes --confirm <name>` | Drop a table. |
| `ganju data table sync <name>` | Read a synced table's spreadsheet again now. |
| `ganju data column add <table> <name> <type> [--input '<json>']` | Add a column; `--input` takes its other settings. |
| `ganju data column rename <table> <name> <new-name>` | Rename a column. |
| `ganju data column change <table> <name> --input '<json>' [--yes]` | Change a column. A type change copies the table and needs `--yes`; `--no-wait` returns before the copy ends. |
| `ganju data column rm <table> <name> --yes` | Drop a column. |

### Schema as code

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ganju data schema pull` | Write the database's tables and saved queries to `ganju.data.json`. |
| `ganju data schema diff` | Show what `push` would change. |
| `ganju data schema push [--yes]` | Apply the file. Drops and type changes need `--yes`. |

`--schema <file>` uses another file instead of `ganju.data.json`.

### Rows

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ganju data rows <table>` | List rows. Takes `--where` (repeatable), `--sort`, `--search`, `--include`, `--limit` (up to 500), `--cursor`, `--all` and `--json`. |
| `ganju data get <table> <id>` | One row. `--include` expands relations. |
| `ganju data insert <table> --input '<json>'` | Add a row, or a list of rows. `--input-file rows.jsonl` reads JSON or JSONL. |
| `ganju data update <table> <id> --input '<json>' [--version <n>]` | Change a row. `--version` refuses the change if the row changed since you read it. |
| `ganju data delete <table> <id>... [--yes]` | Delete rows. `rm` works too. |
| `ganju data history <table> <id>` | A row's change history. |
| `ganju data write --input-file ops.json` | Several writes, all or nothing. |
| `ganju data import <table> <file>` | Import a CSV, Excel or JSONL file. Takes `--map 'Header=column'` (repeatable), `--sheet <name>`, `--decimal-mark . \| ,`, `--out <file>` for the refused rows, and `--replace --yes --confirm <table>` to replace every row. |

### Saved queries

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ganju data queries` | The saved queries, their parameters and what they read. |
| `ganju data query save --input-file <file>` | Save one: `{ "name", "description", "sql", "params", "assistant" }`. |
| `ganju data query rm <name> --yes` | Delete one. |
| `ganju data run <name> [--input '<json>'] [--limit <n>]` | Run one by name, with its parameters. |

### Filters and confirmations

`--where` takes `column=value` and `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `~` (contains),
`^=` (starts with). `status=[open,done]` matches any of the values, and
`note=null` finds empty ones. On a text column the value is text as typed
(`phone=3001234567`); elsewhere, quotes keep a value as text: `code="007"`.
Repeat `--where` to require several conditions, or pass the JSON filter
itself: `--where '{"price":{"lt":30000}}'`.

Anything that drops, deletes or rewrites data needs `--yes`. Dropping the
database or a table also needs its name, typed with `--confirm`. In a terminal
a missing confirmation is asked for; in a script it is refused.

```bash
ganju data rows menu --where 'price<30000' --where size=30cm --sort -price --limit 50
ganju data insert menu --input '{"name":"Margherita","price":28000}'
ganju data import menu menu.xlsx --sheet Menu --map 'Price (COP)=price'
ganju data schema diff
ganju data table rm orders --yes --confirm orders
ganju data export --format csv --out backup/
```

With `GANJU_API_TOKEN` set, writes are recorded as the token, and data
commands wait out a `429` on their own. The details of each command, with
examples, are in the [Data API](/docs/data-api/#from-the-command-line) page.

## Signing in

`ganju login` opens your browser to sign in and comes back to the terminal on
its own. It's the loopback flow `gh` and `wrangler` use: the CLI listens on a
local port for the redirect, with PKCE and no client secret, and registers
itself on first login.

The login is stored in `~/.ganju/credentials.json`, readable only by you,
**per API**, so working against two deployments doesn't log you out of either.
A stored login renews itself when it expires. `ganju logout` deletes it from
this machine; it doesn't change anything you deployed.

`ganju login` refuses to run while `GANJU_API_TOKEN` is set, since that token
would be used instead.

A login can deploy; the token an MCP client like Claude Desktop gets when it
connects to your project can't. Connecting a client never hands it control of
your project.

## CI

A token from `GANJU_API_TOKEN` is never refreshed, and the token a browser
login holds lasts about an hour, so a scheduled job needs a **personal access
token**:

```bash
ganju token create "GitHub Actions" --expires 90
ganju token create ci --expires never --json | jq -r .token
ganju token list
ganju token revoke "GitHub Actions"
```

Then every command works with no browser:

```yaml
- run: npx @ganju/cli deploy
  env:
    GANJU_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GANJU_API_TOKEN }}
```

Commit `ganju.json` with `organizationId` and `projectId` filled in (neither is
secret). A common setup runs `ganju build --strict` on every pull request and
`ganju deploy` on merge. A pipeline has no terminal, so a deploy over a version
made in the app stops unless you pass `--force`.

What to know about tokens:

- **Scoped to one project**, the one `ganju.json` is linked to. A token reaches
  that project's functions and data and nothing else in your account.
- **The value is shown once**, when it's created. Only a hint is kept, so
  `list` shows names, who made each, when it was last used and when it expires.
  With `--json`, `create` prints the whole token object, which is what makes the
  `jq` pipe above work.
- **`--expires`** takes a number of days, or `never`.
- **Revoke by name or id.** A name two tokens share is refused, with their ids.
  Revocation lands on the next request.
- **A token cannot create or revoke tokens.** Run `ganju token create` from a
  browser login, so a leaked token can't mint its own replacement.
- **A token outlives the account that made it**, listed as inactive, and stops
  working the moment its owner is removed.

`ls` works for `list`, `new` for `create`, and `rm`, `remove` or `delete` for
`revoke`.

## Environment

| Variable | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GANJU_API_URL` | Which deployment to talk to. Overrides `apiUrl` in `ganju.json`. |
| `GANJU_API_TOKEN` | A token for a machine with no browser. Replaces the stored login. |
| `GANJU_SECRET_VALUE` | `ganju secret set NAME` reads the value from here. |
| `GANJU_CONFIG_DIR` | Where the login is stored. Default `~/.ganju`. |

## What the CLI doesn't cover

Functions, the database and its triggers, and reading WhatsApp templates. The
rest is done in the app: prompts, knowledge ([resources](/docs/resources/)),
catalog tools and HTTP endpoints, [channels](/docs/channels/), members and
billing.

ganju is the command line for developers. It writes, tests and deploys a project’s functions (the actions your bot runs), manages the project’s database, and runs the same way in CI. It is a client of the same endpoints the app uses, so a deploy from the CLI and a change made by the Assistant land in the same place.

Inside the app, the project’s owner builds by talking to the Assistant and reads the code on the Tools page; nobody edits code in the browser. Reach for the CLI when the functions belong in a repository, in code review and in a pipeline.

npm install -g @ganju/cli

Node 20 or newer. The package is @ganju/cli, and the binary is ganju. To run it without installing, use npx @ganju/cli <command>. Functions and Data need the organization to be on Pro or Enterprise.

Your first deploy

ganju init my-tools     # scaffold a project that deploys as-is
cd my-tools
ganju login             # opens your browser, signs in on this machine
ganju link              # pick the organization and project this deploys to
ganju deploy            # bundle, upload, publish

ganju init writes a working tool rather than an empty file: a ganju.json with one lookup-order tool declared, and src/lookupOrder.js implementing it. The next command succeeds, and you edit from something that ran.

ganju deploy prints each step, and ends with the tools now live:

› bundling 1 tool
  1.1 KB (from 1.6 KB) · 1 entry, router generated
› creating a draft version
› uploading v1
› uploading the source (2 files, 1.9 KB)
› publishing
✓ v1 is live on my-tools — 1 tool
  lookup-order

Every command

Run ganju help (or ganju <command> --help) for the list in your terminal, and ganju --version for the version you have.

Getting started

Command What it does
ganju init [dir] Scaffold ganju.json and a handler in dir (default: the current folder). Refuses if that folder already has a ganju.json, and keeps an existing handler rather than overwriting it.

ganju logout Delete the stored token for this API. Nothing you deployed changes.
ganju whoami Who this machine is signed in as, and against which API.
ganju link Pick the organization and project, and write them into ganju.json. Creates ganju.json when there is none, so a folder that only uses ganju data needs no init.
ganju link --status Show what ganju.json is linked to, without changing it.

Working on functions

Command What it does
ganju build Lint the tools, bundle and minify them to .ganju/bundle.js, and report the size.
ganju deploy Build, upload and publish. Also deploys the triggers in ganju.json, if it has any.
ganju test <tool> Run one tool once, without publishing it.
ganju logs Recent calls and their ctx.log output.

Managing what is live

Command What it does

ganju.json

One file describes the project: the tools it exposes, the rules the code runs under, and optionally the database triggers it deploys. It travels with the deploy, so the code and the permissions it needs are reviewed in the same pull request.

{
  "artifact": "acme-support",  // written by `ganju link`
  "organizationId": "…",       // written by `ganju link`
  "projectId": "…",            // written by `ganju link`
  "uploadSource": true,        // the default: send the readable source too

  // How the code may run. One set of rules for the whole project.
  "connections": ["google-gmail"],
  "allowedHosts": ["api.acme.com"],
  "timeoutMs": 10000,
  "resourceAccess": "own",

  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "lookup-order",
      "title": "Look up order",
      "description": "Find an order by its id. Use when the customer gives an order number.",
      "entry": "src/lookupOrder.js",
      "input": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "orderId": { "type": "string", "description": "The order number the customer gave." }
        },
        "required": ["orderId"]
      },
      "output": { "type": "object", "properties": { "status": { "type": "string" } } },
      "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true },
      "data": { "access": "read", "tables": ["orders"] }
    }
  ]
}

Project settings

Key What it does
artifact, organizationId, projectId Where this deploys. Written by ganju link; none of them is secret, so commit them.
apiUrl Which Ganju deployment to talk to. Default https://api.ganju.ai. GANJU_API_URL overrides it.
main Your own router, for projects whose tools don’t name an entry. Default src/index.ts.
connections The connected accounts the code may ask a token for, and send files as, e.g. google-gmail, google-calendar. Anything else is refused when the tool runs.
allowedHosts The hosts fetch may reach. An entry allows its subdomains too. Empty or left out means any public host. Private and loopback addresses are always blocked.
timeoutMs How long one call may take. Default 10,000, at most 30,000.
resourceAccess How far ctx.resources.create and .delete reach: "own" (the default, only what the tools wrote) or "all".
uploadSource Whether deploy uploads the readable source beside the bundle. On unless false.
tools The tools, below. At least one.
triggers Database triggers to deploy with the functions. Left out, deploy doesn’t touch the database’s triggers; [] removes the ones it deployed. See Triggers.

Only the keys you write are sent; the server applies its own defaults for the rest. The four keys connections, allowedHosts, timeoutMs and resourceAccess are the same settings the Settings dialog on the Tools page shows, so a change in either place shows in the other.

Each tool

Key What it does
name What the model calls, e.g. lookup-order. Letters, digits, _ or -, up to 64 characters.
title The readable label.
description How the model decides whether to call it. Say when to use it, not only what it does.
entry The file whose default export handles this tool. Give it on every tool, or on none.
input JSON Schema of the arguments. Each property is offered to the model.
output Optional JSON Schema. Declare one and the tool must return a matching object; MCP clients get structured output instead of text.
annotations readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint.
data What the tool may do with the project’s database through ctx.data: { "access": "read" | "write", "tables": [...] }. Left out, everything.
expose false deploys the tool for triggers only: the bot never sees it, and it doesn’t count toward the project’s tools.
channels true lets the tool message customers and chats through ctx.channels. Left out, those calls are refused.

annotations are the MCP tool annotations. They reach MCP clients as hints, and they decide what a channel bot confirms when the organization turns on Confirm sensitive actions: a tool that declares neither readOnlyHint: true nor destructiveHint: false is asked about before it runs. Mark lookups read-only; leave anything that sends, charges or deletes as destructiveHint: true.

data, expose and channels are explained in Data from functions.

Secrets are not in this file, and must not be. A value committed beside your source is exactly what secrets exist to avoid. Send them once with ganju secret set.

Two ways to write the router

Give every tool an entry and the map from tool name to handler is generated from ganju.json, so the tool name is written in exactly one place:

// src/lookupOrder.js
import { defineTool } from '@ganju/sdk';

export default defineTool(async (input, ctx) => {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.acme.com/orders/${input.orderId}`, {
    headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${await ctx.secret('ACME_KEY')}` }
  });
  return { status: (await res.json()).status };
});

Or give none of them one and write the map yourself, in the file named by main (default src/index.ts). This is the shape of the functions the Assistant writes, so it’s also what you have if you move them into a repository:

import { createHandler, defineTool } from '@ganju/sdk';

export default createHandler({
  'lookup-order': defineTool(async (input, ctx) => ({ status: 'shipped' }))
});

A mix of the two is refused rather than resolved, because either reading silently drops half of what you wrote.

What the build does

esbuild bundles the project to one ES module, because a deployed script is a single module, and bundling is what lets you split code across files and use npm packages.

@ganju/sdk is not bundled. It’s rewritten to ./ganju-sdk.js, the module the platform attaches beside every upload, so your bundle never carries a copy that could drift from the platform it talks to.

TypeScript works. Types are stripped, not checked, so run tsc --noEmit yourself if you want them enforced. A bundle is capped at 3 MB.

ganju build              # lint, bundle, minify, report the size
ganju build --no-minify  # keep .ganju/bundle.js readable
ganju build --strict     # fail on any lint warning (useful in CI)

deploy bundles on its own from the current source; it never reads a .ganju/bundle.js you built earlier.

The tool linter

Before it bundles, ganju build checks how each tool reads to a model, the things that make a model pick the wrong tool or guess at its arguments. It warns about:

  • a missing or very short description, or one that never says when to use the tool;
  • no annotations: the tool is then treated as one that may change things, and confirmed before every call when the organization confirms sensitive actions, lookups included;
  • input properties with no description;
  • an input property named confirmation, which the platform keeps for itself;
  • two tools that look alike in name or description.

Warnings never stop a build. --strict makes them fail it.

ganju deploy prints the same checks, run by the API against the whole server, so they also cover overlap with the project’s other tools and warn when more than 25 are enabled.

Deploying

ganju deploy             # build, upload, publish
ganju deploy --draft     # upload a version, publish nothing
ganju deploy --force     # don't stop for a live version made in the app

A deploy is three steps: a draft version is created from ganju.json, the bundle (and the readable source) is attached to it, and the draft is published. A deploy that dies partway leaves a draft behind. That’s intended: ganju versions shows it, and the next deploy makes a new one rather than resuming a draft whose bundle never arrived.

A deploy replaces every function of the project with the ones in the folder. A function that isn’t in ganju.json stops existing on the server.

Deploying over changes made in the app

The project’s owner may have changed the functions through the Assistant since your last deploy. When the live version was made in the app, ganju deploy stops before publishing:

! The live version, v14, was made in the app. Deploying replaces it with this folder's code.
  These functions would stop working: check-stock
  Copy any changes made in the app that you want to keep into this project first.
Replace it? [y/N]

It names the functions your folder doesn’t have, which would stop working. In a terminal it asks; in a script, where there is nobody to ask, it stops, and --force deploys anyway. --draft is never stopped, since a draft replaces nothing.

Your source in the app

Beside the bundle, ganju deploy uploads the project’s readable source, so the Tools page shows your real files instead of minified code, and so the project’s Assistant can read them. It is only shown, never run: the bundle is what runs.

The files are what git would commit: tracked files, plus untracked ones that aren’t ignored. Outside a git repository, your .gitignore files are read instead. Some things never go, whatever the ignore rules say: node_modules, .ganju, .git, .env* files, lockfiles and binary files. A file over 256 KB is left out and named in the output; a project over 2 MB or 500 files sends no source at all, with a warning. A failed source upload never fails the deploy. Set "uploadSource": false to send only the bundle.

Because your source is there, the Assistant doesn’t replace code you deploy. When the owner asks it for a code change, it writes a patch for you instead, which they pass on as A change for your developer. Apply it, then deploy as usual.

Testing

ganju test lookup-order --input '{"orderId":"A-1029"}'
ganju test lookup-order --input-file ./fixtures/order.json
ganju test lookup-order --version active    # what is live now
ganju test lookup-order --version latest    # the newest version
ganju test lookup-order --version 12        # one version, by number
ganju test lookup-order --input '{"orderId":"A-1029"}' --json

The version runs on a preview script nothing else calls, once, against real connections, secrets and egress rules, and the preview is deleted afterwards. Your live version keeps serving clients throughout. A tool that sends an email or writes a row does it for real, so point tests at yourself or at test data.

Without --version, test bundles the folder and uploads it as a new draft first (it prints saved as draft vN — not published). With --version, it uploads nothing.

The input is checked against the tool’s input schema before the run, and the result against its output schema after, because those are the two ways a real call fails. You get the tool’s ctx.log lines, then the output or the error, and how long it took. A failed run exits with code 1. Test runs count toward your monthly tool calls.

Logs

ganju logs                       # the last 20 calls
ganju logs --tool lookup-order   # only this one
ganju logs --limit 100
ganju logs --follow              # keep watching; ctrl-c to stop
ganju logs --json

Each entry is one completed call: when, the tool, how long it took, the ctx.log lines it produced, and the error if there was one. Logs travel back with the result, which is why a ctx.log costs nothing extra and why a call arrives as one whole entry. --follow polls every few seconds, since a call appears only when it finishes; it can’t be combined with --json.

Versions and rollback

ganju versions
ganju versions --json
ganju rollback 12
   VERSION  STATUS     TOOLS  SOURCE           CREATED
●  v14      live       3      editor           2026-11-12 21:04:10
   v13      published  2      bundle + source  2026-11-10 15:22:41
   v12      draft      2      bundle + source  2026-11-10 15:20:03

SOURCE says where a version came from: editor is a version made in the app (by the Assistant), bundle one uploaded by the CLI, and + source means its readable source was uploaded too. Times are UTC. A version that failed to publish is listed with its error under the table.

Published and live are not the same thing: every version that has ever been live is published, and exactly one is the project’s live version. ganju rollback takes a version number (or id) that has been live before, and moves the live pointer back to it.

A version is the unit of both code and contract. The tool names your clients see come from that version, not from the running script, so rolling back brings the schemas back with the code.

Secrets

GANJU_SECRET_VALUE=sk_live_… ganju secret set ACME_KEY
ganju secret list
ganju secret rm ACME_KEY

These are the values ctx.secret('ACME_KEY') reads. Three things to know:

  • set replaces rather than adds. Setting an existing name deletes the old value first.
  • list never prints a value. It shows names and when each was set. To change a value, set it again.
  • A secret is live from the next call, with no deploy.

ganju secret set NAME VALUE works too, but puts the value in your shell history. To keep it out, read it without echoing:

read -s GANJU_SECRET_VALUE && export GANJU_SECRET_VALUE
ganju secret set ACME_KEY
unset GANJU_SECRET_VALUE

ls works for list, and remove or delete for rm. Secrets can also be added and removed in the Settings dialog of the Tools page.

Triggers

ganju.json can carry the project’s database triggers, deployed by ganju deploy right after the functions, so a trigger can name a function the same deploy added:

"triggers": [
  { "table": "orders", "on": "insert", "function": "notify-kitchen" },
  {
    "table": "orders",
    "on": "update",
    "when": { "status": { "changedTo": "ready" } },
    "function": "tell-customer"
  },
  {
    "name": "nightly-orders",
    "on": "schedule",
    "every": "day",
    "at": "21:00",
    "query": "todays_orders",
    "email": { "to": "owner@example.com", "subject": "Today's orders", "text": "{{count}} orders on {{date}}" }
  }
]

deploy lists each trigger it deployed, the ones it removed, and the signing secret of a new webhook trigger, shown once. The rules for conditions, time triggers and actions are in Triggers, and schedules have their own page, Schedules.

WhatsApp templates

ganju channel templates
ganju channel templates --json

Lists the message templates of each WhatsApp channel in the project, as Ganju last synced them from Meta: name, language, category, status (with Meta’s reason when rejected), and the variables. It only reads: templates are created in the channel’s Message templates tab in the app, where they are checked before going to Meta for review. A function sends an approved one with ctx.channels.send.

Project data

ganju data manages the project’s database from a terminal. Every command calls the Data API the app uses, so a row written here follows the same rules and is recorded under your login or token. Run ganju data help for the list in your terminal.

Database

Command What it does
ganju data create [--name <name>] Create the project’s database. --replace --yes gives up restoring a deleted one and starts a new one.
ganju data info Status, size, tables and open index suggestions. status works too.
ganju data drop --yes --confirm <name> Delete the database. It can be restored for 7 days.
ganju data restore Undo a delete.
ganju data restore --at <ISO time> --yes Put the database back to a point in time, e.g. 2026-10-30T09:15:00-05:00.
ganju data restore --bookmark <b> --yes Put it back to a bookmark (a drop prints the one that undoes it).
ganju data checkpoint Take a bookmark of right now. Prints it alone, so B=$(ganju data checkpoint) works.
ganju data time-zone [<zone>] Show or set the zone datetimes come back in and schedules run in, e.g. America/Bogota. --clear goes back to UTC.
ganju data export [--format jsonl|csv] [--out <dir>] Download every table (default JSONL) and the schema.
ganju data changes The schema change log. log works too.
ganju data copy [status|wait|dismiss] A table copy running in the background, after a column change.
ganju data index add|dismiss <id> Act on an index suggestion from info.

Tables and columns

Command What it does
ganju data tables The tables and their columns, what the bot may do with each, and which are synced from a spreadsheet.
ganju data table create <name> --schema <file> Create a table from a schema file.
ganju data table rename <name> <new-name> Rename a table.
ganju data table rm <name> --yes --confirm <name> Drop a table.
ganju data table sync <name> Read a synced table’s spreadsheet again now.
ganju data column add <table> <name> <type> [--input '<json>'] Add a column; --input takes its other settings.
ganju data column rename <table> <name> <new-name> Rename a column.
ganju data column change <table> <name> --input '<json>' [--yes] Change a column. A type change copies the table and needs --yes; --no-wait returns before the copy ends.
ganju data column rm <table> <name> --yes Drop a column.

Schema as code

Command What it does
ganju data schema pull Write the database’s tables and saved queries to ganju.data.json.
ganju data schema diff Show what push would change.
ganju data schema push [--yes] Apply the file. Drops and type changes need --yes.

--schema <file> uses another file instead of ganju.data.json.

Rows

Command What it does
ganju data rows <table> List rows. Takes --where (repeatable), --sort, --search, --include, --limit (up to 500), --cursor, --all and --json.
ganju data get <table> <id> One row. --include expands relations.
ganju data insert <table> --input '<json>' Add a row, or a list of rows. --input-file rows.jsonl reads JSON or JSONL.
ganju data update <table> <id> --input '<json>' [--version <n>] Change a row. --version refuses the change if the row changed since you read it.
ganju data delete <table> <id>... [--yes] Delete rows. rm works too.
ganju data history <table> <id> A row’s change history.
ganju data write --input-file ops.json Several writes, all or nothing.
ganju data import <table> <file> Import a CSV, Excel or JSONL file. Takes --map 'Header=column' (repeatable), --sheet <name>, --decimal-mark . | ,, --out <file> for the refused rows, and --replace --yes --confirm <table> to replace every row.

Saved queries

Command What it does
ganju data queries The saved queries, their parameters and what they read.
ganju data query save --input-file <file> Save one: { "name", "description", "sql", "params", "assistant" }.
ganju data query rm <name> --yes Delete one.
ganju data run <name> [--input '<json>'] [--limit <n>] Run one by name, with its parameters.

Filters and confirmations

--where takes column=value and !=, >, >=, <, <=, ~ (contains), ^= (starts with). status=[open,done] matches any of the values, and note=null finds empty ones. On a text column the value is text as typed (phone=3001234567); elsewhere, quotes keep a value as text: code="007". Repeat --where to require several conditions, or pass the JSON filter itself: --where '{"price":{"lt":30000}}'.

Anything that drops, deletes or rewrites data needs --yes. Dropping the database or a table also needs its name, typed with --confirm. In a terminal a missing confirmation is asked for; in a script it is refused.

ganju data rows menu --where 'price<30000' --where size=30cm --sort -price --limit 50
ganju data insert menu --input '{"name":"Margherita","price":28000}'
ganju data import menu menu.xlsx --sheet Menu --map 'Price (COP)=price'
ganju data schema diff
ganju data table rm orders --yes --confirm orders
ganju data export --format csv --out backup/

With GANJU_API_TOKEN set, writes are recorded as the token, and data commands wait out a 429 on their own. The details of each command, with examples, are in the Data API page.

Signing in

ganju login opens your browser to sign in and comes back to the terminal on its own. It’s the loopback flow gh and wrangler use: the CLI listens on a local port for the redirect, with PKCE and no client secret, and registers itself on first login.

The login is stored in ~/.ganju/credentials.json, readable only by you, per API, so working against two deployments doesn’t log you out of either. A stored login renews itself when it expires. ganju logout deletes it from this machine; it doesn’t change anything you deployed.

ganju login refuses to run while GANJU_API_TOKEN is set, since that token would be used instead.

A login can deploy; the token an MCP client like Claude Desktop gets when it connects to your project can’t. Connecting a client never hands it control of your project.

CI

A token from GANJU_API_TOKEN is never refreshed, and the token a browser login holds lasts about an hour, so a scheduled job needs a personal access token:

ganju token create "GitHub Actions" --expires 90
ganju token create ci --expires never --json | jq -r .token
ganju token list
ganju token revoke "GitHub Actions"

Then every command works with no browser:

- run: npx @ganju/cli deploy
  env:
    GANJU_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GANJU_API_TOKEN }}

Commit ganju.json with organizationId and projectId filled in (neither is secret). A common setup runs ganju build --strict on every pull request and ganju deploy on merge. A pipeline has no terminal, so a deploy over a version made in the app stops unless you pass --force.

What to know about tokens:

  • Scoped to one project, the one ganju.json is linked to. A token reaches that project’s functions and data and nothing else in your account.
  • The value is shown once, when it’s created. Only a hint is kept, so list shows names, who made each, when it was last used and when it expires. With --json, create prints the whole token object, which is what makes the jq pipe above work.
  • --expires takes a number of days, or never.
  • Revoke by name or id. A name two tokens share is refused, with their ids. Revocation lands on the next request.
  • A token cannot create or revoke tokens. Run ganju token create from a browser login, so a leaked token can’t mint its own replacement.
  • A token outlives the account that made it, listed as inactive, and stops working the moment its owner is removed.

ls works for list, new for create, and rm, remove or delete for revoke.

Environment

Variable What it does
GANJU_API_URL Which deployment to talk to. Overrides apiUrl in ganju.json.
GANJU_API_TOKEN A token for a machine with no browser. Replaces the stored login.
GANJU_SECRET_VALUE ganju secret set NAME reads the value from here.
GANJU_CONFIG_DIR Where the login is stored. Default ~/.ganju.

Functions, the database and its triggers, and reading WhatsApp templates. The rest is done in the app: prompts, knowledge (resources), catalog tools and HTTP endpoints, channels, members and billing.

## Before you start

You need Node 20 or newer, and a project on **Pro** or **Enterprise**, where
[Functions](/docs/tools/functions/) are available.

```bash
npm install -g @ganju/cli
ganju login

git clone https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju.git
cd ganju/examples/weather
ganju link       # choose the organization and project to deploy to
```

Every example works the same way from here: `ganju build --strict` to check
it, `ganju test` to run a tool once without publishing it, `ganju deploy` to
make it live, and `ganju logs` to see the calls your bot makes.

A deploy replaces the project's whole set of functions with the example's, so
use a project for trying things, not one your customers use. If the project's
functions were made in the app, `ganju deploy` says so and asks before
replacing them.

`ganju link` fills in `organizationId`, `projectId` and `artifact` in
`ganju.json`. The copies in the repository leave them out so they work for
anyone. Run `npm install` in an example if you want `ctx` to autocomplete in
your editor. The build doesn't need it.

Each example is laid out the same way:

```
ganju.json         the tools, their schemas, and what the code may reach
src/<tool>.ts      one file per tool, default-exporting defineTool(...)
src/lib/*.ts       helpers the tools share
```

## Weather

Current conditions and a forecast for any city, from
[Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com). No account and no key, so it's the one
to deploy first.

```bash
ganju test current-weather --input '{"city":"Bogotá"}'
ganju test weather-forecast --input '{"city":"Lisbon","days":5}'
ganju deploy
```

Then ask your assistant *"Do I need an umbrella in Lisbon this week?"*

**The tool is ordinary `fetch`.** The only Ganju code is `defineTool` and
`ctx.log`:

```ts
// src/currentWeather.ts
export default defineTool<{ city: string }>(async (input, ctx) => {
  const place = await findPlace(input.city.trim());
  ctx.log(`${input.city} → ${place.name}`);

  const { current } = await fetchForecast(place, 1);

  return {
    place: place.name,
    ...(place.country ? { country: place.country } : {}),
    conditions: describe(current.weather_code),
    temperatureC: current.temperature_2m
    // …
  };
});
```

**What to notice**

- **`allowedHosts` is what lets `fetch` out.** Every request leaves through the
  platform, which checks the host first. One entry, `open-meteo.com`, covers
  both `api.open-meteo.com` and `geocoding-api.open-meteo.com`, because an
  entry allows its subdomains too.
- **The schema limits the input before your code runs.** `days` is declared
  with `"minimum": 1, "maximum": 7`, so a request for 30 days is refused
  and never reaches the handler.
- **Leave missing fields out rather than setting them to `null`.** An output
  schema has no nullable type, so a `null` in a `string` field fails the whole
  call. `country` is left out when the geocoder doesn't have one.

## GitHub issues

List and open issues in your repositories, so an assistant can check whether a
bug is already reported before filing it.

Create a [fine-grained personal access token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new)
with **Issues: Read and write** on only the repositories you want reachable, and
store it as a secret:

```bash
read -s GANJU_SECRET_VALUE && export GANJU_SECRET_VALUE
ganju secret set GITHUB_TOKEN
unset GANJU_SECRET_VALUE

ganju test github-list-issues --input '{"repo":"your-org/your-repo","limit":5}'
ganju deploy
```

**The token is read at call time, never stored with the code:**

```ts
// src/lib/github.ts
const token = await ctx.secret('GITHUB_TOKEN');

const response = await fetch(`https://api.github.com${path}`, {
  headers: {
    authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
    accept: 'application/vnd.github+json',
    'user-agent': 'ganju-example-github-issues'
  }
});
```

**What to notice**

- **Secrets stay out of the repository.** The token isn't in the code, in
  `ganju.json` or in the bundle. Rotating it is one `ganju secret set` and
  takes effect on the next call, without a redeploy.
- **The schema can check more than types.** `repo` has a `pattern` for
  `owner/name`, `state` is an `enum` of `open`, `closed` and `all`, and `labels`
  is an `array` of strings.
- **Error messages should say what to do next.** A 401 tells the model the
  token needs resetting, and a 404 says the repository is wrong or out of the
  token's reach. The model can pass that on instead of guessing.
- **Mark what writes, and let the platform ask.** `github-create-issue` is
  annotated `destructiveHint: true`: it posts where other people see it. With
  [Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions) on, the
  person is asked before an issue is filed. Its description only tells the
  model to check for a duplicate first. The [order desk](#order-desk) shows the
  pattern in full.

`ganju test` uses the real secret, so testing `github-create-issue` opens a real
issue. Use a scratch repository.

## Team notes

A notebook your assistant can write to and search. Say *"note that the
release moved to Thursday"* in Slack, then ask *"when's the release?"* from
Claude a week later.

```bash
ganju test save-note --input '{"title":"Release checklist","body":"1. Tag\n2. Build\n3. Deploy"}'
ganju test find-notes --input '{"query":"how do we ship"}'
ganju deploy
```

It uses all five `ctx.resources` methods, one per tool:

| Tool | Method |
| --- | --- |
| `save-note` | `ctx.resources.create({ …, index: true })` |
| `list-notes` | `ctx.resources.list()` |
| `read-note` | `ctx.resources.read(uri)` |
| `find-notes` | `ctx.resources.search(query)` |
| `delete-note` | `ctx.resources.delete(uri)` |

```ts
// src/saveNote.ts
const saved = await ctx.resources.create({
  title,
  uri: noteUri(title), // resource://notes/release-checklist
  content: markdown,
  mimeType: 'text/markdown',
  index: true
});

return { uri: saved.uri, created: saved.created, indexed: saved.indexed };
```

**What to notice**

- **A stable uri makes saving idempotent.** Each note lives at
  `resource://notes/<slug-of-title>`, so saving under an existing title replaces
  the note, and `created: false` says so. The shared prefix is also how
  `list-notes` and `find-notes` pick notes out from uploads and crawled pages.
- **`index: true` is a deliberate choice.** What a tool writes isn't searchable
  unless it asks to be. Here it does, so the notes show up in `find-notes` and
  in the assistant's own [knowledge search](/docs/resources/). Indexing takes
  a few seconds and counts toward your plan's storage.
- **Search returns passages, not documents.** One note can match more than
  once, so `find-notes` keeps the best-scoring passage per note.
- **`resourceAccess: "own"` limits what can be deleted.** `delete-note` can
  only remove what a tool wrote, never a file someone uploaded, whatever uri
  it's given.

This one calls no outside hosts. Its `allowedHosts` is empty, and **empty
means any public host**, not none. If you extend it to fetch something, list
that host.

## Calendar free time

Finds the open slots on a day of your Google Calendar that fit a meeting,
within working hours. It can answer *"When am I free Tuesday for an hour?"*
or suggest times to someone.

Connect **Google Calendar** on the project's **Tools** page, then:

```bash
ganju test find-free-time --input '{"date":"2026-09-21","durationMinutes":60}'
ganju deploy
```

```json
{
  "date": "2026-09-21",
  "timeZone": "America/Bogota",
  "busy": [{ "start": "10:00", "end": "11:30" }, { "start": "13:00", "end": "14:15" }],
  "free": [
    { "start": "09:00", "end": "10:00", "minutes": 60 },
    { "start": "11:30", "end": "13:00", "minutes": 90 },
    { "start": "14:15", "end": "17:00", "minutes": 165 }
  ]
}
```

**The connection is one line:**

```ts
// src/lib/google.ts
const { accessToken } = await ctx.connection('google-calendar');

const response = await fetch(`https://www.googleapis.com/calendar/v3${path}`, {
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` }
});
```

**What to notice**

- **The platform handles OAuth.** `ctx.connection` returns a short-lived
  access token and refreshes it as needed. The refresh token never reaches
  your code.
- **`connections` works like a permission.** `ganju.json` declares
  `"connections": ["google-calendar"]`. Without it the call is refused, even
  with the account connected, so a script can't reach accounts it didn't
  declare.
- **Ask for as little as the task needs.** The tool uses Google's free/busy
  endpoint, which returns times only. No event titles or attendees reach the
  conversation.
- **Time zones work without a library.** `src/lib/time.ts` uses `Intl` to turn
  "9:00 in the calendar's time zone" into an exact time, correct on the days
  the clocks change.

## News digest

The Hacker News front page, in the chat or emailed to someone with the list
attached as a Markdown file.

Connect **Gmail** on the project's **Tools** page, then:

```bash
ganju test hn-top-stories --input '{"limit":5}'
ganju test email-hn-digest --input '{"to":"you@example.com","limit":5}'
ganju deploy
```

The second test sends a real email, so send it to yourself.

**Make the file first, then send it:**

```ts
// src/emailDigest.ts
const saved = await ctx.resources.create({
  title: `Hacker News digest — ${date}`,
  uri: `resource://news-digest/${date}`,
  fileName: `hacker-news-${date}.md`,
  mimeType: 'text/markdown',
  content: toMarkdown(stories, date)
});

await ctx.sendFile({
  to: 'gmail',
  uris: [saved.uri],
  message: { to: input.to, subject: `Hacker News digest — ${date}`, body }
});
```

**What to notice**

- **`sendFile` takes uris, never bytes.** The platform reads the file from
  storage and attaches it, so the same call can send a 40MB PDF your code
  could never hold. Swap `to: 'gmail'` for `'outlook'` or `'slack'` to deliver
  somewhere else.
- **Sending needs a declared connection too.** Sending as an account takes the
  same permission as holding its token, so `google-gmail` is in
  `connections`.
- **One uri per day keeps storage from piling up.** Running the tool twice in a
  day replaces the morning's file.
- **Keep the number of requests bounded.** Each story is its own request, made
  in parallel. `limit` stops at 15 because every `fetch` counts toward the
  project's outbound request budget.

## Order desk

A small store's support desk: look up an order, leave an internal note on it,
refund it. Nothing to connect: the orders are sample data in the code, and
notes and refunds are saved on the project. What it's for is the refund, which
asks the person first without the code or the descriptions ever mentioning it.

```bash
ganju build --strict
ganju test order-lookup --input '{"orderId":"A-1001"}'
ganju deploy
```

Then turn on **Confirm sensitive actions** in **Settings → Organization** and
ask *"Order A-1001 arrived with a chipped mug, can you refund that mug?"*

**One tool for each answer to "what does it do?":**

```json
// ganju.json (abridged)
{ "name": "order-lookup",   "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true } },
{ "name": "order-add-note", "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": false } },
{ "name": "order-refund",   "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": true } }
```

With the switch on, the lookup and the note run straight away. The refund
doesn't run until the person says yes:

- **In a channel** (Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack, Discord), the bot holds the call
  and asks in the chat, showing under its question exactly what a yes runs:

  ```
  ⏳ Refund an order
  - orderId: A-1001
  - amount: 14
  - reason: one mug arrived chipped
  ```

  A yes from the same person within 30 minutes runs that stored call, not a
  new one the model writes. Anything else drops it.
- **In an MCP client** (Claude, Cursor), the first call comes back *not run
  yet* with a one-time token. The assistant asks in its own chat, and on a yes
  calls again with the token, which works once, for those exact arguments,
  within 10 minutes.

**What to notice**

- **Annotations are the whole mechanism.** Nothing in `src/orderRefund.ts`
  checks for a confirmation; by the time it runs, the person has said yes.
- **Leave "confirm first" out of the description.** The platform asks, and a
  model told to ask as well asks twice.
- **A tool with no annotations is confirmed every time.** By the MCP defaults,
  a tool that doesn't say it only reads may change things, lookups included.
  `ganju build` warns about it, and `--strict` fails on it.
- **`ganju test` doesn't ask.** It runs the tool directly, so testing
  `order-refund` records a real refund on the sample order.

## Restaurant orders

A restaurant's order desk on the project's own [database](/docs/data/). The
menu, orders and their lines are rows in Data, so the app, the Assistant and
these functions all read the same numbers. It's the `data-orders` folder.

| Tool | What it does | `data` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `place-order` | Saves an order and its lines and takes the dishes out of stock, all or nothing | `write`, three tables |
| `sales-report` | Units and revenue per dish for a period, from a saved query | `read` |
| `notify-kitchen` | Posts each new order to the staff's chat; run by a trigger only | `write`, three tables |
| `tell-customer` | Tells the customer their order is ready; run by a trigger only | `read`, `orders` |

The tables and the saved query live in `ganju.data.json`, beside the code:

```bash
ganju link
ganju data create
ganju data schema push
ganju data insert menu --input '[{"name":"Margherita","price":28000,"stock":10},{"name":"Hawaiana","price":30000,"stock":2}]'
ganju build --strict
ganju test place-order --input '{"customer":"Ana","items":[{"dish":"Margherita","quantity":2}]}'
ganju secret set KITCHEN_CHANNEL_ID   # the Telegram channel's id, from the app
ganju secret set KITCHEN_CHAT_ID      # the staff group's chat id
ganju deploy
```

Then ask *"Two Hawaianas and one Margherita for Ana"*, and then *"and three
more Hawaianas"*: the second is refused, since two were left.

**One write for one order:**

```ts
// src/placeOrder.ts (abridged)
const { results } = await ctx.data.write([
  { op: 'insert', table: 'orders', values: { customer: input.customer, total } },
  // a line per dish, pointing at the order inserted first
  { op: 'insert', table: 'order_lines', values: { order: { $ref: 0 }, dish: dish.id, quantity, price } },
  // and a stock decrement per dish, guarded so stock never goes below zero
  {
    op: 'update',
    table: 'menu',
    id: dish.id,
    set: { stock: { decrement: quantity } },
    where: { stock: { gte: quantity } }
  }
]);
```

**What to notice**

- **`ctx.data` needs no setup.** Every function of a project with a database
  gets it. Calls follow the same rules as the [Data API](/docs/data-api/), and
  each change is recorded as the function that made it.
- **All or nothing.** If one dish is short, the guard fails and the whole order
  is refused with how many are left. Nothing is half-saved.
- **A saved query instead of SQL.** `sales_by_dish` is a `SELECT` saved with
  the tables, and `ctx.data.run` runs it by name. A function never sends SQL.
- **`data` in `ganju.json` narrows a function.** `sales-report` can only read;
  `place-order` reaches only its three tables. The platform enforces it, whatever
  the code does with the model's input.
- **Triggers are deployed with the code.** `"triggers"` in `ganju.json` runs
  `notify-kitchen` on each new order, `tell-customer` when an order's status
  changes to `ready`, and messages the customer when an order is still
  `pending` 30 minutes after it was placed.
- **Functions only triggers run.** `notify-kitchen` and `tell-customer` have
  `"expose": false`, so the bot never sees them and they don't count toward its
  tools, and `"channels": true`, so they can message through
  `ctx.channels`.

More on all of this in [Data from functions](/docs/data/functions/) and
[Triggers](/docs/data/triggers/).

## Make it yours

The quickest way to write a new tool is to copy the example closest to it:

1. **Copy the folder** and run `ganju link` in it.
2. **Rename the tool** in `ganju.json`. The router is generated from the
   manifest, so the name only lives there.
3. **Rewrite the description.** It's how the model decides when to call the
   tool, so say *when* to use it, not only what it does.
4. **Set `annotations`.** `readOnlyHint: true` if it only reads,
   `destructiveHint: false` if its changes can be undone, `destructiveHint:
   true` if it sends, deletes, spends or can't be undone. `ganju build`
   tells you what's missing.
5. **List exactly the hosts and connections you need.** Anything else is
   refused when the tool runs.
6. **`ganju test` until it passes, then `ganju deploy`.** If a deploy goes
   wrong, `ganju rollback` puts the previous version back.

They are for developers. If you’d rather describe what your bot should do, the Assistant writes functions like these for you.
