Before you start

You need Node 20 or newer, and a project on Pro or Enterprise, where Functions are available.

npm install -g @ganju/cli
ganju login

git clone https://github.com/MontoyaAndres/ganju.git
cd ganju/examples/weather
ganju link       # choose the organization and project to deploy to

Every example works the same way from here: ganju build --strict to check it, ganju test to run a tool once without publishing it, ganju deploy to make it live, and ganju logs to see the calls your bot makes.

A deploy replaces the project’s whole set of functions with the example’s, so use a project for trying things, not one your customers use. If the project’s functions were made in the app, ganju deploy says so and asks before replacing them.

ganju link fills in organizationId, projectId and artifact in ganju.json. The copies in the repository leave them out so they work for anyone. Run npm install in an example if you want ctx to autocomplete in your editor. The build doesn’t need it.

Each example is laid out the same way:

ganju.json         the tools, their schemas, and what the code may reach
src/<tool>.ts      one file per tool, default-exporting defineTool(...)
src/lib/*.ts       helpers the tools share

Weather

Current conditions and a forecast for any city, from Open-Meteo. No account and no key, so it’s the one to deploy first.

ganju test current-weather --input '{"city":"Bogotá"}'
ganju test weather-forecast --input '{"city":"Lisbon","days":5}'
ganju deploy

Then ask your assistant “Do I need an umbrella in Lisbon this week?”

The tool is ordinary fetch. The only Ganju code is defineTool and ctx.log:

// src/currentWeather.ts
export default defineTool<{ city: string }>(async (input, ctx) => {
  const place = await findPlace(input.city.trim());
  ctx.log(`${input.city} → ${place.name}`);

  const { current } = await fetchForecast(place, 1);

  return {
    place: place.name,
    ...(place.country ? { country: place.country } : {}),
    conditions: describe(current.weather_code),
    temperatureC: current.temperature_2m
    // …
  };
});

What to notice

  • allowedHosts is what lets fetch out. Every request leaves through the platform, which checks the host first. One entry, open-meteo.com, covers both api.open-meteo.com and geocoding-api.open-meteo.com, because an entry allows its subdomains too.
  • The schema limits the input before your code runs. days is declared with "minimum": 1, "maximum": 7, so a request for 30 days is refused and never reaches the handler.
  • Leave missing fields out rather than setting them to null. An output schema has no nullable type, so a null in a string field fails the whole call. country is left out when the geocoder doesn’t have one.

GitHub issues

List and open issues in your repositories, so an assistant can check whether a bug is already reported before filing it.

Create a fine-grained personal access token with Issues: Read and write on only the repositories you want reachable, and store it as a secret:

read -s GANJU_SECRET_VALUE && export GANJU_SECRET_VALUE
ganju secret set GITHUB_TOKEN
unset GANJU_SECRET_VALUE

ganju test github-list-issues --input '{"repo":"your-org/your-repo","limit":5}'
ganju deploy

The token is read at call time, never stored with the code:

// src/lib/github.ts
const token = await ctx.secret('GITHUB_TOKEN');

const response = await fetch(`https://api.github.com${path}`, {
  headers: {
    authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
    accept: 'application/vnd.github+json',
    'user-agent': 'ganju-example-github-issues'
  }
});

What to notice

  • Secrets stay out of the repository. The token isn’t in the code, in ganju.json or in the bundle. Rotating it is one ganju secret set and takes effect on the next call, without a redeploy.
  • The schema can check more than types. repo has a pattern for owner/name, state is an enum of open, closed and all, and labels is an array of strings.
  • Error messages should say what to do next. A 401 tells the model the token needs resetting, and a 404 says the repository is wrong or out of the token’s reach. The model can pass that on instead of guessing.
  • Mark what writes, and let the platform ask. github-create-issue is annotated destructiveHint: true: it posts where other people see it. With Confirm sensitive actions on, the person is asked before an issue is filed. Its description only tells the model to check for a duplicate first. The order desk shows the pattern in full.

ganju test uses the real secret, so testing github-create-issue opens a real issue. Use a scratch repository.

Team notes

A notebook your assistant can write to and search. Say “note that the release moved to Thursday” in Slack, then ask “when’s the release?” from Claude a week later.

ganju test save-note --input '{"title":"Release checklist","body":"1. Tag\n2. Build\n3. Deploy"}'
ganju test find-notes --input '{"query":"how do we ship"}'
ganju deploy

It uses all five ctx.resources methods, one per tool:

Tool Method
save-note ctx.resources.create({ …, index: true })
list-notes ctx.resources.list()
read-note ctx.resources.read(uri)
find-notes ctx.resources.search(query)
delete-note ctx.resources.delete(uri) 
// src/saveNote.ts
const saved = await ctx.resources.create({
  title,
  uri: noteUri(title), // resource://notes/release-checklist
  content: markdown,
  mimeType: 'text/markdown',
  index: true
});

return { uri: saved.uri, created: saved.created, indexed: saved.indexed };

What to notice

  • A stable uri makes saving idempotent. Each note lives at resource://notes/<slug-of-title>, so saving under an existing title replaces the note, and created: false says so. The shared prefix is also how list-notes and find-notes pick notes out from uploads and crawled pages.
  • index: true is a deliberate choice. What a tool writes isn’t searchable unless it asks to be. Here it does, so the notes show up in find-notes and in the assistant’s own knowledge search. Indexing takes a few seconds and counts toward your plan’s storage.
  • Search returns passages, not documents. One note can match more than once, so find-notes keeps the best-scoring passage per note.
  • resourceAccess: "own" limits what can be deleted. delete-note can only remove what a tool wrote, never a file someone uploaded, whatever uri it’s given.

This one calls no outside hosts. Its allowedHosts is empty, and empty means any public host, not none. If you extend it to fetch something, list that host.

Calendar free time

Finds the open slots on a day of your Google Calendar that fit a meeting, within working hours. It can answer “When am I free Tuesday for an hour?” or suggest times to someone.

Connect Google Calendar on the project’s Tools page, then:

ganju test find-free-time --input '{"date":"2026-09-21","durationMinutes":60}'
ganju deploy
{
  "date": "2026-09-21",
  "timeZone": "America/Bogota",
  "busy": [{ "start": "10:00", "end": "11:30" }, { "start": "13:00", "end": "14:15" }],
  "free": [
    { "start": "09:00", "end": "10:00", "minutes": 60 },
    { "start": "11:30", "end": "13:00", "minutes": 90 },
    { "start": "14:15", "end": "17:00", "minutes": 165 }
  ]
}

The connection is one line:

// src/lib/google.ts
const { accessToken } = await ctx.connection('google-calendar');

const response = await fetch(`https://www.googleapis.com/calendar/v3${path}`, {
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` }
});

What to notice

  • The platform handles OAuth. ctx.connection returns a short-lived access token and refreshes it as needed. The refresh token never reaches your code.
  • connections works like a permission. ganju.json declares "connections": ["google-calendar"]. Without it the call is refused, even with the account connected, so a script can’t reach accounts it didn’t declare.
  • Ask for as little as the task needs. The tool uses Google’s free/busy endpoint, which returns times only. No event titles or attendees reach the conversation.
  • Time zones work without a library. src/lib/time.ts uses Intl to turn “9:00 in the calendar’s time zone” into an exact time, correct on the days the clocks change.

News digest

The Hacker News front page, in the chat or emailed to someone with the list attached as a Markdown file.

Connect Gmail on the project’s Tools page, then:

ganju test hn-top-stories --input '{"limit":5}'
ganju test email-hn-digest --input '{"to":"you@example.com","limit":5}'
ganju deploy

The second test sends a real email, so send it to yourself.

Make the file first, then send it:

// src/emailDigest.ts
const saved = await ctx.resources.create({
  title: `Hacker News digest — ${date}`,
  uri: `resource://news-digest/${date}`,
  fileName: `hacker-news-${date}.md`,
  mimeType: 'text/markdown',
  content: toMarkdown(stories, date)
});

await ctx.sendFile({
  to: 'gmail',
  uris: [saved.uri],
  message: { to: input.to, subject: `Hacker News digest — ${date}`, body }
});

What to notice

  • sendFile takes uris, never bytes. The platform reads the file from storage and attaches it, so the same call can send a 40MB PDF your code could never hold. Swap to: 'gmail' for 'outlook' or 'slack' to deliver somewhere else.
  • Sending needs a declared connection too. Sending as an account takes the same permission as holding its token, so google-gmail is in connections.
  • One uri per day keeps storage from piling up. Running the tool twice in a day replaces the morning’s file.
  • Keep the number of requests bounded. Each story is its own request, made in parallel. limit stops at 15 because every fetch counts toward the project’s outbound request budget.

Order desk

A small store’s support desk: look up an order, leave an internal note on it, refund it. Nothing to connect: the orders are sample data in the code, and notes and refunds are saved on the project. What it’s for is the refund, which asks the person first without the code or the descriptions ever mentioning it.

ganju build --strict
ganju test order-lookup --input '{"orderId":"A-1001"}'
ganju deploy

Then turn on Confirm sensitive actions in Settings → Organization and ask “Order A-1001 arrived with a chipped mug, can you refund that mug?”

One tool for each answer to “what does it do?”:

// ganju.json (abridged)
{ "name": "order-lookup",   "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true } },
{ "name": "order-add-note", "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": false } },
{ "name": "order-refund",   "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": true } }

With the switch on, the lookup and the note run straight away. The refund doesn’t run until the person says yes:

  • In a channel (Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack, Discord), the bot holds the call and asks in the chat, showing under its question exactly what a yes runs:

    ⏳ Refund an order
- orderId: A-1001
- amount: 14
- reason: one mug arrived chipped

    A yes from the same person within 30 minutes runs that stored call, not a new one the model writes. Anything else drops it.

  • In an MCP client (Claude, Cursor), the first call comes back not run yet with a one-time token. The assistant asks in its own chat, and on a yes calls again with the token, which works once, for those exact arguments, within 10 minutes.

What to notice

  • Annotations are the whole mechanism. Nothing in src/orderRefund.ts checks for a confirmation; by the time it runs, the person has said yes.
  • Leave “confirm first” out of the description. The platform asks, and a model told to ask as well asks twice.
  • A tool with no annotations is confirmed every time. By the MCP defaults, a tool that doesn’t say it only reads may change things, lookups included. ganju build warns about it, and --strict fails on it.
  • ganju test doesn’t ask. It runs the tool directly, so testing order-refund records a real refund on the sample order.

Restaurant orders

A restaurant’s order desk on the project’s own database. The menu, orders and their lines are rows in Data, so the app, the Assistant and these functions all read the same numbers. It’s the data-orders folder.

Tool What it does data
place-order Saves an order and its lines and takes the dishes out of stock, all or nothing write, three tables
sales-report Units and revenue per dish for a period, from a saved query read
notify-kitchen Posts each new order to the staff’s chat; run by a trigger only write, three tables
tell-customer Tells the customer their order is ready; run by a trigger only read, orders

The tables and the saved query live in ganju.data.json, beside the code:

ganju link
ganju data create
ganju data schema push
ganju data insert menu --input '[{"name":"Margherita","price":28000,"stock":10},{"name":"Hawaiana","price":30000,"stock":2}]'
ganju build --strict
ganju test place-order --input '{"customer":"Ana","items":[{"dish":"Margherita","quantity":2}]}'
ganju secret set KITCHEN_CHANNEL_ID   # the Telegram channel's id, from the app
ganju secret set KITCHEN_CHAT_ID      # the staff group's chat id
ganju deploy

Then ask “Two Hawaianas and one Margherita for Ana”, and then “and three more Hawaianas”: the second is refused, since two were left.

One write for one order:

// src/placeOrder.ts (abridged)
const { results } = await ctx.data.write([
  { op: 'insert', table: 'orders', values: { customer: input.customer, total } },
  // a line per dish, pointing at the order inserted first
  { op: 'insert', table: 'order_lines', values: { order: { $ref: 0 }, dish: dish.id, quantity, price } },
  // and a stock decrement per dish, guarded so stock never goes below zero
  {
    op: 'update',
    table: 'menu',
    id: dish.id,
    set: { stock: { decrement: quantity } },
    where: { stock: { gte: quantity } }
  }
]);

What to notice

  • ctx.data needs no setup. Every function of a project with a database gets it. Calls follow the same rules as the Data API, and each change is recorded as the function that made it.
  • All or nothing. If one dish is short, the guard fails and the whole order is refused with how many are left. Nothing is half-saved.
  • A saved query instead of SQL. sales_by_dish is a SELECT saved with the tables, and ctx.data.run runs it by name. A function never sends SQL.
  • data in ganju.json narrows a function. sales-report can only read; place-order reaches only its three tables. The platform enforces it, whatever the code does with the model’s input.
  • Triggers are deployed with the code. "triggers" in ganju.json runs notify-kitchen on each new order, tell-customer when an order’s status changes to ready, and messages the customer when an order is still pending 30 minutes after it was placed.
  • Functions only triggers run. notify-kitchen and tell-customer have "expose": false, so the bot never sees them and they don’t count toward its tools, and "channels": true, so they can message through ctx.channels.

More on all of this in Data from functions and Triggers.

Make it yours

The quickest way to write a new tool is to copy the example closest to it:

  1. Copy the folder and run ganju link in it.
  2. Rename the tool in ganju.json. The router is generated from the manifest, so the name only lives there.
  3. Rewrite the description. It’s how the model decides when to call the tool, so say when to use it, not only what it does.
  4. Set annotations. readOnlyHint: true if it only reads, destructiveHint: false if its changes can be undone, destructiveHint: true if it sends, deletes, spends or can’t be undone. ganju build tells you what’s missing.
  5. List exactly the hosts and connections you need. Anything else is refused when the tool runs.
  6. ganju test until it passes, then ganju deploy. If a deploy goes wrong, ganju rollback puts the previous version back.

Your own tools in code: the Assistant writes them for you, developers deploy them with the CLI, and the Tools page shows what is live, lets you test it and roll back.

**Functions** are tools written in code. In the app they're called
**actions**: "check if a pizza is in stock", "save a booking", "email me each
new order". A function is the way to do anything that isn't one HTTP request
or an integration we ship: several steps, logic, a call to your own API
combined with a key, reading and writing the project's
[database](/docs/data/).

Your code runs on Cloudflare's edge, in an isolate we deploy for you. There is
no server to run and no pipeline to wire up. Connected accounts, file sending,
the database and your channels reach the code as **host capabilities**, so it
never handles a refresh token or a 40 MB attachment.

> Functions are part of **Pro** and **Enterprise**. On Free, the Functions tab
> shows **Write your own tools** with **Upgrade to Pro**, and
> [HTTP Endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/) are the custom tool that needs
> no code.

![The Functions tab on the Free plan: "Write your own tools" with a code sample and Upgrade to Pro](/images/tools-functions-free.webp)

## Who writes them

Nobody types code into the app. A project's functions come from one of two
places:

- **The [Assistant](/docs/assistant/).** The owner describes what the bot
  should do, and the Assistant writes the function, tests it, and turns it on
  when the owner presses **Apply**. This is how most projects get their
  actions.
- **A developer with the [`ganju` CLI](/docs/tools/cli/).** The functions live
  in a repository, and `ganju deploy` uploads them.

Both write to the same versions, so the **Tools** page, `ganju versions` and
the Assistant always agree on what is live. When a developer deploys, the
Assistant stops writing code for that project: it answers a code change with a
patch for the developer instead. When the Assistant changed the functions
since the developer's last deploy, `ganju deploy` warns before replacing them.

## The Functions tab

**Tools → Functions** shows the project's functions: what is live, every
earlier version, and the code, read-only.

![The Functions tab: the info box with "Open the assistant", the version picker, the version details and the functions with their switches and Run](/images/functions-assistant-readonly.webp)

Across the top:

- **Version**, a picker with every version (`v14 · live`, `v13 · published`,
  `v12 · draft`). Choose one and its functions and code open.
- **Roll back to v13**, only on projects without the Assistant: shown when the
  open version was live before but isn't now, it puts that version back. Where
  the Assistant writes the actions, ask it to go back instead.
- **Settings**, what the code may reach. See [Settings](#settings).

When the Assistant writes the project's functions, an info box says so:
**Your actions are written by the assistant. You can read them here; to add or
change one, ask it.**, with **Open the assistant**. A project with no
functions yet shows the same button.

Under it, a row describes the open version: **Version**, **Status** (`live`,
`published`, `draft` or `archived`), how many **Functions** it has, its
**Source**, and when it was **Created** and **Published**. The source is one
of:

| Source | Where it came from |
| --- | --- |
| **Dashboard editor** | Written in the app, by the Assistant. |
| **CLI (source)** | Deployed with the CLI, with its readable source. The page shows your files. |
| **CLI bundle** | Deployed with the CLI without its source. The page shows the compiled bundle. |

A version that failed to publish shows its error in a banner.

### Each function

Every function is a row with its title, description, name, how many inputs it
takes, and tags: **structured output** when it declares an output schema, and
**Triggers only** when only database triggers run it.

- The **switch** (on the live version) decides whether the server offers the
  function, **without a redeploy**. Turning one off keeps its code and shortens
  the tool list the model reads on every turn. At least one has to stay on.
- **Run** expands the function and runs it with its sample input. See
  [Test before anyone sees it](#test-before-anyone-sees-it).
- Expanding the row shows its **Input schema** and **Output schema**.

### The code

Below the functions is the open version's code, marked **read-only**, with a
file explorer beside it. `index.js` is the entry the platform calls, and
`ganju-sdk.js` is shown dimmed as **attached**: the platform adds it to every
deploy. A version from the CLI with its source shows your project's files
instead, with a note that it changes in the project, with `ganju deploy`.

## What a function looks like

A project is one script holding all its functions. The entry module exports a
router, and each function is an async handler that gets the model's arguments
and a `ctx`:

```js
import { createHandler, defineTool } from './ganju-sdk.js';

const checkStock = async (input, ctx) => {
  const { rows } = await ctx.data.query({
    table: 'stock',
    where: { pizza: input.pizza }
  });
  return { pizza: input.pizza, left: rows[0]?.quantity ?? 0 };
};

export default createHandler({ 'check-stock': defineTool(checkStock) });
```

Beside the code, each version carries a **manifest** that declares every
function the way the model sees it:

| Field | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| **name** | What the model calls, e.g. `check-stock`. It must be a key of the router. |
| **title** | The readable label. |
| **description** | How the model decides whether to call it. It says **when** to use it ("Use when a customer asks whether a pizza is available"). |
| **input schema** | JSON Schema. Every property is offered to the model as an argument. |
| **output schema** | Optional. With one, the function must return a matching object, and MCP clients get structured output instead of text. |
| **annotations** | What it does: only reads, changes things that can be undone, or sends, deletes, charges or can't be undone. Decides what a channel bot confirms first. |
| **data** | What it may do with the database: read or write, and which tables. |
| **expose** | Off: only triggers run it, and it doesn't count toward the project's tools. |
| **channels** | On: it may message customers and chats through `ctx.channels`. |

Code the Assistant writes is plain JavaScript modules with no build step and no
npm packages, at most 25 files. A developer deploying with the CLI can use
TypeScript and packages, since the CLI bundles them. The `ganju.json` fields
for all of the above are in the [CLI reference](/docs/tools/cli/#each-tool).

## What your code can do

| `ctx` member | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| `ctx.connection(provider)` | A short-lived access token for a connected account, e.g. `google-calendar`. Never the refresh token. |
| `ctx.secret(name)` | A key stored in **Settings** or with `ganju secret set`, read at call time. |
| `ctx.resources.search / read / list` | The same knowledge your bot answers from. |
| `ctx.resources.create / delete` | Write a file or note to the project, or remove one. Not searchable unless created with `index: true`. |
| `ctx.sendFile(options)` | Email or post stored files as real attachments through Gmail, Outlook or Slack (up to 10 per call). The bytes never pass through your code. |
| `ctx.data` | The project's database: `describe`, `query`, `search`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `write` (all or nothing) and `run` (a saved query). |
| `ctx.channels` | Message a customer the bot has talked to (`send`), post to a chat the bot is in (`post`), and list approved WhatsApp templates (`templates`). |
| `ctx.log(...)` | Lines that show in the test panel, in the logs the Assistant reads, and in `ganju logs`. |
| `fetch` | The global you know, screened on the way out. |

`ctx.data` and `ctx.channels` are covered in
[Data from functions](/docs/data/functions/), along with functions that only
triggers run.

`ctx.sendFile` is the thing your code couldn't do on its own: a function's
memory is capped, so large attachments are sent by the platform from storage.
`ctx.resources.create` takes up to 1 MB of text or 10 MB of file bytes.

## Settings

**Settings** opens **Function settings**: what the code may reach, and what it
may spend doing it. None of it lives in the code, on purpose: a limit the code
could widen isn't a limit. They can be changed here, and a developer sets the
same values in `ganju.json`; a change in either place shows in the other.

![The Function settings dialog: Connections with their status, then Secrets](/images/function-settings-live.webp)

- **Connections**: the accounts the code may ask a token for, and send files
  as. Each shows whether it's **Connected**, **Needs re-authorization** or
  **Not connected**. Anything not switched on is refused when the function
  runs. Switching on one you haven't connected yet is allowed: the call fails
  with a message saying so.
- **Secrets**: the values `ctx.secret()` reads. Encrypted, read on each call,
  and never sent back to the browser. Adding or removing one takes effect on
  the next call, with no redeploy. The Assistant asks for the ones it needs
  with a card where you paste the key.
- **Allowed hosts**: a comma-separated allowlist for outbound requests. **Empty
  means any public host**, not none. Private and loopback addresses are always
  blocked.
- **Timeout (ms)**: how long one call may take. Default 10,000, at most 30,000.
- **Resource access**: how far `ctx.resources.create` and `.delete` reach.
  **Only what this tool wrote** is the default and the safe one; **Every
  resource in this project** lets a function replace and remove uploaded and
  crawled resources too.

Connections, hosts, timeout and resource access save together with **Save**; a
secret acts the moment you add or remove it.

## Test before anyone sees it

Expand a function and use **Run** with a **Sample input**.

![A function expanded to its input and output schemas, with a sample input field, Format and Run](/images/functions-test.webp)

A test runs the open version on a preview script nothing else calls, once,
and deletes it. That means it runs **the real thing** (real connections,
secrets and egress rules) while your live version keeps serving clients.
A function that sends an email or saves a row does it for real.

You get back the output, the `ctx.log` lines, the error if there was one, and

the run, and the result against the output schema after, because those are
the two ways a real call fails.

## Versions, turning on and rolling back

A version is the unit of both **code and contract**: the tool names your
clients see come from the version, not from the running script, so going back
brings the schemas back with the code.

- The Assistant saves **drafts** while it works. Nobody sees a draft. It turns
  one on through a change set, which goes live when the owner presses
  **Apply**, and **Undo** on that card goes back.
- Ask the Assistant to go back ("put the actions back the way they were
  yesterday") and it finds the version that was live then and stages it, saying
  which actions added since would go.
- A developer publishes with `ganju deploy` and goes back with
  `ganju rollback`.

**Published** and **live** are different: every version that has been live is

## Limits and cost

- **Per call**: 5 seconds of CPU, and your timeout (at most 30 seconds) for
  the whole call. A result over 256 KB is cut short.
- **Per minute**: 60 calls per tool.
- **Per script**: up to 50 functions, and a 3 MB bundle.
- **Per month**: 1,000,000 tool calls included on Pro and Enterprise, then $5
  per million. Only calls into **your own code** count; the integrations we
  ship and remote MCP servers you connect don't.
- **Outbound requests** are screened: private, loopback and link-local
  addresses are always refused, and your allowed hosts apply on top.

The Assistant watches the functions it built. When one fails often, or an
account it uses needs signing in again, the Assistant tab shows **Something
stopped working**, and **Fix it with the assistant** asks it to read the logs
and propose a fix. See
[When an action stops working](/docs/assistant/#when-an-action-stops-working).
Developers read the same calls with [`ganju logs`](/docs/tools/cli/#logs).

Functions are tools written in code. In the app they’re called actions: “check if a pizza is in stock”, “save a booking”, “email me each new order”. A function is the way to do anything that isn’t one HTTP request or an integration we ship: several steps, logic, a call to your own API combined with a key, reading and writing the project’s database.

Your code runs on Cloudflare’s edge, in an isolate we deploy for you. There is no server to run and no pipeline to wire up. Connected accounts, file sending, the database and your channels reach the code as host capabilities, so it never handles a refresh token or a 40 MB attachment.

Functions are part of Pro and Enterprise. On Free, the Functions tab shows Write your own tools with Upgrade to Pro, and HTTP Endpoints are the custom tool that needs no code.

Who writes them

Nobody types code into the app. A project’s functions come from one of two places:

  • The Assistant. The owner describes what the bot should do, and the Assistant writes the function, tests it, and turns it on when the owner presses Apply. This is how most projects get their actions.
  • A developer with the ganju CLI. The functions live in a repository, and ganju deploy uploads them.

Both write to the same versions, so the Tools page, ganju versions and the Assistant always agree on what is live. When a developer deploys, the Assistant stops writing code for that project: it answers a code change with a patch for the developer instead. When the Assistant changed the functions since the developer’s last deploy, ganju deploy warns before replacing them.

Tools → Functions shows the project’s functions: what is live, every earlier version, and the code, read-only.

  • Settings, what the code may reach. See Settings.

When the Assistant writes the project’s functions, an info box says so: Your actions are written by the assistant. You can read them here; to add or change one, ask it., with Open the assistant. A project with no functions yet shows the same button.

Source Where it came from

A version that failed to publish shows its error in a banner.

Each function

Every function is a row with its title, description, name, how many inputs it takes, and tags: structured output when it declares an output schema, and Triggers only when only database triggers run it.

  • The switch (on the live version) decides whether the server offers the function, without a redeploy. Turning one off keeps its code and shortens the tool list the model reads on every turn. At least one has to stay on.
  • Run expands the function and runs it with its sample input. See Test before anyone sees it.
  • Expanding the row shows its Input schema and Output schema.

The code

Below the functions is the open version’s code, marked read-only, with a file explorer beside it. index.js is the entry the platform calls, and ganju-sdk.js is shown dimmed as attached: the platform adds it to every deploy. A version from the CLI with its source shows your project’s files instead, with a note that it changes in the project, with ganju deploy.

What a function looks like

A project is one script holding all its functions. The entry module exports a router, and each function is an async handler that gets the model’s arguments and a ctx:

import { createHandler, defineTool } from './ganju-sdk.js';

const checkStock = async (input, ctx) => {
  const { rows } = await ctx.data.query({
    table: 'stock',
    where: { pizza: input.pizza }
  });
  return { pizza: input.pizza, left: rows[0]?.quantity ?? 0 };
};

export default createHandler({ 'check-stock': defineTool(checkStock) });

Beside the code, each version carries a manifest that declares every function the way the model sees it:

Field What it’s for
name What the model calls, e.g. check-stock. It must be a key of the router.
title The readable label.
description How the model decides whether to call it. It says when to use it (“Use when a customer asks whether a pizza is available”).
input schema JSON Schema. Every property is offered to the model as an argument.
output schema Optional. With one, the function must return a matching object, and MCP clients get structured output instead of text.
annotations What it does: only reads, changes things that can be undone, or sends, deletes, charges or can’t be undone. Decides what a channel bot confirms first.
data What it may do with the database: read or write, and which tables.
expose Off: only triggers run it, and it doesn’t count toward the project’s tools.
channels On: it may message customers and chats through ctx.channels.

Code the Assistant writes is plain JavaScript modules with no build step and no npm packages, at most 25 files. A developer deploying with the CLI can use TypeScript and packages, since the CLI bundles them. The ganju.json fields for all of the above are in the CLI reference.

ctx.secret(name) A key stored in Settings or with ganju secret set, read at call time.

Connect GitHub's official remote MCP server to give your assistant repositories, issues, and pull requests.

**GitHub** isn't a set of tools we build; it's GitHub's **official remote MCP
server**, connected through Ganju. Ganju links to GitHub's hosted server, lists
the tools *it* offers, and exposes the ones you pick to your assistant. You get
GitHub's own, up-to-date toolset (repositories, issues, pull requests and more),
maintained by GitHub, not re-implemented by us.

## How it works

The **GitHub** card sits in **Tools → Catalog** next to the other
integrations, marked *Remote MCP server · connect to enable tools* until you
connect it. Ganju talks to GitHub's server (`https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`)
over streamable HTTP. Every tool you allow is registered on your MCP server as
`github__<tool>` (for example `github__search_repositories`); when the
assistant calls one, Ganju forwards the call to GitHub with your token and
returns the result.

## Connect it

GitHub's server authenticates with a **personal access token** (PAT).

1. In GitHub, go to **Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens**
   and create a token. Give it access only to the repositories and permissions
   you want the assistant to have, because the token is the ceiling of what it
   can do.
2. In Ganju, open **Tools → Catalog** and select the **GitHub** card.
3. Paste the token in **GitHub token** and select **Connect & list tools**. If
   GitHub refuses it, you'll see *Could not list tools with this token.*
4. Choose the tools (see below) and select **Connect GitHub** to save.

The token is encrypted and never shown again.

## Choose the tools

After listing, the dialog shows **Tools (x/y)** with every tool GitHub's server
offers, each with its own checkbox, plus **All** and **None**. Each tool you
allow counts as one toward your [tool limit](/docs/tools/catalog/#the-tool-budget),
and the dialog tells you how many more you can turn on. GitHub's server offers
many tools; pick the handful your assistant needs.

Under the list:

- **Trust this server's read-only labels**: tools GitHub itself marks as
  read-only skip confirmation. A server could mislabel a tool, so turn this on
  only for servers you trust.
- **Only reads: looks things up, changes nothing**: mark tools yourself, so
  they run without asking for confirmation, even after the assistant has read
  outside content. Everything else is treated as a sensitive action.
- **Resources & prompts (optional)**: if the server offers resources or
  prompts, they're off by default; only the ones you enable here are exposed.

![The GitHub tools dialog: the tool count, trust read-only labels, each tool with "Only reads", Exposed, Disconnect and Save](/images/tools-mcp-github-tools.webp)

## Change, turn off, disconnect

Open the GitHub card again to change which tools are allowed, then **Save**.
The **Exposed** switch at the bottom turns the whole server off without losing
the setup (*Kept, but not on your MCP server*); **Disconnect** removes it and
its token.

## Available tools

The tools come from GitHub's server and can change as GitHub updates it,
typically covering repositories, files, issues, pull requests and related
workflows. The dialog always shows the current list. Responses are capped in
size before they reach the model, and results from the server are treated as
outside content.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Could not list tools with this token."** The token is wrong, expired or
  lacks access. Create a new one and connect again.
- **A tool fails with a permission error.** The token doesn't cover that
  repository or permission; widen the token in GitHub.
- **"Could not reach the remote MCP server".** GitHub's server didn't answer;
  try again later.

Want another vendor's server? See [Notion](/docs/tools/notion/), or expose your
own API with [HTTP Endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/).

Send, read, search, and manage email from a connected Gmail account: 18 tools across sending, triage, labels, threads, and drafts.

The **Gmail** integration lets your assistant work with email on a connected
Google account: starting new messages, replying in-thread, triaging the inbox,
organizing with labels, and managing drafts. It offers **18 tools**; turn on
only the ones your assistant needs.

## Connect it

1. Open **Tools → Catalog** and select the **Gmail** card.
2. Select **Connect Gmail**, choose the Google account and approve.
3. Back on the Tools page, turn on the tools you want.

One connection serves all 18 tools. Connecting asks Google for these
permissions: read (`gmail.readonly`), send (`gmail.send`), modify
(`gmail.modify`), compose drafts (`gmail.compose`) and labels (`gmail.labels`).
Each tool row shows the one it uses under **Scopes**.

![Gmail connected: the Connected chip, Disconnect, and each tool with its switch](/images/tool-gmail-enabled.webp)

The tools have no per-tool settings. The tool names in parentheses are what
MCP clients and logs show.

## Sending

- **Send Email** (`gmail-send-email`): composes and sends a new message,
  starting a new thread. Takes `to`, `subject` and `body` (HTML), with optional
  `cc` and `bcc` (comma-separated) and `attachmentUris` (files from your
  [resources](/docs/resources/), up to ~18 MB combined). Returns the new message
  and thread IDs.
- **Reply Email** (`gmail-reply-email`): replies to a message by `messageId`,
  keeping it in the same Gmail thread and adding "Re:". Set `replyAll` to include
  the original To and Cc recipients; `attachmentUris` works as above. Use this
  rather than Send Email to keep a conversation together.
- **Forward Email** (`gmail-forward-email`): forwards a message (`messageId`)
  to `to`, with an optional intro `body` above it and optional `cc`. Adds "Fwd:"
  and starts a new thread.

## Reading & searching

- **List Emails** (`gmail-list-emails`): lists messages (from / subject / date /
  ID), filtered with Gmail search syntax in `query` (`is:unread`,
  `from:a@b.com`, `after:2025/01/01`, `has:attachment`). Empty lists recent inbox
  messages. `maxResults` 1–50, default 10.
- **Read Email** (`gmail-read-email`): opens one message by `messageId` and
  returns its headers and decoded body.
- **List Threads** (`gmail-list-threads`): lists conversations (thread ID and
  latest snippet), with the same `query` syntax. `maxResults` 1–50, default 10.
- **Get Thread** (`gmail-get-thread`): summarizes every message in a thread
  (`threadId`): date, from, subject, snippet and message ID, without full
  bodies. Scan a conversation cheaply, then Read Email the one you want.
- **Get Profile** (`gmail-get-profile`): reports which address is connected and
  its message and thread totals.

## Organizing

- **List Labels** (`gmail-list-labels`): lists every label with its ID,
  including system ones (`INBOX`, `UNREAD`, `STARRED`, `IMPORTANT`, `SPAM`). The
  label tools take IDs, not names, so this comes first.
- **Modify Labels** (`gmail-modify-labels`): adds or removes labels on one
  message: `messageId` plus `addLabelIds` and/or `removeLabelIds`. Archive =
  remove `INBOX`, mark read = remove `UNREAD`, star = add `STARRED`.
- **Batch Modify Labels** (`gmail-batch-modify-labels`): the same change on many
  messages at once (`messageIds`, up to 1,000). Ideal for bulk archive or
  mark-all-as-read.
- **Move to Trash** (`gmail-trash-email`): moves a message to Trash, where Gmail
  keeps it for 30 days. The safe choice whenever someone asks to "delete" an
  email.

## Drafts

- **Create Draft** (`gmail-create-draft`): saves a message in Drafts without
  sending it. Same fields as Send Email, attachments included. Use it when the
  person wants to review first, or when it's not clear they want it sent.
- **List Drafts** (`gmail-list-drafts`): lists drafts with their IDs,
  recipients and subjects. `maxResults` 1–50, default 10.
- **Get Draft** (`gmail-get-draft`): reads a draft in full by `draftId`, to
  confirm exactly what will go out.
- **Update Draft** (`gmail-update-draft`): replaces a draft entirely: pass
  `draftId` with the full `to`, `subject` and `body` even when changing one of
  them, and `attachmentUris` again to keep attachments; anything left out is
  removed. Doesn't send it.
- **Send Draft** (`gmail-send-draft`): sends a saved draft as it is and returns
  the message ID.
- **Delete Draft** (`gmail-delete-draft`): permanently deletes an unsent draft
  (it doesn't go to Trash).

## Sensitive actions

With [Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions) on,
the assistant asks before **Send Email**, **Reply Email**, **Forward Email**,
**Send Draft**, **Move to Trash** and **Delete Draft**. Reading, labels and
creating or editing drafts run without asking. A common pattern is to enable
**Create Draft** but not **Send Email**, so a person always presses send.

## Use the connection from your own code

A [function](/docs/tools/functions/) can call the Gmail API with the same
connection: add `google-gmail` to its connections and call
`ctx.connection('google-gmail')` for a short-lived access token. An
[HTTP endpoint](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/) can use it as its **Connected
account**.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Google credential not connected".** Gmail was disconnected. Connect it
  again from the card.
- **The card shows Expired.** Google stopped accepting the sign-in (password
  changed or access revoked in the Google account). Connect again; your tools
  are kept.
- **"Attachments exceed Gmail's 18MB raw cap".** Send fewer or smaller files, or
  share a link instead.
- **A label change fails.** Use IDs from List Labels; user labels have IDs like
  `Label_12`, not their display names.

Prefer Microsoft mail? See [Outlook](/docs/tools/outlook/), which offers the same
set via Microsoft Graph.

  • Batch Modify Labels (gmail-batch-modify-labels): the same change on many messages at once (messageIds, up to 1,000). Ideal for bulk archive or mark-all-as-read.
  • Move to Trash (gmail-trash-email): moves a message to Trash, where Gmail keeps it for 30 days. The safe choice whenever someone asks to “delete” an email.

Drafts

  • Create Draft (gmail-create-draft): saves a message in Drafts without sending it. Same fields as Send Email, attachments included. Use it when the person wants to review first, or when it’s not clear they want it sent.
  • List Drafts (gmail-list-drafts): lists drafts with their IDs, recipients and subjects. maxResults 1–50, default 10.
  • Get Draft (gmail-get-draft): reads a draft in full by draftId, to confirm exactly what will go out.
  • Update Draft (gmail-update-draft): replaces a draft entirely: pass draftId with the full to, subject and body even when changing one of them, and attachmentUris again to keep attachments; anything left out is removed. Doesn’t send it.
  • Send Draft (gmail-send-draft): sends a saved draft as it is and returns the message ID.
  • Delete Draft (gmail-delete-draft): permanently deletes an unsent draft (it doesn’t go to Trash).

Sensitive actions

With Confirm sensitive actions on, the assistant asks before Send Email, Reply Email, Forward Email, Send Draft, Move to Trash and Delete Draft. Reading, labels and creating or editing drafts run without asking. A common pattern is to enable Create Draft but not Send Email, so a person always presses send.

Use the connection from your own code

A function can call the Gmail API with the same connection: add google-gmail to its connections and call ctx.connection('google-gmail') for a short-lived access token. An HTTP endpoint can use it as its Connected account.

Troubleshooting

  • “Google credential not connected”. Gmail was disconnected. Connect it again from the card.
  • The card shows Expired. Google stopped accepting the sign-in (password changed or access revoked in the Google account). Connect again; your tools are kept.
  • “Attachments exceed Gmail’s 18MB raw cap”. Send fewer or smaller files, or share a link instead.
  • A label change fails. Use IDs from List Labels; user labels have IDs like Label_12, not their display names.

Prefer Microsoft mail? See Outlook, which offers the same set via Microsoft Graph.

Create and manage calendar events, invite attendees, and find open time slots on a connected Google account.

The **Google Calendar** integration lets your assistant read and manage a
schedule on a connected Google account: listing calendars, browsing and editing
events, and finding open time to meet. It offers **6 tools**, and you set which
calendar and time zone they use once, for the whole integration.

## Connect it

1. Open **Tools → Catalog** and select the **Google Calendar** card.
2. Select **Connect Google Calendar**, choose the Google account and approve.
3. Turn on the tools you want, then set the defaults below.

Connecting asks Google for `calendar.readonly` (calendars, events and free/busy)
and `calendar.events` (create, change and delete events).

## Integration defaults

Once connected and with at least one calendar tool on, the group header shows
three settings that apply to every calendar tool (a tool you turn on later
inherits them):

- **Default calendar**: which calendar events and free/busy lookups use,
  unless a call names another. The account's primary calendar is used until you
  pick one.
- **Default time zone**: how event times are read, and the zone the working
  hours of Find Free Slots are in. Without one, the zone set in Google Calendar
  is used.
- **Attendee notifications**: whether Google emails guests when events are
  created, changed or cancelled: **Notify everyone**, **Notify external guests
  only** or **Don't send notifications**.

![Google Calendar connected: Default calendar, Default time zone, Attendee notifications and the tools](/images/tools-calendar-defaults.webp)

## Per-tool settings

Three tools have extra settings, under the pencil icon (**Configure**) on their
row:

**Create Event**

- **Default duration (minutes)**: used when an event has no end time (60 if
  unset).
- **Add a Google Meet link**: attaches a Meet conference to every new event.
- **Default location**: used when the call gives none.
- **Visibility**: **Calendar default**, **Public** or **Private**.

**List Events**

- **Default max results**: how many events a call returns when it doesn't
  say (1–50; 10 if unset).
- **Default look-ahead (days)**: with no end time, events this many days
  ahead are listed.

**Find Free Slots**, your booking policy:

- **Working hours start (0–23)** and **Working hours end (1–24)**: local hours,
  in the default time zone (or the one set in Google Calendar).
- **Working days**: which weekdays count.
- **Default slot length (minutes)**: the shortest gap worth returning.
- **Buffer between meetings (minutes)**: kept free around every busy block.
- **Minimum notice (hours)**: nothing sooner than this from now.
- **Max advance (days)**: nothing further out than this.

## Tools

The names in parentheses are what MCP clients and logs show. Every tool except
List Calendars takes an optional `calendarId` to use another calendar than the
default.

- **List Calendars** (`calendar-list-calendars`): lists every calendar on the
  account with its ID, name, time zone, access role and whether it's the
  primary one.
- **List Events** (`calendar-list-events`): lists events between `timeMin` and
  `timeMax` (ISO 8601), with recurring events expanded into single instances,
  ordered by start. `timeMin` defaults to now; `query` searches event text;
  `maxResults` 1–50, default 10. Returns summary, start, end, location and event
  ID.
- **Create Event** (`calendar-create-event`): adds an event. Needs `summary`
  and `startTime`; give `endTime` or `durationMinutes`, or the default duration
  applies. Times are the local time meant (e.g. `2026-09-30T15:00:00`) in the
  event's time zone; the model turns "tomorrow at 7am" into that. Optional
  `description`, `location`, `timeZone` (IANA) and `attendees` (emails, who get
  an invite). Returns the event ID and a link.
- **Update Event** (`calendar-update-event`): changes an event by `eventId`;
  only the fields passed change (`summary`, `startTime`, `endTime`,
  `description`, `location`, `timeZone`, `attendees`). Passing `attendees`
  **replaces** the whole guest list.
- **Delete Event** (`calendar-delete-event`): permanently removes an event by
  `eventId`; guests are notified according to **Attendee notifications**.
- **Find Free Slots** (`calendar-find-free-slots`): returns the open gaps
  between `timeMin` and `timeMax` (both required), from Google's free/busy,
  after applying your booking policy. `durationMinutes` asks for gaps at least
  that long.

The typical flow is **Find Free Slots → Create Event**.

## Sensitive actions

With [Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions) on,
the assistant asks before **Create Event**, **Update Event** and **Delete
Event**, since guests can be emailed about each. The three reading tools run
without asking.

## Use the connection from your own code

A [function](/docs/tools/functions/) can call the Google Calendar API with the
same connection: add `google-calendar` to its connections and call
`ctx.connection('google-calendar')`.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Could not load calendars. Reconnect Google Calendar and try again."** The
  connection lapsed; connect again from the card.
- **"Google Calendar credential not connected".** The integration was
  disconnected.
- **Events land an hour off.** Set a **Default time zone**, or tell the
  assistant the zone; a time with `Z` or an offset is taken as that exact
  instant.
- **"No free slots: the search window is empty after applying the booking
  policy".** Minimum notice or max advance cut the whole window. Ask for a
  different range or relax the policy.

Booking through a scheduling page instead? See [Cal.com](/docs/tools/calcom/).

Point your bot at an API you already run: describe one request and it becomes a named tool, with no code and no deploy.

**HTTP Endpoints** turn an API you already run into a tool. You describe one
request (method, URL, headers, arguments) and it becomes a named tool the
model can call. No code, no bundle, no deploy step.

This is the middle rung between the catalog and
[functions](/docs/tools/functions/): more flexible than an integration we ship,
and far less work than code. It's also the custom tool available on **every
plan**, including Free.

You can fill in the form yourself, or ask the [Assistant](/docs/assistant/):
it can add and change an HTTP endpoint as part of a change set you apply.

## The tab

![The HTTP Endpoints tab, empty, with the New endpoint button](/images/new-http-function.webp)

Each endpoint you add becomes its own tool, listed here with a switch, an edit
button and a remove button. **Off keeps the endpoint and everything configured
on it** (the row shows **Off · settings kept**); **Remove deletes it with its
settings**. Use the switch when you want the tool to go quiet, and remove it
when you're done with it. On Free, the tab shows how many of your 3 endpoints
you've used.

## Add an endpoint

**New endpoint** opens **Add HTTP endpoint**. **Form** guides you field by
field; **JSON** lets you write the whole configuration at once (to use a saved
secret or a connected account there, set `auth.credentialId` to its id).

![The Add HTTP endpoint dialog with method, URL, headers, inputs, authentication and advanced options expanded](/images/new-http-function-advanced-options.webp)

### Name and description

- **Tool name**: what the model calls, e.g. `lookup-order`. Letters, digits,
  `_` or `-`.
- **Description**: tell the model **when** to call this tool. It's how the
  model decides.

### The request

- **Method** (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`) and **URL**. Use
  `{{arg}}` anywhere in the URL to drop in an input.
- **What it does**: whether the call only reads or changes something. The
  default, **Decide from the method: GET reads, anything else is sensitive**,
  fits most APIs. Pick **Only reads: looks things up, changes nothing** for a
  `POST` that just searches, **Changes things that can be undone**, or
  **Sends, deletes, charges or can't be undone**. When the organization turns
  on [Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions), a
  channel bot asks before calling a sensitive endpoint.
- **Headers** and **Query parameters**: fixed values, or `{{arg}}`
  placeholders filled in at call time.
- **Body**, for `POST`, `PUT` and `PATCH`: a **Format** (**None**, **JSON**,
  **Form (urlencoded)** or **Text**) and a **Body template** built from the
  same placeholders. A JSON template must parse once the arguments are filled
  in, e.g. `{"id":"{{orderId}}"}`.
- **Inputs (model arguments)**: what the model provides when it calls the
  tool. Each one has a name, a **Type** (**String**, **Number** or
  **Boolean**), whether it's **Required**, and a **Description**, which is how
  the model knows what to put there.

### Authentication

Pick an **Auth type**:

| Auth type | What is sent |
| --- | --- |
| **None** | Nothing. |
| **Bearer token** | The stored token as an `Authorization: Bearer` header. |
| **Basic (user:pass)** | The stored `username:password` as basic auth. |
| **API key** | The stored key, in a **Header** or a **Query param** with the **Parameter name** you choose. |
| **Connected account** | An account you connected from the [catalog](/docs/tools/catalog/). Its access token is refreshed and sent as a Bearer header on every call. |

A key is stored encrypted, applied just before the request leaves, and never
shown back to you or sent to the model. You can **Add new secret** with a
**Label** to recognize it, or **Use an existing secret** you saved before.

### Advanced options

- **Response type**: **Auto-detect**, or force **JSON** or **Text**.
- **JSON path**: extract a sub-tree, e.g. `data.items`, so the model gets the
  part it needs rather than the whole envelope.
- **Output schema (optional)**: declare one and a JSON response comes back to
  MCP clients as **structured output** instead of text. The response must then
  be a JSON object, or the call is reported as an error.
- **Success statuses**: comma-separated, e.g. `200, 201`. Defaults to any 2xx.
- **Timeout (ms)**: default 10,000, at most 30,000.
- **Allowed hosts**: a comma-separated allowlist. Private and loopback hosts
  are always blocked, whatever this says.

**Add endpoint** saves it.

## How a call runs

When the model decides to use the tool, Ganju fills your placeholders with its
arguments, applies the stored credential, and makes the request from our
infrastructure. The response, narrowed by your JSON path and shaped by your
output schema, goes back to the model to finish its reply.

Every request is screened, so an endpoint can never be pointed at an internal
address, and each endpoint is limited to 60 calls a minute so a chatty model
can't hammer your service. Failures come back marked as errors rather than as
text that happens to start with "Error", which is what lets the model tell
"the call failed" from "the answer is no".

## When to use which

| | Reach for |
| --- | --- |
| The vendor is in our catalog | **[Catalog](/docs/tools/catalog/)**: connect once, done |
| The vendor publishes a remote MCP server | **Catalog**: connect the server and get its whole maintained toolset |
| One request against your own API | **HTTP Endpoints** |
| Several steps, logic, your database, or a key combined with a computation | **[Functions](/docs/tools/functions/)**, written by the [Assistant](/docs/assistant/) |

## Limits

Free allows **3 endpoints** per project. Pro and Enterprise have no endpoint
limit; every endpoint that is on still counts toward the project's
[tools](/docs/tools/#turning-tools-on-and-off). HTTP endpoint calls aren't
metered as tool calls: only calls into [your own code](/docs/tools/functions/)
are.

Connect Notion's official remote MCP server to search, read, and update pages and databases.

**Notion** isn't a set of tools we build; it's Notion's **official remote MCP
server**, connected through Ganju. Ganju links to Notion's hosted server, lists
the tools *it* offers, and exposes the ones you pick to your assistant. You get
Notion's own, up-to-date toolset (searching, reading and updating pages and
databases), maintained by Notion, not re-implemented by us.

## How it works

The **Notion** card sits in **Tools → Catalog** next to the other
integrations, marked *Remote MCP server · connect to enable tools* until you
connect it. Ganju talks to Notion's server (`https://mcp.notion.com/mcp`) over
streamable HTTP. Every tool you allow is registered on your MCP server as
`notion__<tool>`; when the assistant calls one, Ganju forwards the call to
Notion and returns the result.

## Connect it

Notion's server signs you in with **OAuth**, so there's no token to copy.

1. Open **Tools → Catalog** and select the **Notion** card.
2. Select **Connect Notion**. You're sent to Notion to sign in and choose the
   workspace and the pages the assistant may reach.
3. You come back to the Tools page with the Notion dialog open. Choose the
   tools (see below) and **Save**.

Ganju stores the resulting credential encrypted and refreshes it for you. The
assistant only reaches the pages you shared during sign-in.

![The Connect Notion dialog before signing in to Notion](/images/tools-mcp-notion-connect.webp)

## Choose the tools

After connecting, the dialog shows **Tools (x/y)** with every tool Notion's
server offers, each with its own checkbox, plus **All** and **None**. Each tool
you allow counts as one toward your
[tool limit](/docs/tools/catalog/#the-tool-budget), and the dialog tells you how
many more you can turn on.

Under the list:

- **Trust this server's read-only labels**: tools Notion itself marks as
  read-only skip confirmation. Turn this on only for servers you trust.
- **Only reads: looks things up, changes nothing**: mark tools yourself, so
  they run without asking for confirmation, even after the assistant has read
  outside content. Everything else is treated as a sensitive action.
- **Resources & prompts (optional)**: if the server offers resources or
  prompts, they're off by default; only the ones you enable here are exposed.

The dialog works the same way as GitHub's; see the screenshot on
[GitHub](/docs/tools/github/#choose-the-tools).

## Change, turn off, disconnect

Open the Notion card again to change which tools are allowed, then **Save**.
The **Exposed** switch at the bottom turns the whole server off without losing
the setup; **Disconnect** removes it and its sign-in.

## Available tools

The tools come from Notion's server and can change as Notion updates it,
typically searching your workspace and reading, creating or updating pages and
databases. The dialog always shows the current list. Responses are capped in
size before they reach the model, and results from the server are treated as
outside content.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Could not start the Notion connection."** Try again; if it persists, the
  sign-in page couldn't be reached.
- **A page isn't found.** It wasn't shared during sign-in. Disconnect and
  connect again, choosing that page.
- **A call says the credential needs to be re-authorized.** Open the Notion card
  on the Tools page and connect again.

Want another vendor's server? See [GitHub](/docs/tools/github/), or expose your
own API with [HTTP Endpoints](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/).

  2. Select Connect Notion. You’re sent to Notion to sign in and choose the workspace and the pages the assistant may reach.
  3. You come back to the Tools page with the Notion dialog open. Choose the tools (see below) and Save.

Ganju stores the resulting credential encrypted and refreshes it for you. The assistant only reaches the pages you shared during sign-in.

Choose the tools

After connecting, the dialog shows Tools (x/y) with every tool Notion’s server offers, each with its own checkbox, plus All and None. Each tool you allow counts as one toward your tool limit, and the dialog tells you how many more you can turn on.

Under the list:

  • Trust this server’s read-only labels: tools Notion itself marks as read-only skip confirmation. Turn this on only for servers you trust.
  • Only reads: looks things up, changes nothing: mark tools yourself, so they run without asking for confirmation, even after the assistant has read outside content. Everything else is treated as a sensitive action.
  • Resources & prompts (optional): if the server offers resources or prompts, they’re off by default; only the ones you enable here are exposed.

The dialog works the same way as GitHub’s; see the screenshot on GitHub.

Change, turn off, disconnect

Open the Notion card again to change which tools are allowed, then Save. The Exposed switch at the bottom turns the whole server off without losing the setup; Disconnect removes it and its sign-in.

Available tools

The tools come from Notion’s server and can change as Notion updates it, typically searching your workspace and reading, creating or updating pages and databases. The dialog always shows the current list. Responses are capped in size before they reach the model, and results from the server are treated as outside content.

Troubleshooting

  • “Could not start the Notion connection.” Try again; if it persists, the sign-in page couldn’t be reached.
  • A page isn’t found. It wasn’t shared during sign-in. Disconnect and connect again, choosing that page.
  • A call says the credential needs to be re-authorized. Open the Notion card on the Tools page and connect again.

Want another vendor’s server? See GitHub, or expose your own API with HTTP Endpoints.
Microsoft 365 mail for your assistant, backed by Microsoft Graph: 18 tools across sending, triage, folders, threads, and drafts.

The **Outlook** integration gives your assistant Microsoft 365 / Outlook email,
backed by **Microsoft Graph**. It mirrors the [Gmail](/docs/tools/gmail/) set
(send, read, organize and draft) with **18 tools**, using mail *folders* where
Gmail uses labels.

## Connect it

1. Open **Tools → Catalog** and select the **Outlook** card.
2. Select **Connect Outlook**, sign in with the Microsoft account and approve.
3. Back on the Tools page, turn on the tools you want.

One connection serves all 18 tools. Connecting asks Microsoft for `Mail.ReadWrite`,
`Mail.Send`, `User.Read` and `offline_access` (so the connection keeps working
without signing in again). Each tool row shows the permission it uses under
**Scopes**. If your organization's Microsoft 365 admin restricts third-party
apps, they may need to approve it first.

![Outlook before connecting: Connect Outlook, the banner and the tools greyed out](/images/tools-catalog-not-connected.webp)

The tools have no per-tool settings. Bodies are HTML unless the call passes
`contentType: "text"`. The tool names in parentheses are what MCP clients and
logs show.

## Sending

- **Send Email** (`outlook-send-email`): sends a new message, starting a new
  conversation. Takes `to`, `subject` and `body`, with optional `cc`, `bcc`
  (comma-separated), `contentType` and `attachmentUris` (files from your
  [resources](/docs/resources/), up to 150 MB per file; large files are uploaded
  in chunks).
- **Reply** (`outlook-reply-email`): replies to a message by `messageId`,
  keeping the conversation. Set `replyAll` to include every original recipient;
  attachments are allowed.
- **Forward** (`outlook-forward-email`): forwards a message (`messageId`) to
  `to`, with an optional intro `body` above the quoted original, optional `cc`
  and attachments. Starts a new conversation.

## Reading & searching

- **List Emails** (`outlook-list-emails`): lists messages (from / subject /
  received / ID), newest first. `query` is a full-text search; field operators
  like `from:` are matched as plain words, not filters. `folderId` restricts it
  to one folder (default: the inbox). `maxResults` 1–50, default 10.
- **Read Email** (`outlook-read-email`): reads one message by `messageId`; HTML
  bodies are turned into plain text for the model.
- **List Threads** (`outlook-list-threads`): lists conversations (one entry per
  conversation, with its latest subject and sender), with optional `query`.
  `maxResults` 1–50, default 10.
- **Get Thread** (`outlook-get-thread`): summarizes every message in a
  conversation (`conversationId`) without full bodies; then Read Email the one
  you want.
- **Get Profile** (`outlook-get-profile`): reports the connected account's
  name, address and inbox totals.

## Organizing

- **List Folders** (`outlook-list-folders`): lists every mail folder, system
  and your own, with its ID and unread count.
- **Move Message** (`outlook-move-message`): moves one message (`messageId`) to
  `destinationId`: a well-known name (`inbox`, `drafts`, `sentitems`,
  `deleteditems`, `junkemail`, `archive`) or a folder ID from List Folders.
  Archive, mark as spam, or restore from Deleted Items.
- **Batch Move Messages** (`outlook-batch-move-messages`): moves up to 20
  messages (`messageIds`) to the same folder in one call; extra IDs are ignored.
- **Move to Trash** (`outlook-trash-email`): moves a message to Deleted Items,
  where it can still be restored. The safe choice for "delete".

## Drafts

- **Create Draft** (`outlook-create-draft`): saves a message in Drafts without
  sending it; same fields as Send Email, attachments included.
- **List Drafts** (`outlook-list-drafts`): lists drafts with ID, recipient,
  subject and last-modified time. `maxResults` 1–50, default 10.
- **Get Draft** (`outlook-get-draft`): reads a draft in full by `draftId`.
- **Update Draft** (`outlook-update-draft`): overwrites a draft's `to`,
  `subject` and `body` (all three required). Omit `attachmentUris` to keep the
  existing attachments, or pass a list to replace them. Doesn't send it.
- **Send Draft** (`outlook-send-draft`): sends a saved draft as it is.
- **Delete Draft** (`outlook-delete-draft`): permanently deletes an unsent
  draft (it doesn't go to Deleted Items).

## Sensitive actions

With [Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions) on,
the assistant asks before **Send Email**, **Reply**, **Forward**, **Send Draft**,
**Move to Trash** and **Delete Draft**. Reading, moving between folders and
creating or editing drafts run without asking.

## Use the connection from your own code

A [function](/docs/tools/functions/) can call Microsoft Graph with the same
connection: add `microsoft-outlook` to its connections and call
`ctx.connection('microsoft-outlook')`. An
[HTTP endpoint](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/) can use it as its **Connected
account**.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Microsoft Outlook credential not connected".** Outlook was disconnected.
  Connect it again from the card.
- **The card shows Expired.** Microsoft stopped accepting the sign-in (password
  changed, access revoked, or an admin policy). Connect again; your tools are
  kept.
- **A search with `from:` finds nothing useful.** Outlook search is full-text;
  search for the sender's name or address as plain words.

Post messages, browse channels, look up users, and upload files in a Slack workspace.

The **Slack** integration lets your assistant act in a Slack workspace:
posting messages and thread replies, finding channels and people, and sharing
files from your resources. It offers **4 tools**. Message **search** is a
separate integration, [Slack Search](/docs/tools/slack-search/), because Slack
doesn't let a bot token search.

This is about Slack as a set of *tools* the assistant calls. To put the
assistant itself in Slack, so people can talk to it there, see the
[Slack channel](/docs/channels/slack/).

## Connect it

1. Open **Tools → Catalog** and select the **Slack** card.
2. Select **Connect Slack**, pick the workspace and approve.
3. Back on the Tools page, turn on the tools you want.

Connecting installs a bot in the workspace with these permissions:
`chat:write`, `channels:read`, `groups:read`, `mpim:read`, `im:read`,
`users:read`, `users:read.email` and `files:write`. Each tool row shows the ones
it uses under **Scopes**.

The bot posts as itself and only sees what a bot can see: to post in a channel,
or to list a private one, invite the bot to it first (`/invite @YourBot` in
Slack).

![Tools, Catalog tab: the tools-exposed bar, search, filters and the integration cards](/images/tools-catalog.webp)

## Tools

The names in parentheses are what MCP clients and logs show.

- **Send Message** (`slack-send-message`): posts `text` to a channel, DM or
  thread. `channel` takes an ID (`C…`, `G…`, `D…`, preferred) or a name
  (`#general`); `threadTs` replies inside an existing thread. Text uses Slack's
  mrkdwn (`*bold*`, `_italic_`, `<@U123>` mentions) unless `mrkdwn` is `false`.
  Returns the message `ts`, so later replies can thread onto it.
- **List Channels** (`slack-list-channels`): lists conversations the bot can
  see, with name, member count, archived state, topic and channel ID. `types`
  defaults to `public_channel,private_channel` (also `mpim`, `im`);
  `includeArchived` adds archived ones; `query` filters by name; `maxResults`
  1–200, default 50. Use it to turn a channel name into an ID before posting.
- **Get User** (`slack-get-user`): looks up a person by `userId` **or**
  `email` (exactly one). Returns the ID, display and real name, email (if
  visible), bot and deleted flags, and status. Use it to turn an email into a
  Slack ID before a DM.
- **Upload File** (`slack-upload-file`): shares a stored resource
  (`resourceUri`) into a `channel`, with an optional `title`,
  `initialComment` and `threadTs`. Up to 100 MB per file. Use this rather than
  Send Message to share a document or image.

## Sensitive actions

With [Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions) on,
the assistant asks before **Send Message** and **Upload File**. List Channels
and Get User run without asking.

## Searching the workspace

Connect [Slack Search](/docs/tools/slack-search/) to add **Search Messages**:
search for prior context, then reply with Send Message using the `ts` the search
returned as `threadTs`.

## Use the connection from your own code

A [function](/docs/tools/functions/) can call the Slack Web API with the bot
token: add `slack` to its connections and call `ctx.connection('slack')`.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Slack credential not connected".** Slack was disconnected. Connect it again
  from the card.
- **`not_in_channel` or `channel_not_found`.** The bot isn't a member of that
  channel. Invite it in Slack, or use List Channels to check the ID.
- **Get User returns no email.** The person's email isn't visible to the bot in
  that workspace; look them up by `userId` instead.

Workspace-wide message search for Slack, a separate connection because Slack blocks bot tokens from searching.

**Slack Search** adds workspace-wide message search to your assistant. It's a
separate integration from [Slack](/docs/tools/slack/) for a technical reason:
Slack does **not** let bot tokens call `search.messages`, so search runs on a
**user token** (`xoxp`) instead of the bot token the other Slack tools use.

## Connect it

1. Open **Tools → Catalog** and select the **Slack Search** card.
2. Select **Connect Slack Search**, pick the workspace and approve.
3. Turn on **Search Messages**.

It asks for a single permission, `search:read`, and you can connect it with or
without the main Slack integration.

Because it's a *user* token, search sees what **the person who connected it**
can see in Slack, including private channels and DMs they're in. Connect it
with an account whose visibility you're comfortable giving the assistant, such
as a dedicated account.

## Tool

- **Search Messages** (`slack-search-messages`): searches messages across the
  workspace. `query` accepts Slack's own modifiers: `in:#channel`,
  `from:@user`, `before:YYYY-MM-DD`, `has:link`. `sort` is `score` (relevance,
  the default) or `timestamp` (newest first); `maxResults` 1–50, default 10.
  Each match comes with the channel, user, `ts`, a text snippet and a
  permalink.

It only reads, so it's never held for
[Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions).

Pair it with the [Slack](/docs/tools/slack/) tools: search for the thread
("what did support say about the refund?"), then **Send Message** with the
match's `ts` as `threadTs` to reply inside it.

## Use the connection from your own code

A [function](/docs/tools/functions/) can use the same user token: add
`slack-user` to its connections and call `ctx.connection('slack-user')`.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Slack credential not connected".** Slack Search isn't connected (connecting
  the main Slack card isn't enough). Connect it from its own card.
- **A message you can see isn't found.** Search only covers what the connecting
  account can see. Connect with an account that's in that channel.

Search the live web and read full page content, powered by Tavily.

The **Web Search** integration gives your assistant access to the live web,
powered by **Tavily**, so it can answer with current facts and cite sources
when the answer isn't in your resources. It offers **2 tools**.

## Connect it

Web Search uses your own **Tavily API key**; searches are billed to your Tavily
account.

1. Create an account at Tavily and copy an API key from its dashboard.
2. In Ganju, open **Tools → Catalog**, select the **Web Search** card and choose
   **Add Web Search API key**.
3. Paste the key and **Save**. We run a tiny test search with it before storing
   it; it's encrypted and never shown again.
4. Turn on **Web Search** and, if you want, **Web Extract**.

To swap the key later, use **Update API key**; **Disconnect** removes it.

![The API key dialog for an integration, with Cancel and Save](/images/tools-api-key-dialog.webp)

## Tools

The names in parentheses are what MCP clients and logs show.

- **Web Search** (`web-search`): searches the web for a `query` and returns the
  top results (title, URL and a snippet), plus a synthesized answer when one is
  available. Options:
  - `maxResults`: 1–20, default 5.
  - `searchDepth`: `basic` (default) or `advanced`, which digs deeper but is
    slower and costs more Tavily credits.
  - `topic`: `general` (default) or `news`, with `days` to keep only the last
    N days.
  - `includeDomains` / `excludeDomains`: restrict results to, or drop them
    from, given sites.

  The assistant is told to cite the URLs it relies on.
- **Web Extract** (`web-extract`): fetches the full, cleaned text of one or
  more pages (`urls`). `extractDepth` is `basic` (default) or `advanced`, which
  also pulls tables and embedded data at a higher cost. Use it after a search,
  or when the person shares a link, to read a page rather than rely on the
  snippet. Pages that can't be fetched are reported separately.

The typical flow is **Web Search** to find sources → **Web Extract** to read the
most relevant ones in full. Both only read, so neither is held for
[Confirm sensitive actions](/docs/settings/#confirm-sensitive-actions).

## Troubleshooting

- **"Invalid Tavily API key (or Tavily could not be reached)".** The key was
  refused when saving. Copy it again from Tavily.
- **"Web search is not connected".** The key was removed. Add it again from the
  card.
- **Searches start failing after working.** Check your Tavily plan's credits.
- **The assistant answers from the web instead of your documents.** Make sure
  your [resources](/docs/resources/) cover the topic; the assistant searches
  them first, and you can steer it in the bot's instructions.

The API key is only used by these tools; [functions](/docs/tools/functions/)
can't borrow it. For a narrower lookup against one site you control, an
[HTTP endpoint](/docs/tools/http-endpoints/) may be a better fit.

Connect your AI to your files, tools, and apps, then offer it to anyone through the channels they already use.

Welcome to the Ganju docs. Ganju connects AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT,
and Gemini to your own files, tools, and apps, with no servers to run, and no
code to write.

Then it lets you **offer that AI to whoever you want** (clients, your team, or
individual people) through the channels they already use: Telegram, WhatsApp,
Slack, and Discord. One workspace, delivered everywhere.

These guides take you from a blank workspace to a live assistant you can share
with anyone.

## How the app is laid out

Everything happens inside a **project**: one bot, with its own knowledge,
actions, and channels. A project's left rail has the same sections every time:

| Section | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| **Home** | The project's dashboard: its MCP URL, activity, tool health, and recent activity. |
| **Assistant** | Describe in your own words what your bot should know or do, and it builds it with you. Pro and Enterprise. |
| **Knowledge** | What your bot knows: the **Resources** tab (files, websites, Drive folders) and the **Prompts** tab (reusable templates). |
| **Data** | The project's own database: tables your bot reads and writes. Pro and Enterprise. |
